Sports.title: Verstappen warns COTA bumps are “unacceptable” and “out of control”
Sports.content:
When the United States Grand Prix came up during the Formula 1 press conference in Singapore, Max Verstappen immediately joked that he would have to order a new spine. The four-time world champion had followed the World Endurance Championship round in Texas – The Lone Star Le Mans, held over the weekend of 6 September – and said he was shocked by the condition of the circuit.

Although Verstappen was still able to laugh about it with Kimi Antonelli at the time, he made it clear during the media day in Austin that he is genuinely concerned about the “unacceptable” track conditions.

“From what I saw in WEC, it was extremely badly bumpy. I'm not really looking forward to that, to be honest, for your spine,” said Verstappen. “I was joking about that in the last race, but it's not really a joke to be honest. We mentioned this already for years, that it's actually getting a bit out of control.”

The problem stems from the ground beneath the circuit. Built on Texas’ infamous high-plasticity clay, the track suffers from a severe shrink-swell effect as weather conditions change. This constant shifting leaves the circuit extremely bumpy, particularly in the heavy braking zones where the asphalt is subjected to the greatest stress.

Ahead of the 2026 race, certain sections have been resurfaced again, including the stretch between Turns 9 and 11. In addition, repair work was carried out to address the bumps between Turns 12 and 19. Two years ago, ahead of the 2024 United States Grand Prix, the entire track was resurfaced.

When Autosport asked Verstappen whether he believes more needs to be done, the four-time world champion stressed that the location itself should not be used by the organisers as an excuse.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

“It's very bad. Of course, you can use the excuse that the soil is the problem, but then you should have known that and you need to make sure that you reinforce it more,” the Dutchman said.

“I mean, I love this track, I love this place. It's one of the best layouts ever and it's one of the, I would say, best venues and best cities to be at. But for me, the bumps that we have are unacceptable.

“Over time, they've been grinding a little bit here and there, but you're putting a plaster on the big problem and that's just what's underneath. That's what you actually need to tackle in the first place.”

According to Verstappen, far-reaching measures are needed, with attention being paid not only to the tarmac itself, but also to the soil beneath it.

“But that, of course, means you need to really fully open up the track,” he added. “That costs a lot of money and time, but honestly, that's the only way to get rid of it. Because yeah, these bumps are not natural and they are out of control.”

Why F1's 2026 cars could make things even worse for drivers

At first glance, it might seem like a blessing in disguise that F1 no longer uses the ground-effect cars of recent years. After all, those cars had to be run particularly low and stiff, but when asked by Autosport, Verstappen made it clear that the 2026 machinery could actually make things even more painful.

Race start Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

“It's probably worse because we have very low ride heights while cornering,” said Verstappen. “On the straights you have the SM mode, so you go up. But in most places under the braking especially, you actually bottom out more than before. And most of the bumps are under braking or in the corner, not on the actual straight.

“Under braking, it's like actually a very stressful moment – especially when there are these kind of awkward bumps, not just bumps from the track getting older, but bumps from the surface underneath, the soil just moving up and down. Sometimes it's very hard to know what to expect, or if you’re a tiny bit offline, you don't know what is there because no one really drives there. So, yeah, it's really not nice.”

All of this means that drivers' backs take a considerable beating. Verstappen says he has already experienced this at COTA in previous years.

“Last year, for example, you pull around 5-6G in a corner, but I had some impacts, the vertical load, which was like over 9G on my spine,” he said. “I can tell you that it’s really not fun and especially the older you get, you think about that more and more. That's not what you want.”

Verstappen added that his spine is already not in the best possible condition after more than 11 seasons in F1: “I think sometimes people don't really understand that. I can tell you from the checks that I've done from my spine, the bottom end of the spine doesn't look that great.

“I know that's part of racing and I know that can be part of sport, but it's of course also further damage from the cars that we had the last few years. And now if we continue finding this acceptable to drive on, then you are going to suffer from that much more.

“People can say, yeah, but there are worse sports out there for damage to parts of your body. For sure, but that's why I'm not doing them. So, yeah, it's not nice.”

Sports.title: Why Colapinto spoke out against abuse targeting his own F1 team
Sports.content:
It has become a recurring topic during Franco Colapinto's media sessions throughout the 2026 Formula 1 season: the Argentine feeling the need to speak out against abuse on social media.

Colapinto discussed the issue at length during an exclusive interview with Autosport in Monaco, as well as during many of the race weekends that have followed since.

After the Singapore Grand Prix last time out, however, the Alpine driver felt the urgency to go a step further and address his fanbase directly in a video message. Among other things, he said he appreciated all the support from his fans, but added that directing hate towards others does nothing to help his own F1 career.

“First of all, I've always been very grateful for all the fans supporting me,” said Colapinto, when asked by Autosport about his statement ahead of this weekend’s United States Grand Prix.

“But I think in every sport and fan base, it's got a bad side as well, the hate side of people putting bad comments and not helping athletes perform at their best. To me, it crossed a few lines lately.

“I think it was probably the last thing I could do, to put out a statement of me talking in a video like that. It was always going to be positive, so I was keen to do it.”

Franco Colapinto, Alpine Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Explaining what he meant when he said that certain lines had recently been crossed, Colapinto revealed that even members of his own team had been targeted on social media. Colapinto found that unacceptable, prompting him to speak out once again.

“Especially my mechanics got a lot of hate,” revealed the 23-year-old. “My engineers as well, people from my team that want me to do well and that help me to perform. I'm working with them daily and seeing them getting these kind of messages, it just hurts me in general.”

Asked whether these were comments on the team's official Instagram account or personal messages sent to team members, Colapinto replied: “I don’t have their phones, but from what I understand, they receive messages and comments. Again, it just crossed the line for me.”

In practice, this includes mechanics who work on Colapinto's car and make adjustments to, for example, the front wing from one qualifying segment to the next.

They are then wrongly held responsible for a difficult session and subsequently receive hateful messages on their accounts, although Autosport understands that Alpine has taken measures to minimise the impact.

Team members are advised to keep their personal social media accounts private and not show any team logos, in order to minimise the risk of receiving unwanted messages.

Franco Colapinto, Alpine Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Nevertheless, that does not address the actual problem at its root, which is precisely why Colapinto has once again made an urgent appeal to fans. He also stressed that the problem is not limited to F1, but affects society as a whole.

“I've been talking about this for the last 10 races probably,” he said. “I do my best, but I think it kept crossing some lines. So this was the last thing I could do, making a video, and I think it helped.

“You saw it with Max as well. He also made a statement about it. It's happening a lot around us. It's an issue that we’ve got in sports nowadays, in sports and in many different areas of life. Artists, actors, it's everywhere.

“Personally, it doesn’t hurt me too much. I don't look at those comments too much, I don't put too much attention. But for some it does [affect them]. And that’s why we need to put attention on it. We need to improve it and hopefully this video does improve it slightly.”

Sports.title: Sainz yet to be "convinced" that F1 2026 will finish in the Middle East
Sports.content:
Carlos Sainz has admitted that it's "difficult" to be convinced by Formula 1's chiefs that its final rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi can go ahead as planned despite the ongoing Middle Eastern conflict.

Both F1 management and governing body the FIA have maintained the position that the final two rounds of 2026 in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, scheduled back-to-back at the end of November and first weekend of December, can go ahead as planned.

With no resolution in sight for the ongoing conflict between the US and its ally Israel, and Iran, and new strikes on Saudi Arabia by the Houthi rebels, the situation in the Middle East remains extremely volatile.

The outlook is also likely to be influenced by the US midterm elections on 3 November, with several outlets reporting the US and Israel are preparing for fresh attacks on Iran afterwards.

F1 has been working on a contingency plan with an alternative season finale in Imola, on the weekend of the planned Abu Dhabi race, but all indications from series chiefs are that they are very keen to press ahead with the Middle Eastern double-header based on the current information and assurances they have received from various stakeholders.

But Sainz, who acts as director of the F1 drivers association GPDA, feels it is "difficult" and "premature" to envisage a finish in the region based on the current news cycle.

Abu Dhabi GP 2025 Photo by: Nicolas Economou / NurPhoto via Getty Images

"They seem very convinced that it's going to go ahead," Sainz said on Thursday ahead of this weekend's United States Grand Prix in Austin. "I think on my personal side, and not speaking as a GPDA, it's very difficult to be convinced right now because there's still plenty of things happening in the Middle East.

"And also there is obviously an election that is going to happen in the US and things that are going to happen in the political side of the world that could affect the next month and a half very suddenly. So, I think it's relatively premature to be so convinced."

But Sainz also felt that the drivers have little choice but to put their faith in what series executives decide, as they have more information on what is happening on the ground.

"As it stands, we would go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi and if the FIA and Formula 1 decide that's still safe and a good scenario, I think we as drivers have to go with whatever they say," the Spaniard added.

"It's not like we don't have as much inside information as they have, so we need to follow their lead and trust in their decision making.

"But only as it stands, I think the world can change a lot in the next month and a half. So we need to be [reactive] to whatever happens and not just go because we want to go right now."

Sports.title: When Cadillac will open its F1 engine factory
Sports.content:
Cadillac has revealed its Formula 1 engine factory will open on 18 December.

General Motors was approved by the FIA in 2025 as a power unit supplier from the 2029 season onwards, hence the construction of new F1 engine facilities at the manufacturer’s base in Charlotte, North Carolina.

“We're opening our whole engine factory, if you will, in Charlotte, North Carolina on 18 December,” General Motors president Mark Reuss announced in a conference at Autosport Business Exchange in New York. “So that's coming really well.”

General Motors now has another couple of years to design its own power unit, though the timing may be suboptimal – FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has committed to F1 switching back to V8 engines – potentially running on sustainable fuel with a smaller share of electric power – by 2031. In that case, GM’s powertrain would get two seasons in action at best, potentially just one if the switch is brought forward to 2030.

In the meantime, Cadillac is running customer Ferrari power units, and the team’s maiden season has been tricky thus far. It is the only outfit yet to score a point in 2026, and the MAC-26 has qualified slowest of all at the last four rounds.

General Motors president Mark Reuss presents Cadillac's one-off shakedown F1 livery for Barcelona Photo by: Cadillac Communications

“You know, we’re not here to finish last, so we’ve got to follow through and build this team, build the powertrain and build the car, like we did in GTP,” Reuss said. “That takes a little more time here, because this is a place where we've never raced. You’ve got to get the right people with the right engineers and the right drivers, and we’ve got to get that process really going, and it's logarithmic, it's not linear.”

Veterans Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas have been bringing invaluable experience in that context, but they have also been recording their worst career results.

“You can't win every race – no one can win every race – so when it happens, when they have a day that is unfortunate, or mistakes were made, they move on from that race and perfect their craft – whether it's with the car or themselves, or their physicality, or whatever that is – and they drive for that perfection,” Reuss said.

“Both of these gentlemen in the race for us do that, and they really understand what it takes and the process. I'm very, very happy that they're patient with us, to be honest; that takes a special person.”

Sports.title: Slater set for F1 practice debut with Audi in Mexico
Sports.content:
Audi junior Freddie Slater will make his debut at the wheel of a Formula 1 car with a couple of Free Practice 1 outings in Mexico City and Sao Paulo.

Audi took over the Sauber team ahead of 2026 for the German brand’s maiden F1 season, incidentally launching a new driver academy, which has largely rested on Slater’s shoulders.

Previously an Italian F4 and Formula Regional European champion, Slater has lived up to expectations by taking second place in Formula 3 behind Ugo Ugochukwu – the 18-year-old Briton was the highest-placed rookie in the standings.

Ahead of his step up to Formula 2 with Invicta – following in the footsteps of fellow Trident F3 racers Gabriel Bortoleto, Leonardo Fornaroli and Rafael Camara – Slater will be in action in FP1 at the Mexican and Brazilian grands prix, helping Audi fulfil the rules’ young-driver requirements.

Alpine reserve Paul Aron was loaned to Audi on two occasions earlier this season for free practice sessions, and Slater is getting the team’s last two mandatory rookie outings, replacing Nico Hulkenberg and Bortoleto once each.

“Getting behind the wheel of a Formula 1 car at a grand prix weekend is a big moment for me and something I’ve been dreaming of since I was a kid,” Slater said. “I’ve learned a lot this year, and these free practice outings with Audi will be another opportunity to keep gaining on-track experience.

Freddie Slater, TRIDENT Photo by: Dom Gibbons - Formula 1 via Getty Images

“Being part of the Audi Driver Development Programme has already given me some incredible opportunities, and I am grateful for their trust and support. I’m really looking forward to getting out on track: my focus will be on doing the best job I can, helping the team with its programme and taking as many learnings as possible from both sessions.”

Audi racing director Allan McNish added: “We have seen Freddie making great progress throughout recent years, both on and off the track; it is the right time for Freddie to step up.

“These appearances in Mexico and Brazil will give him valuable experience of a Formula 1 race weekend, and another chance to continue his development before he steps up to Formula 2 next season.

"We are looking forward to seeing him in the R26 and supporting him through these two important FP1 sessions.”

Colton Herta in at COTA

Earlier, Cadillac test and development driver Colton Herta will be in action at this weekend's United States Grand Prix, driving Sergio Perez’s car. Austin will mark the Californian’s fourth FP1 session of the year, though his latest, in Monza, was cut short by a suspected hydraulic issue.

“Driving the MAC-26 in front of the American fans at COTA is going to be special,” Herta said. “I have great memories at this track – winning my first IndyCar race here back in 2019 was a huge moment in my career, so stepping into an F1 car on this layout feels like coming full circle.

Colton Herta, Cadillac Racing Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“I’ve built up a good rhythm with the team through my previous FP1 runs in Barcelona, Budapest, and Monza, so my goal for Friday morning is straightforward: execute the test programme cleanly, help the engineers gather good data on the set-up, and hand the car back to Checo with some useful feedback to support the team for the rest of the weekend.”

Team principal Marcin Budkowski added: “The high-speed sweeping section in sector one [at COTA] and the tight, low-speed turns at the end of the lap are a tricky for car set-up, and the bumps always add an extra dimension.

“We are looking forward to having Colton back in the car for FP1 on Friday, and we also plan to bring some small floor and cooling upgrades for evaluation.

"Colton knows this circuit very well from his IndyCar career, so his feedback will be valuable as we establish our baseline for the weekend.”

Currently a lowly 19th in the F2 standings, Herta told Autosport he was still aiming at F1 by 2028, while his plans for next year remain unclear.

Sports.title: MotoGP "can’t just copy" F1’s Drive to Survive success – Chase Carey
Sports.content:
Liberty Media director Chase Carey believes MotoGP “can’t just copy” Netflix’s Formula 1 docuseries Drive to Survive to gain widespread recognition.

Liberty acquired F1 in January 2017, and one of the major events under the American company was the release of the Netflix show’s opening season two years later, which substantially contributed to the world championship’s increased popularity.

Liberty then bought 84% of Dorna Sports (now known as MotoGP Sports Entertainment Group) in July 2025. The group is seeking to make motorcycle grands prix more diverse – 11 of the top 12 riders in the 2026 MotoGP championship are Spanish or Italian – while increasing its presence in the United States.

“Certainly there are elements of what teams need to do in MotoGP that will have similarities to Formula 1,” Carey said in a conference at Autosport Business Exchange in New York. “Obviously, it is a global franchise.

“In some ways, MotoGP is even crazier. When you look at these guys, they look like they're lying on the pavement riding the motorcycles around. But it is a sport that also has its unique characteristics. And I think you can't just cookie-cutter [the approach].

“It's early days. They're working on it, developing the strategies, the opportunities of how you take that sport and grow it in the way we've tried to with Formula 1.”

Drive to Survive has been credited with introducing F1 to a brand-new audience, boosted by the COVID-19 pandemic’s lockdowns, which first occurred a couple of weeks after season two was released.

“Drive to Survive is probably the most obvious example,” Carey acknowledged. “We recognised we needed to have the personalities that make up the sport, give them a bigger platform and let fans engage.

“The digital world today is a 24/7 world. The premium experience is still that live race, but at the end of the day people are connecting with the race, following the race and clips of the race, clips of what people are doing, things going on behind the scenes.

“They're following that 24/7. So we need to continue to find ways to feed that appetite and that desire to connect with their sport, provide the vehicles that enable fans to connect with the sport in that way.

Liz Claman and Chase Carey Photo by: Bryan Bedder / Getty Images

“Right now the US is the biggest YouTube market for our sport. So it tells you about the connection we're having through [those] vehicles.

“Drive to Survive has become a centerpiece in the digital efforts. A lot of efforts are going on with digital, but that certainly is the centerpiece. It has been an incredibly important, valuable franchise for us.”

Many competitions, in motorsport and beyond, have attempted to emulate this success, but Carey doesn’t believe that would be right for MotoGP.

“You should look for opportunities,” the American insisted. “Realistically, everybody saw Drive to Survive and then everybody tried to do it. Golf tried to do their Full Swing, tennis tried to do Break Point – everybody.

“Usually, you can't just copy something. I think we learned that at Fox with American Idol. American Idol sort of captured the world's imagination, and there were shows that came behind and did well, but there was only one American Idol that really did that.

“I think generally you can't go out and do the same thing. You've got to find ways to use opportunities, use personalities, use digital platforms, develop great partners.

“A partner in Formula 1 like Apple, I think this is where Apple has brought a whole new perspective to how you broadcast and connect with fans. So I think that type of opportunity, you've got to then see what you can do with it, how you develop it.

“They have to follow their own path and find their own opportunities. The Formula 1 movie was a great opportunity for that, but you can't just go out and do a MotoGP movie. That may not be the right opportunity.

“But there may be something else – there will be something else. It's probably not just doing the same things you did, it's finding those opportunities, finding those personalities.”

Sports.title: Horner reveals Red Bull call to thank him for F1 engine project after maiden win
Sports.content:
Christian Horner has revealed Red Bull shareholders called him on the back of the Red Bull Ford Powertrains engine’s maiden Formula 1 victory in Malaysia.

Horner joined the Milton Keynes-based squad as its team principal when the brand acquired the Jaguar outfit ahead of the 2005 season, but was sacked and replaced by Laurent Mekies in July 2025.

Across two decades at the helm of the team, Horner not only led it to eight drivers’ and six constructors’ titles but also oversaw its transition from an engine customer into a power unit manufacturer, following Honda’s exit from F1 at the end of the 2021 season.

Red Bull was able to keep using the Japanese powertrains until last year; its own power unit, designed in collaboration with Ford, debuted in 2026.

The Red Bull engine clinched its first victory at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, courtesy of Max Verstappen, with the Dutchman making it back-to-back wins one week later in Singapore.

“We managed to do it on the chassis side and then the challenge came, could we do it on the engine side?” Horner related in a conference at Autosport Business Exchange in New York.

“You know, we needed to have an engine after Honda announced their withdrawal in 2020. So we created this start-up company, Red Bull Powertrains, with the same philosophy of attracting the talent, giving people a chance, giving people the opportunity, and then empowering them and encouraging them to push the boundaries.

“I've been super proud to see how that engine has developed and delivered this year.”

Christian Horner Photo by: Autosport

Horner’s contribution was acknowledged by the brand itself, as he received the aforementioned phone call from its leaders.

“It was an appreciated gesture, seeing that engine and knowing what went into it, you know, the sweat and tears along the way,” the Briton continued.

“For all the men and women involved, it was an incredible, incredible achievement. And their 16th attempt to win a grand prix, which is very hard at the best of times.

“I was very grateful to both the shareholders who reached out, and [Red Bull CEO] Oliver Mintzlaff who reached out to thank me as well. It was quite a different call than I had from him 15 months earlier.”

Horner is referring to the phone call that led to his dismissal, as his position had become increasingly precarious following Red Bull cofounder Dietrich Mateschitz’s death.

Errol Barnett and Christian Horner Photo by: Bryan Bedder / Getty Images

Horner did not have the Verstappen camp on his side and was losing the support of the Yoovidhya family – Chalerm Yoovidhya is a majority owner of the company – but still describes the news as “pretty abrupt and quite brutal”.

“I felt that things were changing,” he added. “Nothing stays the same forever, and after the founder, Dietrich Mateschitz, sadly passed at the end of ‘22, it was always going to be the case that the company was going to evolve and was going to change.

“Dietrich, he was Red Bull, he was the power behind it, he made all the big decisions. And suddenly, obviously, trying to replace somebody like that is impossible.

“Inevitably, as the group evolved and took on that challenge, it was just different. There was a drive to bring more control back into the head office, and that sat differently from the autonomy that we'd enjoyed at Red Bull Racing and in Milton Keynes.

“It was a different path that essentially what we were on, and you could feel that that was changing. It wasn't that it was right or wrong, it was just different. And I didn't feel, certainly, that it was what had allowed us to achieve so much success over the years.

“So, inevitably, it came to an end.”

Sports.title: “Difficult to be convinced” F1’s Qatar and Abu Dhabi rounds will happen – Sainz | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Carlos Sainz Jnr has doubts whether the final two rounds of the Formula 1 season in the Middle East will go ahead as planned.

The November and December rounds in Losail, Qatar and Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates have been in doubts for months due to the ongoing war between the US and Iran. The war previously led to the cancellation of the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian grands prix in April (the former took place earlier this month, in name only, after being relocated 6,000 kilometres away to Malaysia).

The series’ CEO Stefano Domenicali previously indicated a decision was needed by mid-September. However no final announcement has yet been made. While FOM and the FIA has repeatedly stated the races will go ahead, they have made arrangements for Imola in Italy to take over as the venue for the finale if needed.

Sainz acknowledged F1’s governing body and commercial rights holder “seem very convinced that it’s going to go ahead.” But the Grand Prix Drivers’ Association director said he personally has doubts due to the political situation, including the potentially significant midterm elections in the USA which are less than two weeks away.

“On my personal side and not speaking as a GPDA [director], it’s very difficult to be convinced right now, because there are still things happening, plenty of things happening in the Middle East, and also there is obviously an election that is going to happen in the US, and things that are going to happen in the political side of the world that could affect the next month, month and a half, very suddenly.

“So I think it’s relatively premature to be so convinced, but as it stands, we will go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi. If the FIA and Formula 1 decide that it’s still safe and a good scenario, I think we, as drivers, have to go with whatever they say.

“We don’t have as much political information, as much inside information as they have, for sure, so we need to follow their lead and trust in their decision-making, but only as it stands.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“The world can change a lot in the next month, month and a half, and we need to stay diligent and reactive to whatever happens, and not just go because we want to go right now.”

The Losail International Circuit issued a press release yesterday drawing attention to its two major events next month: the F1 grand prix and the rescheduled round of the Moto GP championship which was originally due to take place in April.

Sainz said the GPDA is prepared to follow the FIA’s guidance.

“The GPDA, as united as we are, we don’t have half of the information that Formula 1 and FIA have with all the political battles that are happening in the world,” he said.

“I think the GPDA can help a lot to understand the sport, or make the FIA and F1 understand the sport, what makes racing better, what makes a race track better, what needs to be changed in order to get more safety. But about political matters, realistically none of us have the information and the contacts that F1 and FIA have.

“So, similar to [the media], you need to trust in a way the decision that F1 and FIA take about that matter, but as I said before, we need to stay reactive and see how situations change, I think they will do that and they will take the right decision when it comes.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Oscar Piastri agreed the drivers were prepared to put “our trust in the FIA and F1.”

“There have been difficult situations in the past through conflicts and all kinds of things,” he said. “So we’ll put our trust in F1 and the FIA and listen to their advice.”

“We might have to get some snowploughs out if we race in Imola,” he added. “But I think I’ll leave it to F1. I think Imola has just been touted as the replacement, then hopefully it’s above zero. That’s all I ask for.”

Update: Williams has issued a further statement from Sainz regarding his comments on the Qatar and Abu Dhabi grands prix:

“Following some reporting of my comments in the press conference earlier today about ending the season in the Middle East, I want to be clear that I know the FIA and Formula 1 will put safety first and completely trust them to make the right decision. We look forward to racing in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.”

Sports.title: Slater to make F1 practice debut for Audi in Mexico | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Audi’s junior driver Freddie Slater will make his first appearance in a Formula 1 practice session at the Mexican Grand Prix next week.

Slater, who finished runner-up in the Formula 3 championship this year, will also drive for the team in the following round in Brazil one week later.

Audi has already completed two of its four obligations to run inexperienced drivers in its cars during practice sessions this year. It handed two outings to Paul Aron, one in each of its cars.

The team is yet to confirm which cars Slater will drive in the upcoming two practice sessions. By dividing Slater’s two appearances between its cars, it can fulfil its obligation to run drivers on four occasions over the course of the season.

Slater, 18, is due to move into Formula 2 next year with Invicta.

Aston Martin has also announced it will satisfy its practice driver obligations in Mexico by handing its fourth outing to Jak Crawford. They will become the third team to do so, joining Audi and Cadillac. Colton Herta will make his fourth appearance for the latter this weekend.

Sports.title: “Free Congo!”: Hamilton welcomes F1’s return to Africa, with reservations over Rwanda | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton indicated he has mixed feelings over Formula 1’s choice of Rwanda as the venue for its first grand prix in Africa since 1993.

The seven-times world champion has repeatedly called for the series to return to the continent and lobbied F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali on the matter. However he acknowledged the criticism F1 has faced for choosing to race in Rwanda.

“I’ve been advocating for a race in Africa for many, many, many years,” he said, describing his “countless meetings with the stakeholders, so many meetings with Stefano at his office in London, but also race weekends.”

“Countless calls. ‘What’s happening?’, ‘where are we going?’, ‘who are you meeting with?’. Many meetings with different presidents from different countries, lots of phone calls with different presidents in different countries within Africa.

“For me it’s a place that deserves to have a grand prix. It’s [about] more than just one country, it is about the continent in itself and there’s so many beautiful countries within it and the people are so lovely.

“The culture is so rich and I think it’s important that we get to show that to the world and we get to do that with our sport. We get to go to all these different countries and people see some of these countries they didn’t really know too much about and all of a sudden it’s on the screen and kids are talking about it. They go to school talking about. So I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix.”

However the Rwandan government has been accused of backing a rebel militia in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo. Amnesty International claims the M23 group has committed human rights abuses which “may amount to war crimes”.

Therese Kayikwamba Wagner, the DR Congo’s minister of foreign affairs, said she told Domenicali last year it would be “morally indefensible” for F1 to hold a race in Rwanda. She called for F1 to guarantee its race will not be paid for using wealth Rwanda has taken from DR Congo.

Hamilton, who has previously spoken out against human rights abuses in and by other countries F1 visits, indicated he is aware of the concerns over visiting Rwanda and said the series should not overlook them.

“Of course I don’t get to choose where we go and naturally there’s problems all over the world today,” he said. “I’ve seen many of the stories, but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. Growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum: a lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism and the west intervening.

“But if you see the people, you see so many designs that are out there today, top brands come from Africa and it’s got all the richest resources.

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.

Sports.title: Verstappen would have won Singapore GP in a Ferrari, says Hadjar: ‘It was the fastest car’ | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen’s Singapore Grand Prix victory would have been even more dominant if he had been driving for Ferrari, according to his team mate.

“I don’t think we have the fastest car,” said Isack Hadjar ahead of this weekend’s race in Austin.

His team mate Verstappen has won the last two grands prix in a row. He beat Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc by seven seconds in Singapore.

However Hadjar believes his team mate is getting more from his car than Ferrari’s drivers are from theirs.

“The car is still very hard to drive,” he explained. “In Malaysia it was dominant but I don’t think in Singapore it was the fastest car. That’s what I believe.

“I think if you put Max in the Ferrari he would have won the race with more margin so that’s my opinion. In Singapore I think [the Ferrari] was the fastest car.”

Verstappen beat Charles Leclerc to pole position by five hundredths of a second. Lewis Hamilton, who was quickest in Q1 and Q2, was another seven hundredths of a second behind in the other Ferrari.

Hadjar finished 10th in Singapore after starting from the pit lane due to a penalty for replacing a failed power unit. He is eager to have a more competitive weekend in Austin.

“It was one of those weekends where you get a failure in each session, so you learn from it and we just move on,” he said. “I’m happy to be here in Texas. I like that track and the car’s been, performance-wise, working really well the last couple of weekends.

“We’re confident as a team, but of course we are aware of the upgrades in the other garages so we’re still down to earth. We still know our weaknesses on the car, we’re still working on it.

“So I just want to go out there and have another clean one because the last two weekends have been very frustrating considering the car I have been given.”

Sports.title: FIA’s new Formula 1 Race Operations Centre opens at FOM’s Biggin Hill base | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The FIA is using Formula 1’s base at Biggin Hill in the UK as the site of its new Race Operations Centre.

Biggin Hill is the home of F1’s broadcasting operations, where raw footage from the hundreds of camera operators which cover every session are combined into the video feeds seen by millions of viewers worldwide.

The governing body of motorsport announced the opening of the new facility which will allow its officials to manage events around the world without being present in person.

A key part of the facility’s functions will involve providing support to race control and stewards on decisions during sessions. It will assist in detecting when drivers have jumped the start or lined up incorrectly on the grid, exceeded track limits or committed offences in the pit lane.

The ROC will also use new artificial intelligence systems to automate processes and detect incidents.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem and Formula 1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali were among those who attended the formal inauguration of the new facility.

“As the championship grows globally, it is vital that we continue to invest in the people, technology and infrastructure that underpin world-class race operations,” said Ben Sulayen. “This state-of-the-art facility will strengthen our ability to support accurate, consistent and efficient decision-making, ensuring that our sport continues to operate at the highest possible standards.”

Sports.title: “I’ll probably need to order a new spine” – Verstappen braced for bumpy weekend at COTA | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen expects a rough ride from the notorious bumps at the Circuit of the Americas this weekend.

The track in Austin, Texas has a reputation for being one of the bumpiest on the calendar. The race promoters have attempts to ease the bumps on several occasions and F1’s latest generation of cars are supposed to offer a less harsh ride than the ‘ground effect’ designs used last year.

However after watching footage of the World Endurance Championship round at COTA last month (below), Verstappen expects a tough time this weekend.

“From what I saw in WEC, the track is incredibly bumpy,” he said. “Oh my God, yeah, I’ll probably need to order a new spine, I think, after the weekend. I’ll become like RoboCop. That’s a new challenge for everyone, to deal with those bumps.”

Red Bull go into this weekend’s race as the favourites to win, having performed strongly across the three previous rounds. Verstappen has taken two grand prix wins, one sprint race win and second place in a grand prix over that time.

However he says the different characteristics of the upcoming circuits makes it unclear how competitive they will be.

“I don’t want to say now that I will be in the fight in Austin,” said Verstappen. “The last few weekends have been great.

“But I just take it race by race and once we are in Austin, then we’ll see how it will go there. It’s again a very different track.”

“From there we have to go to Mexico [which is] high altitude, everything will run super-hot,” he added. “We need to see how the engine is going to perform in that altitude, how the car is behaving, because it’s very different.

“So there are so many different things that you can get right or wrong in those races, but we’ll see.”

Sports.title: Eddie Hearn Expects Conor Benn To Leave Zuffa
Sports.content:
Eddie Hearn doubts Conor Benn will fight for Zuffa again, suggesting the price of his comeback could lead to a disagreement over the opponent.

The Matchroom promoter believes Zuffa will want Benn to accept a difficult fight to justify his purse. However, Hearn admits he does not know whom the company intends to offer, making this his forecast rather than evidence of a breakdown between Benn and his promoter.

“He’s got a comeback fight. Watch who they try and make him fight for that comeback fight,” Hearn told reporters. “I don’t believe he’ll fight for Zuffa again.”

Hearn referred to a $15 million payment to Benn while discussing fighter pay, but did not provide contract details establishing what Benn would receive for his next appearance.

Asked to identify the opponent, Hearn made clear he was describing what he expects to happen.

“I don’t know, but what they’ll do is they’ll give him an opponent he doesn’t want to fight because he’s on a lot of money for a comeback fight,” he said.

That is the potential difficulty with an expensive comeback. The fighter may want an opponent who allows him to rebuild, while the promoter wants a bout that earns back some of its investment. Finding someone who satisfies both sides becomes harder when the purse is already high.

Demanding a tough fight hardly proves Zuffa wants rid of Benn. Any company committing serious money can reasonably expect a competitive contest. Benn’s actual reaction will come down to the exact opponent, the financial terms, plus what his contract requires.

Hearn’s critique must also be weighed against the source. As a competing promoter who spent much of the conversation taking aim at Zuffa’s boxing footprint, his forecast carries an obvious commercial angle.

Concrete matchmaking offers will give this situation substance. For now, Hearn has put his name to a blunt forecast, betting Benn’s negotiations end with him walking away rather than returning to the ring for Zuffa.

Handing Conor Benn a soft touch on a massive guarantee is financial malpractice for an outfit trying to establish a foothold in boxing.

Zuffa is not running a charity or operating like an old school promoter willing to absorb red ink just to build a fighter’s confidence. If they are cutting an eight-figure check or anything close to it, they need eyeballs, gate revenue, and platform buzz to offset the layout. A walkover against an unranked body does none of that.

Benn has spent years fighting sporadic rounds, dealing with layoffs, and avoiding the elite tier at 147. His ring identity was built on aggressive matchmaking against aging veterans rather than proven, prime operators.

Even pulling an elite light welterweight up to a catchweight or a soft 147 presents a nightmare. Fighters like Subriel Matias, Richardson Hitchins, or Gary Antuanne Russell possess the precision, hand speed, and technical discipline to exploit Benn’s reckless attacks inside six rounds.

The welterweight division may be transitional, but throwing Benn in with someone like Brian Norman Jr., Richardson Hitchins, or even a rugged veteran who can take a shot means Benn is live to get completely exposed.

If Benn’s camp expects a showcase fight while cashing an elite purse, the negotiations are doomed from the jump. Zuffa’s natural move is to demand a real fight where the outcome is genuinely in doubt. The moment they slide a dangerous name across the table, Benn either has to take the gamble of his life or walk away from the payday entirely.

Sports.title: Denzel Bentley Loses Appeal To Bypass Yoenli Hernandez
Sports.content:
Denzel Bentley’s November 7 fight against Shane Mosley Jr. now threatens his hold on the WBO middleweight title after the sanctioning body rejected his appeal and ordered him to face Yoenli Hernández next.

The ruling leaves Bentley’s planned Zuffa Boxing debut in conflict with his mandatory obligation. If he intends to keep the WBO championship, the committee’s decision requires Hernández to come first.

The WBO announced Thursday that its Complaint and Grievance Committee had denied Bentley’s appeal and upheld the mandatory order.

“Both parties have been ordered to confirm their intention to proceed within 24 hours of service of the Award.”

That deadline concerns whether Bentley and Hernández intend to proceed. It does not mean they must complete negotiations or fight within 24 hours. Nor does the announcement say Bentley has already been stripped.

Still, Bentley has lost the appeal he hoped would allow him to retain his championship while taking the Mosley fight. He previously argued that he should be permitted a voluntary defense before meeting Hernández. The WBO has refused to approve that route. talksport.com

Bentley’s team booked Mosley while the title issue remained unresolved. That decision now puts pressure on the November 7 plans, with the WBO insisting its mandatory challenger cannot be made to wait through another opponent.

The financial side helps explain Bentley’s reluctance. The mandatory fight already went through purse bids, with the WBO’s official minutes recording a $200,000 bid. That is the total bid for staging the contest, rather than Bentley’s individual purse. wboboxing.com

A better-paying opportunity elsewhere may appeal to Bentley, but it does not remove Hernández’s right to challenge for the belt. Allowing a champion to book another fight and then postpone his mandatory would leave the challenger paying the price for a deal he had no part in making.

Bentley can decide which opportunity he wants to pursue. What he cannot currently count on is taking the Mosley fight with the WBO’s approval while Hernández waits. The appeal was his attempt to keep both options available. Thursday’s ruling closes that route unless the sanctioning body subsequently changes its position.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia vs Floyd Mayweather: Is It Good Or Bad For Boxing?
Sports.content:
Boxing fans received an unexpected announcement as the reigning WBC welterweight world champion Ryan Garcia (26-2, 21 KOs) claims he and boxing legend Floyd “Money” Mayweather (50-0, 27 KOs) have agreed to a fight.

On October 21st, Ryan Garcia posted the breaking news on all of his social media platforms. Garcia claims his bout with Mayweather will be a real match, and the WBC strap will be at stake.

“Trust me at first I thought this was bull***,”Garcia said. “But it’s real Floyd and I agree to a fight 147 for the WBC welterweight championship of the world 50-0 vs The current champ.”

Garcia doubled down on the claim as he posted another message on his Instagram account, and this message included a photo of Garcia and Mayweather in what appears to be a FaceTime call.

“Talking about fighting- it’s real, and he wants to do a real fight 147. He and I both agreed to post this! Let’s Rumble.”

When you glance at the tale of the tape, Ryan Garcia is 28 years old, and in four months Floyd Mayweather will be 50. That along with a few other red flags make boxing fans question why Garcia is interested in this bout?

Garcia blames Mayweather for changing the fight game in the worst way due to the fact that boxers in Garcia’s era try to mimic Mayweather by protecting their 0. It would be satisfying for Garcia to put the blemish on Mayweather’s record.

This bout is good for Mayweather because a fight against Garcia guarantees a big payday. Also, a victory over Garcia would take down Bernard Hopkins’ record, and it would make Mayweather the oldest boxer in history to win a world title.

This fight is good for boxing because a Mayweather vs. Garcia bout would grab the attention of the casuals. Casual fans will be intrigued by the star power and the fact that this bout will feature boxers from two different eras.

This potential fight is bad for boxing because some boxers have been fighting and clawing their way up the rankings trying to position themselves for a title shot. If the Mayweather vs. Garcia bout takes place, it means Floyd skipped the line.

Floyd Mayweather hasn’t fought a legitimate boxer since his bout against Andre Berto back in 2015. If the WBC approves Mayweather’s bid to skip the line, it would be egregious.

Speaking of the sanctioning body, as of now the WBC hasn’t approved this proposed Mayweather vs. Garcia bout. The news of this matchup is trending, but it may end up being clickbait.

It’s puzzling why Garcia wants this fight. Garcia could have matchups against Teofimo Lopez, Devin Haney, or Isaac “Pitbull” Cruz, but yet he wants to box an opponent who is 11 years removed from legitimate competition.

For Ryan Garcia, this appears to be a losing situation. If Floyd Mayweather beats him, it’s kind of embarrassing considering the circumstances. If he defeats Mayweather, he won’t receive the credit because by the time the fight takes place, Mayweather will be 50 years old!

This Ryan Garcia vs Floyd Mayweather situation has a few pluses, but it has a number of minuses. In the coming days and weeks, boxing fans and boxing pundits will give their opinions as it relates to the question, is this potential bout good or bad for boxing?

Sports.title: Devin Haney Gets Favorable Matchup In Liam Paro
Sports.content:
Devin Haney has agreed to meet Liam Paro in a WBO and IBF welterweight unification before the close of the year in the United States, according to Mike Coppinger of The Ring. Official confirmation on the date and venue remains pending.

The matchup offers Haney an ideal path toward a second belt. Facing an opponent recently beaten by Richardson Hitchins represents a noticeably safer route than the scrapped Shakur Stevenson clash. Paro carries championship hardware, yet that December 2024 split decision defeat gives Haney a transparent blueprint.

Hitchins took Paro’s 140-pound belt by controlling distance, working behind a disciplined jab, and forcing the Australian to play catch-up all night. Haney possesses the precise reach, jab, and ring generalship required to run the exact same play.

Because of that dynamic, this unification leans toward comfortable territory for Haney. Paro holds a world title, yet Haney does not have to invent a fresh game plan. The tape exists, showing Paro struggling against an opponent armed with a very similar skill set.

The main wildcard rests on Haney’s activity level. He has remained completely inactive since his points win over Brian Norman Jr. on November 22, 2025. Spending 11 full months dining out on that performance makes a Liam Paro unification feel like an underwhelming comeback. High-profile names like Shakur Stevenson, Ryan Garcia, Conor Benn, Teofimo Lopez, and Keyshawn Davis represented the true blockbuster options the boxing public demanded. Two world titles supply formal sanctioning prestige, yet belts alone cannot transform Paro into a premier box-office draw.

To his credit, Paro rebuilt his standing with three straight victories following the Richardson Hitchins setback. He seized the IBF welterweight crown by unanimous decision over Lewis Crocker in June, walking into this contest as a two-weight world champion with a 28-1 resume. Still, the manner in which Hitchins systematically dismantled him leaves Haney holding every stylistic trump card.

The collapse of the Stevenson talks makes this matchup feel even more like a consolation prize. Reports from The Ring indicated that weight limits and rehydration clauses ultimately wrecked that fight. Haney secures a tidy opportunity to pocket a second 147-pound belt, yet outpointing Paro will do nothing to settle whether he can survive against the division’s most lethal stars.

Paro must avoid turning this bout into a fruitless footrace. To take the victory, he has to cut off the ring, hammer the body, and make Haney pay for retreating. Stalking without throwing and waiting for clean openings will merely walk him straight into the WBO champion’s rhythm.

The upside for Haney is massive: capturing a second belt and securing major leverage for future paydays. Defeating Paro takes him one step nearer to an undisputed run at 147, even if it leaves lingering questions about how he handles the division’s truly dangerous punchers.

Sports.title: David Benavidez Returns To PPV Against Michal Cieslak
Sports.content:
David Benavidez taking on Michal Cieslak on December 5 is landing on DAZN pay-per-view, but convincing boxing fans to shell out extra cash for this one is going to be a tough sell. The fight looks completely lopsided in favor of Benavidez, while Cieslak barely registers with mainstream fans.

Having three cruiserweight belts on the line does not move the needle either. Cieslak picked up the WBC belt simply by getting elevated from interim status. When fans already see someone as a paper champion, handing over an official sanctioning belt does nothing to turn him into a credible threat.

DAZN locked in the date, stamping PAY PER VIEW across the official fight poster alongside PBC. They have not dropped the price tag yet, but asking subscribers to dig deeper into their pockets for this headliner feels overly ambitious.

That puts the heavy lifting squarely on Benavidez. Being an elite talent inside the ring has never guaranteed monster pay-per-view numbers. He brings real fireworks once the bell sounds, but generating buy rates demands relentless promotional buzz outside the ring.

Benavidez rarely brings that promotional heat. He stays relatively quiet between training camps. His media appearances lean dead serious, skipping the colorful banter that grabs casual viewers who do not follow every twist in boxing.

Nobody expects him to fake a circus persona. Still, without that natural promotional spark, his headliners rely heavily on having an electric opponent. Cieslak does not move the needle there at all. Putting Benavidez on pay-per-view without an elite foil exposes the gap between being a respected champion and being a genuine ticket seller.

From a purely competitive standpoint, the move makes sense for Benavidez. Picking up the WBC crown lets him unify alongside his WBA and WBO straps, pushing him closer to a massive clash with Jai Opetaia. Taking the fight serves his personal goals, but that does not give regular fans a compelling reason to buy the broadcast.

Stacking the undercard might soften the blow. Taken solely as a main event, the booking comes across as an uncompetitive mismatch anchored by a single recognizable name whose solo box office power is unproven. Slapping three world titles onto the promotional artwork will not fix that reality.

Sports.title: Joe Cordina Agrees Terms To Fight Manny Pacquiao
Sports.content:
Joe Cordina has agreed to terms to fight Manny Pacquiao, putting the Welshman in position for a major payday if the proposed contest goes ahead.

The bout is being discussed for the December 11 Fury–Joshua card, although Eddie Hearn’s latest update confirms only that Cordina’s side has accepted the terms. He is still waiting to find out whether the fight will happen.

“We’ve agreed terms to fight Manny Pacquiao, but we don’t know if that’s happening,” Hearn told reporters. “From our side, we’ve agreed to do it.”

That leaves Cordina waiting on a fight that would bring him attention far beyond his usual audience. Pacquiao’s name would make this one of the most watched nights of his career, even with the Filipino well past his best years.

Cordina has every reason to take the opportunity. A fight against Pacquiao offers a different financial ceiling from the conventional route through the lightweight division. Adding it to Fury–Joshua would also give the former super featherweight champion a huge platform in front of a British audience.

The boxing question is what each man would bring at the agreed weight. Hearn did not reveal that detail, and it would have a considerable effect on the matchup. Cordina’s sharp punching and timing would be tested differently against a naturally smaller opponent than against someone accustomed to competing above his weight.

Pacquiao’s age would inevitably dominate the buildup. The name still sells, but the fighter taking the punches must perform on the night. Cordina would need to approach him as an opponent to beat, rather than let the occasion become a celebration of the former champion’s career.

Agreeing terms removes one obstacle from Cordina’s side. It also shows that his team sees enough reward in the proposed fight to accept it.

The next step is getting Pacquiao’s participation settled, and the contest announced. Cordina has accepted his end of the deal; Hearn’s wording makes clear that he cannot yet promise the fight.

Sports.title: Jack Catterall Refuses To Move For Teofimo Lopez
Sports.content:
Jack Catterall refuses to move out of Teofimo Lopez’s way, rejecting any payment to surrender his place in the WBA welterweight title queue as their October 22 negotiation deadline arrives.

His message leaves little room for bargaining. Catterall wants the fight he was promised, while Lopez seeks permission to bypass him for a unification against WBC champion Ryan Garcia.

“NO there isn’t an amount of money you can give me to step aside end of discussion,” Catterall posted on X. “I want what i deserve I want what I signed up for and I want to become a world champion and I won’t except any fucking offer to move out the way.”

Teofimo’s team has requested an exception from the WBA to pursue Garcia. Catterall can refuse to cooperate, but the sanctioning body still controls whether its order produces a fight or another delay.

That is where Catterall has reason to worry. The WBA also ordered Jaime Munguia to defend against Bektemir Melikuziev, yet Munguia is scheduled to face little-known Nikita Zon on October 31 instead. The organization has stated that it did not approve that matchup and is reviewing the situation. Bek is still waiting for his ordered opportunity.

Issuing an order does little for a mandatory challenger if the champion continues arranging other fights. The WBA’s response to Munguia has yet to put Bek in the ring with him. Catterall needs more than another statement confirming his position.

Eddie Hearn wants Teofimo to fight Catterall or vacate the belt. If Teofimo prefers the Ryan Garcia payday, Catterall shouldn’t have to put his career on hold to accommodate him.

Catterall won’t move. Now the WBA needs to decide whether Lopez must honor the order or gets to choose another opponent while keeping the title.

Even a promise that the Teofimo-Ryan winner must fight Catterall offers little protection. A lucrative immediate rematch could push him aside again. And if the WBA finally enforces its order, the winner could simply vacate and keep the WBC belt. Catterall would be left without the fight or any compensation for waiting—the same position another promise was supposed to prevent.

Sports.title: Alberto Puello Believes He Can Beat Dalton Smith Easily
Sports.content:
Alberto Puello expects to have an easy night at Dalton Smith’s expense this Saturday in Sheffield. The Dominican challenger does not rate the local belt-holder anywhere near his hardest fights, making it clear that Smith will quickly realize finding a target against him is nothing like teeing off on Subriel Matias.

Puello is counting on his slick defense, ring smarts, and footwork to carry the night. In his eyes, Smith had it easy against a flat-footed brawler like Matias, but trying to pin down an awkward southpaw who refuses to stand in the pocket is going to give the champion fits from the opening bell.

“With my experience, hitting him without getting hit, and my skills, I think I can beat him easily,” Puello said to Fight Wire ahead of their October 24 fight in Sheffield.

When asked if Smith is the toughest test of his career, Puello laughed it off with a quick “Not at all.” He pointed right to Gary Antuanne Russell as a far rougher night, and even put Matias above Smith on the danger scale.

“He beat Subriel Matias, of course, but I also think Subriel Matias is a little more difficult than him,” Puello said.

That take is bound to stir up plenty of noise considering Smith stopped Matias. But Puello is looking strictly at styles. Teeing off on an aggressive slugger who marches straight into range is night and day compared to trying to catch a slick technician who makes you swing at fresh air all night.

“I’m a boxer with plenty of defense. I know how to move around the ring. Subriel Matias only has one way of fighting: going forward, taking punches and throwing them. I know how to hit without getting hit.”

Smith will have to work for every opening instead of banking on a sitting target to stay in punching range. If Puello sticks and moves, the local champion could burn serious fuel chasing a ghost all night instead of enjoying the pocket exchanges he had against Matias.

Puello also expects the roaring Sheffield arena to work against Smith. The champion will feel the heat to put on a show and satisfy his hometown crowd, while Puello can relax, stay patient, and stick to the blueprint without any outside pressure.

He is not just planning to scrape by on the cards, either. Puello made it clear his camp has him ready to take a clean twelve-round decision or jump on a stoppage the second Smith gets reckless and leaves an opening.

We already know how the boxing community will treat Smith if he loses to Puello. It will be merciless. The second the final bell sounds, skeptics will point out that the undefeated record was built on domestic fodder and that Matias was simply a flat-footed slugger tailor-made for Smith to counter.

The defeat would leave Smith’s promoter, Eddie Hearn, standing in the ring, needing to tell the fans what went wrong, and likely talking about a rematch.

Ghana News.title: Speaker Bagbin urges RUWA-Ghana to promote the politics of options among women
Ghana News.content:
The Speaker of Parliament, Rt. Hon. Alban Sumana Kingsford Bagbin, has urged RUWA-Ghana LBG to encourage grassroots women to engage in “politics of options” rather than allow political differences to breed hatred and division.

He gave the advice when he received the organisation’s Board of Trustees at the Sir Emmanuel Charles Quist Conference Hall in Parliament House on Wednesday, October 14, 2026.

The Speaker commended RUWA-Ghana for its contributions to women’s economic empowerment and political participation, particularly in the Northern and Upper West Regions. He cited the organisation’s role in supporting three women who were elected in the 2019 District Assembly elections.

RUWA-Ghana’s Board Chair, Dr. Sylvia Josephine Anie, and Executive Director, Masud Aziz Rauf, lead the delegation in presenting an appeal for support to the Speaker of Parliament.

“Women are agents of development,” Mr Bagbin said, emphasising their contributions to household management, childcare, agriculture and community development.

He observed that women in rural communities often bear significant domestic and economic responsibilities, leaving them with limited opportunities to participate in public discourse. He cited intervention such as providing grinding mills to reduce women’s workload as an example of how practical support could improve their livelihoods and create opportunities for greater participation in development.

Mr Bagbin urged RUWA-Ghana to educate women to assess political leaders based on their performance and contributions to their communities rather than party affiliations. He also encouraged the organisation to work with religious leaders, traditional authorities and other stakeholders to strengthen women’s confidence and leadership capacity.

“Education is not only the formal one; the informal one is also important,” he stressed, highlighting the importance of community education and partnerships in changing attitudes towards women’s leadership.

The Speaker further advised the organisation to consolidate its existing achievements, identify communities where targeted interventions could make a difference and build partnerships to expand its work. He expressed willingness to facilitate further engagement with Parliament and encouraged RUWA-Ghana to provide details of the communities and constituencies it intended to target.

The Speaker’s remarks followed a presentation by RUWA-Ghana’s Executive Director, Mr Masud Aziz Rauf, titled “Empowering Women Economically and Politically: Lessons from Community-Level Action and Opportunities for National Impact.”

Mr Rauf disclosed that RUWA-Ghana had supported 54 Village Savings and Loans Associations (VSLAs), reaching 1,350 women across six districts and supporting more than 200 businesses in the Northern and Upper West Regions.

He explained that the savings groups provide women with access to small loans, support their businesses and strengthen their confidence, leadership skills and collective action.

Presenting lessons from the organisation’s 2019 District Assembly elections campaign, Mr Rauf said the initiative targeted 30 women, but 21 filed to contest and three were successfully elected.

“The national figure in 2019 was 229. So out of that 229, we contributed three from our campaign,” he said, referring to the national number of women elected to District Assemblies.

Building on this experience, RUWA-Ghana proposed a new initiative ahead of the 2027 District Assembly elections to identify, train and mentor more women, strengthen community support and encourage qualified women to contest. The initiative will be non-partisan and will not endorse political parties or individual candidates.

The organisation is seeking institutional collaboration with Parliament and other stakeholders to promote civic education, public awareness and women’s representation in local governance.

Speaking on behalf of the Board of Trustees, the Chairperson, Dr Sylvia Josephine Anie, thanked the Speaker for sharing his experiences and insights. She also appealed for support for RUWA-Ghana’s fundraising initiative to expand its women’s empowerment programmes and requested guidance in identifying potential partners.

In response, Mr Bagbin assured the delegation: “You will definitely hear from us.”

Other members of the RUWA-Ghana delegation included Alhaji Salifu Abdul-Rahaman, former Editor of the Ghanaian Times and Board Member; Madam Issah Fuseina, Secretary to the Board of Trustees; Kwabena Ahudey Sr., supporting staff; and Mr Hudu Hafiz, Media and Communications Officer.

The Speaker was accompanied by Mr Inusah Mohammed, Assistant Deputy Clerk, Speakership, Leadership and Member Service; Prof. Turosong Damasus, Executive Secretary to the Speaker; and Col. Francis Anemana (Rtd.), Aide to the Speaker – Special Duties.

RUWA-Ghana LBG has more than two decades of experience in women’s economic empowerment, gender equality, governance, community mobilisation and advocacy. The organisation remains committed to promoting women’s economic independence, inclusive governance and social justice.

Ghana News.title: Student accused of stealing Bishop Obinim’s GH¢1.5m granted bail
Ghana News.content:
Bishop Daniel Obinim

An Adenta Circuit Court has granted bail to a 23-year-old student accused of stealing GH¢1.5 million belonging to Bishop Daniel Obinim, founder of the International Godsway Church.

Ohemaa Serwaa Abigail Owusu Ansah faces charges of conspiracy to commit a crime, to wit, theft. She has not yet entered her plea.

The court admitted her to bail with two sureties, one of whom must be justified with landed property. She is expected to reappear on October 29, 2026.

Chief Inspector Maxwell Lanyo, prosecuting, told the court that the complainant, Bishop Obinim, was a friend of the accused.

The prosecution said the accused visited the complainant at his Lakeside residence on October 13, 2026.

During their conversation in the complainant’s room, he left for church, leaving the accused at the house.

The following morning, at about 0700 hours, the complainant discovered that his safe had been broken into and GH¢1.5 million stolen.

When confronted, the accused allegedly told the complainant she had contacted her father’s worker, Owusu, who sent two young men to the house.

The prosecution said the accused led the two men into the room and showed them the safe. They allegedly broke it open, took the money and left.

On October 16, at about 1400 hours, the accused was arrested and taken to the Criminal Investigations Department (CID) headquarters.

In her caution statement, she allegedly admitted to inviting the two men to the complainant’s house to break into the safe and steal the money.

The prosecution said investigations were ongoing.

Ghana News.title: Court grants bail to two in multiple land grant case
Ghana News.content:
An Accra Circuit Court has granted two persons accused of making conflicting grants of the same parcel of land bail of GH¢2 million each.

The court admitted Nene Ebenezer Mormo Kissiedu Nyamaa II, a farmer, and George Kenneth Tetteh, a retired educationist, to bail with three sureties each, one to be justified.

Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP) Seth Frimpong told the court that the accused allegedly granted the same land to different persons despite prior transactions involving the property.

The court directed the accused to report weekly to the Police investigator and adjourned the case to November 16, 2026.

The prosecution said the complainant, Francis Godsway Ntem, a trader resident in Tema, was introduced to the accused between 2021 and 2022 while searching for land for development.

The accused allegedly represented that they had land around Asutsuare Junction on the Akosombo main road and subsequently sold 1,009 acres to the complainant, who was issued with an indenture.

The court heard that when the complainant tried to develop the land, Ibrahim Yakubu, also known as Sariki Awala, confronted him and claimed ownership of the property.

The prosecution said investigations revealed that Yakubu had acquired 628.12 acres at Luom-Osudoku in 2010 from the late Chief of Luom and had since developed the land, including establishing a livestock farm and granting portions to third parties.

ASP Frimpong said ownership claims later emerged following court decisions involving the land.

He said the accused, acting as Stool Priest and Secretary of the Gbesedorm Clan, together with other clan representatives, relied on a Supreme Court judgment dated July 7, 2021, and re-granted the land to Yakubu through an indenture dated January 3, 2022.

The prosecution further alleged that in October 2019, the Gbesedorm Clan granted 3,211 acres, including Yakubu’s parcel, to the Aworteye Narh Family.

ASP Frimpong said the accused knew of earlier transactions involving the land but allegedly accepted money from the complainant and granted the same property to him.

The prosecution said the accused were arrested, cautioned and charged, and were later granted Police enquiry bail.

Nyamaa II and Tetteh have denied conspiring to grant land to more than one person.

Ghana News.title: Accused seeks removal from 3.9-tonne cocaine trial
Ghana News.content:
The Kwabenya Circuit Court has adjourned to November 5 an application seeking to strike out one of six accused persons standing trial in the alleged 3.9-tonne cocaine case.

The application was filed by Helena Akua Denkyi, a contract staff member of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA), who is the sixth accused person in the case.

Her counsel told the court that she filed the application on September 30, 2026, and served it on the Office of the Attorney-General, along with a hearing notice.

The lawyer said the court had not received an affidavit in opposition to the application.

Mr Prince Osei Owusu, the presiding judge, noted that the application had been filed several weeks earlier but was brought to the court’s attention only at the latest sitting.

The court said it needed time to consider the application and adjourned proceedings to November 5, 2026, for a ruling.

The judge also indicated that the substantive prosecutor was not in a position to respond to bail applications and other requests filed by defence counsel.

On bail, the court directed defence lawyers to file formal applications instead of making oral requests.

Chief Inspector Godwin T. Achondo, leading the prosecution, informed the court that the prosecution was filing the necessary disclosures and requested a one-month adjournment.

Lawyers for the accused persons argued that filing the disclosures suggested investigations had been completed and renewed calls for bail for their clients.

The court had earlier dismissed bail applications filed on behalf of the six accused persons.

The accused are Francis Narh Amanor, a freight forwarder; Frank Adu-Boahen, a self-styled evangelist; Togbe Agbeti; Andrews Tetteh Amponsah; Daniel Laryea; and Helena Akua Denkyi, all public servants except the first two.

Amanor and Adu-Boahen have been charged with conspiracy to commit crime, namely the exportation of narcotic drugs, and exportation of narcotic drugs.

The prosecution alleged that they conspired to export 3.9 tonnes of suspected narcotic substances in four containers from the Tema Port to the Netherlands without a licence from the Minister of Health.

Agbeti, Amponsah, Laryea, and Denkyi face charges of abetment of crime.

They are alleged to have failed to properly analyse abnormal scan images of the four containers, thereby facilitating the attempted exportation of the suspected narcotic substances.

The six accused persons remain in custody and are expected to reappear before the court on November 5, 2026.

Four other accused persons in a related case have also been remanded by the High Court.

In all, 10 persons have been arraigned following the interception of the alleged narcotic substances at Tema Port on August 12, 2026.

Ghana News.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
Ghana News.content:
A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.

Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Charles Tobin, a lawyer representing the BBC, said in court that "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff" with two months left in the discovery period, during which both sides are legally required to exchange information with each other on their case.

Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance" while he was campaigning in Georgia.

In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings.

The judge in the case, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, said that Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December, unless the discovery period is extended.

Last week, attorneys asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.

On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his property in Mar-a-Lago in Florida.

In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year, and claimed that the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action."

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

In July, Trump's lawyers conceded that they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC select or through US broadcasters.

Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, its commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

Typically, depositions take place in a lawyer's office - rather than a courtroom - without a judge physically present.

Depositions, however, carry legal weight and take place under oath. They are recorded verbatim by a court reporter, and the transcripts can later be used as evidence during trials.

In defamation cases, lawyers for both sides are normally present for depositions.
