World.title: Massive strikes hit Kyiv hours after Putin agrees to fresh peace talks
World.content:
Russia attacked the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv in a massive missile attack overnight into Thursday, hours after President Vladimir Putin said the Kremlin was ready to resume trilateral peace talks next month.

At the request of US special envoy Steve Witkoff during their three-hour meeting on Wednesday, Putin said he would be willing to resume talks with Ukraine and the United States after November 10. But the latest diplomatic push – during which Witkoff controversially called Putin a “humanitarian” because he freed a detained American citizen – was followed by an attack on Ukraine involving 21 missiles and 210 drones.

US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that his administration is “the closest we’ve been” to settling the war in Ukraine. The first explosions hit Kyiv three minutes before he made those comments.

The large-scale strikes killed two people and injured 34 others, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday. Ukrainian officials said central Kyiv was also hit with a cluster warhead.

“Russian ‘humanitarians’ have launched three waves of ballistic strikes against Kyiv since this evening,” Zelensky said. “This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening.

“When Russian ballistic missiles are the response to negotiations, real pressure must be applied on Russia to take other steps – steps to stop the killings,” he added, calling for a rapid delivery of air defense missiles.

Firefighters try to extinguish a fire after a Russian missile attack in central Kyiv, Ukraine, on Thursday. Efrem Lukatsky/AP

None of the ballistic missiles that hit Kyiv were intercepted, according to the Ukrainian Air Force, which comes as the country faces a critical shortage of US-made Patriot defense missiles. Air raid sirens continued to blare in Kyiv on Thursday, with warnings of further incoming ballistic missile attacks.

A separate Russian attack hit the central market in the city of Lozova, Kharkiv region, killing at least two people and injuring dozens more as they were shopping on Thursday, according to the mayor.

Meanwhile in Russia, Moscow’s mayor said that 630 drones flew toward the region overnight, in an attack that injured two people in the rural Voronovo area. Most of those were intercepted.

Despite the positive comments on potential future negotiations, there are no indications so far that Russia has budged on any of its maximalist positions.

Russia’s previous demands amount to near-total victory – calling for Ukraine to give up the entire eastern Ukrainian Donbas region, which is now mostly under Russian occupation. Moscow has also called for Ukraine to dramatically reduce the size of its military and pledge to never join NATO.

Ukraine skeptical about fresh trilateral talks in November

According to a post-meeting briefing by Putin’s aide Yury Ushakov, the Kremlin would like to discuss the establishment of a “security framework” for both Russia and Ukraine following the end of the conflict, without offering further details on what Russia would demand as part of that framework.

The next trilateral round could take place in Abu Dhabi, the capital city of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Ushakov said in response to a question on Russian state news channel Russia 24.

Zelensky said on Wednesday that he would like the meeting to happen “no later than the beginning of November.”

“Russia said many times it is ready for a meeting and then things changed and got canceled,” Zelensky added. “Let’s see what happens this time.”

The meeting in St. Petersburg came a day after Witkoff’s summit with Zelensky in Norway. The US envoy described the meetings with both leaders as “constructive” in a post on X later Wednesday, and said the discussions would continue with the trilateral talks.

“While there is still important work left to do, President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end and achieving a comprehensive, durable peace,” he wrote.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff meet inside the Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg Wednesday. Obtained by CNN

During the latest talks, Putin also expressed interest in the topic of restoring economic cooperation with the United States and the possibility of a meeting with China to discuss Ukraine. That follows recent moves by the Trump administration to waive sanctions on Russia and strike a deal on diesel exports.

Speaking to media after the meeting, Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev said there was “no question” that US-Russian economic cooperation would continue, and added that a recently-announced diesel deal between the two countries would go ahead despite European criticism.

A key outcome of the meeting was Witkoff announcing that Russia had released 74-year-old American prisoner Stephen Hubbard, who had been detained in the country for more than four years. A video obtained by CNN after the meeting showed the freed American detainee speaking with Witkoff at the airport in St. Petersburg.

Putin, Witkoff and translators sat around a large round table as they also discussed a wide range of issues including Russia’s willingness to help resolve the war in Iran, potential Russian fertilizer exports to the US and Hubbard’s release. The meeting continued behind closed doors, and Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law who has also been involved in the peace negotiations, joined remotely given he has the flu.

The US and Ukraine made “meaningful progress” in the Norway talks on Tuesday, a US official previously told CNN, adding that the two sides are now in “strong alignment” on what the next steps will be.

“Discussions covered key elements of a comprehensive peace framework, including long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic and prosperity plan, and a broader European security architecture designed to create lasting stability,” the US official said.

But Kremlin aide Ushakov poured cold water on those discussions, saying that while Witkoff had highlighted to Putin “certain new approaches and developments in the positions taken by the Europeans and Kyiv… in truth, these contained little of actual value for resolving the Ukrainian crisis.”

Ukraine and its allies have reiterated the key red lines set by Kyiv for any peace negotiations, including the need for future security guarantees – to ensure Russia doesn’t invade again – and a rejection of any demands to give up territory it controls.

In an Fox News interview on Wednesday, Zelensky repeated a long-held position that Ukraine would accept a ceasefire deal that involves a freeze along the current frontline – something that would involve retaining only about 75 percent of Ukrainian land – and would then ask allies for meaningful security guarantees.

Zelensky also said that Ukraine also wants trilateral negotiations involving Trump, Putin and himself, but the process would be “better with Europeans.”

“I always said that we are open to negotiate in any format, any topics, but don’t speak about us without us, please,” he said, balking at the prospect of any Russia-China-US negotiations.

A European official in Oslo told CNN: “I think plans – or lack of – isn’t as much of a problem as getting Russia to treat any plan seriously.”

This story has been updated with additional developments.

World.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in New Mexico case over Cambridge Analytica scandal
World.content:
New York — A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after the company was found to have misled users about its privacy practices in a case related to A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after the company was found to have misled users about its privacy practices in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal

The Wednesday ruling marks one of the largest-ever legal penalties for a tech giant — and just the latest court loss for Meta this year.

The company, then known as Facebook, disclosed in 2018 that the private information of as many as 87 million Facebook users was improperly obtained by political analytics firm Cambridge Analytica. The firm used that information to build profiles of American voters.

New Mexico sued Facebook in 2021, accusing it of mishandling state residents’ personal information and deceiving those users about its policies in connection with the incident.

A jury found in September that Meta had violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act more than 43 million times. State District Court Judge Francis Mathew criticized the company for what he described as a “coherent strategy designed to mislead the public” in his Wednesday penalty decision.

“Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model,” Mathew wrote.

After Wednesday’s penalty decision, Meta said it will appeal the decision and has accused New Mexico’s attorney general of conflating privacy and speech issues.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”

Meta’s legal battles threaten to strain its business, though court penalties and settlements remain relatively small compared to the company’s earnings so far.

The company reported earnings for the quarter ended in September on Wednesday, including lower quarterly profits than Wall Street had expected. It attributed the miss to a charge from the $18 billion multistate settlement it agreed to in August to resolve claims that its platforms have addicted and harmed young people.

New Mexico was not a party to that settlement, which also resolved the participating states’ outstanding claims related to Cambridge Analytica.

Meta posted income from operations of nearly $13 billion during the quarter, compared to nearly $23 billion that it said it would have earned without the settlement.

Meta CFO Susan Li said on a call with analysts following the earnings report that the company is monitoring “active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” including additional youth-related trials set for later this year and next.

Meta was also ordered to pay nearly $1 billion in a separate New Mexico case earlier this year over claims that its platforms addicted and harmed young people. Meta, along with YouTube, also lost a case in March in Los Angeles brought by a young woman with similar addiction and harm claims. The companies plan to appeal.

Meta earnings

Still, Meta’s business continues to grow at a strong clip thanks in large part to its investments in artificial intelligence. The company posted sales growth of 26 percent year-on-year to more than $64 billion in the quarter.

Meta’s stock (META) jumped more than three percent in after-hours trading following the report on Wednesday.

Meta launched its Muse AI personal assistant app in September. The app quickly rocketed to the top of app stores and has gained more than 10 million users, according to the company. It also launched its latest foundation model, Muse Wonder, last month.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg presents the Muse Charm at the company’s headquarters in Menlo Park, California, on September 23. Carlos Barria/Reuters

The company said Wednesday that its AI investments are boosting its core advertising business “through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetization.” Its average price per ad, a key metric for the company, jumped 14 percent year-over-year in the September quarter.

Across the industry, tech companies face questions about their heavy spending on AI infrastructure. Meta’s capital expenditures during the quarter reached nearly $35 billion, up 80 percent from the year-ago quarter. And the company narrowed its full-year capital expenditure guidance to between $135 billion to $145 billion, the upper end of the range it had previously provided. Meta declined to provide spending guidance for next year.

But investors are signaling they’re willing to give Meta some leeway, given the success of Muse, said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com.

“The market has shifted from punishing Meta for spending to rewarding it for having a compelling product story,” Cohen wrote in emailed commentary.

World.title: US-Ukraine relationship worsens amid Trump and Zelensky’s mutual distrust
World.content:
The relationship between Ukraine and the United States is facing increasing strain over intelligence sharing, sanctions, Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy and the path to peace.

There also appears to be deepening mutual distrust between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky.

Trump on Monday accused Zelensky of not knowing what he was talking about and suggested it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”

Over the weekend Kyiv launched one of its biggest drone attacks this year on Russia, hitting a key oil terminal, in defiance of Trump’s demand that Ukraine stop hitting Russian refining plants.

The White House is trying to relieve pressure on oil and diesel prices in the US ahead of crucial midterm elections, as diesel prices are at a record high.

Last week Trump called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace” and said Zelensky was more difficult to deal with than Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

In an interview on Sunday, Zelensky hit back, saying it was “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face,” an apparent reference to Trump’s relationship to Russia.

Trump again criticized Zelensky on Sunday, claiming in a Truth Social post that he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”

The relationship now seems to be at its lowest ebb since the explosive meeting at the White House 18 months ago.

Zelensky has consistently said he is open to peace negotiations if Ukraine’s security can be guaranteed.

The Ukrainian president said he spoke to US envoy, Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner on Sunday as part of “nonstop communication” to work towards the goal of peace.

The trio will speak again on Tuesday, with Zelensky and Witkoff set to meet in Norway’s capital Oslo, according to Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. Kushner will join the meeting remotely.

Kremlin ‌spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday he hoped for a meeting between Witkoff, his team and Putin in the near future, allowing the US side to brief the Russian leader “on their contacts with both the Ukrainians and the Europeans.”

CNN has reached out to the White House for comment on the meetings.

“We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer,” Zelensky posted on X.

“Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end,” Zelensky added on Monday.

Zelensky also spoke to Pope Leo XIV on Monday, according to the Vatican.

The pope spoke to the Ukrainian president just days after a phone call with Putin in which he expressed his concern about the “grave humanitarian situation” in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where Ukrainian authorities say around 2,000 civilians are stuck without access to food or basic medicine.

Trump has defended recent concessions to Russia on sanctions, which have included a waiver to allow Russian diesel exports and another exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress.

“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote in his Sunday post.

In an interview Sunday with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Zelensky said the waivers strengthened Putin’s war against Ukraine while Moscow was failing on the battlefield.

There is growing anxiety in Kyiv and Europe that the Trump administration will make further concessions to Moscow in an effort to get Putin to agree to a peace deal.

Zelensky told “Meet the Press” that the US siding with Russia would be a “historic mistake.” He said he wanted to trust Trump and hoped he would change his attitude to Putin.

Asked if Trump was an ally of Ukraine, Zelensky said: “I hope so.”

On Monday, Zelensky appealed directly to the US Congress, holding an online meeting with a group of lawmakers from both parties. He described the current situation as “the most difficult situation from the very beginning of this war” and saying that it appears as if “some political decision has been made to slow down support for us.”

Ukraine is also perturbed by reports of a possible three-way meeting involving the US and China next month on settling the conflict – without Ukrainian involvement.

“I think there’s been talk of a meeting. I don’t know if anything’s been finalized,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said during a visit to Uzbekistan Monday.

Trump said on Monday that he’d consider a trilateral meeting with Putin and the Chinese leader Xi Jinping — but said that the sitdown would focus on denuclearization, not Russia’s war with Ukraine.

But Ukraine criticized the idea, arguing such a meeting would not help peace but “would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Monday.

“Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandizement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” Sybiha wrote on X.

The Kremlin said Monday that “no concrete proposals or agreements – neither regarding the meeting itself nor its potential agenda and content – have been discussed or put forward by anyone.”

Attacks persist

Defying Trump’s demands, Ukraine is keeping up long-range strikes into Russia. One target at the weekend was the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal. The terminal can handle up to 12.5 million tons per year. Ukraine’s Fire Point company, which makes the drones used in the attack, said there was a fire on the terminal’s grounds following the strike.

A logistics center in St. Petersburg was also attacked, according to Ozon, a Russian distribution company, as well as a data center for the Russian VKontakte social media platform.

One person was killed and five wounded in the attacks, with residential homes damaged as well, according to local authorities.

A week ago, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure.

Neither Kyiv nor Moscow acknowledged such an agreement. Ukraine briefly halted such attacks, but Russia never stopped pounding Ukraine’s energy plants and cities.

“Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ​ago, Russia has ​deliberately ‌attacked ​Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors ⁠76 times,” Zelensky ​wrote on X Sunday.

On Monday, Zelensky said a Russian drone attack in the Kharkiv region killed six people, including three children. Sharing a blurred photograph of one of the victims – a small child in a stroller – Zelensky said the horrific image showed “the truth about this war.”

“Lives must be protected. Ukraine needs air defense. You can’t think about making money with Russia as long as it continues its asinine war,” he said on X.

Accusations have also flown over the cuts in US satellite intelligence provided to the Ukrainian military.

Zelensky repeated on Sunday that changes in the Starlink system owned by billionaire Elon Musk was limiting the speed of its short-range and battlefield drones, describing it as a “message from the American government.”

Musk said last week that the systems are owned and controlled by the US government, meaning that only the government could decide to place limits on their speed or usage.

The Trump administration has denied it ordered the service restricted. On Monday, Trump said he didn’t know who it was that restricted it, but would “like to find out.”

Similarly the Trump administration has pushed back on accusations from Kyiv that intelligence on incoming ballistic missiles is not being shared.

Zelensky said on Monday that Kyiv had received no advance warning of ballistic missile attacks on Sunday night – something he claims has occurred multiple times in the past week.

“Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners.”

US satellite networks are critical in providing the Ukrainian military with warnings of incoming missiles. Russian ballistic missile attacks are aimed at crippling civilian life and destroying essential infrastructure.

“I don’t know where he’s getting these things or why he’s saying these things to the press,” Rubio told ‌reporters Monday. “You should go back and ask him. There’s been no pause.”

“What he should be focused on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That’s what he should be focused ​on,” Rubio said of Zelensky.

Kyiv and Washington see very different paths to that goal.

CNN’s Daria Tarasova, Anna Chernova, Julia Benbrook, Jennifer Hansler, Christopher Lamb, Kristen Holmes and Ivana Kottasová contributed to this report.

World.title: France promises ‘massive’ police presence this weekend as cities impose more curfews after protest violence
World.content:
French authorities promised a “massive” police presence for planned protests on Saturday and imposed localized curfews for a second consecutive night as the country grapples with the fallout from its worst rioting in years.

The moves come after protests over education and the cost of living spiraled into a wave of deadly, nationwide violence over the weekend that has sparked a political blame game at home and threatens to spill over into its European neighbors.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu credited the “targeted curfews” with helping maintain calm overnight into Tuesday. He admitted that intelligence services had failed to identify the severity of the situation and said previous security arrangements had been too static.

Paris police announced an overnight curfew from 11 p.m. Tuesday in the worst-hit areas around the Place de la République and Les Halles, while cities including Bordeaux and Lille will also impose curfews.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told MPs at the National Assembly he deeply regretted the weekend violence and accepted some responsibility, while also pointing to the role of political opponents and those involved in the destruction.

“I accept my share of the responsibility, but I would not want us to forget the significant responsibility of a certain political camp that does not hesitate to add fuel to the fire, nor the responsibility of the troublemakers,” Nuñez said.

France’s main student union UNEF has called for further protests on Saturday and said they won’t give up until their demands are met. The CGT, one of France’s biggest trade unions, has said it will join, calling for peaceful protests.

Curfews were introduced after more than 2,000 people were arrested this past weekend, with at least two deaths and reports of serious injuries, including two people who lost their hands.

Police fired tear gas into crowds and fought running battles with black-clad, hooded rioters who set fires and broke into thousands of shops and government buildings, with images showing historic buildings ablaze.

The political fallout could prove significant, deepening faultlines between the major parties with an election to succeed French President Emanuel Macron just six months away.

The vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, authorities and political leaders stress – but the level of fighting and destruction has shaken the nation and prompted forceful condemnations from leaders and the public alike.

“Those who destroyed must pay,” Macron said on Sunday evening. “Those who looted must pay back. Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”

He also promised to hold meetings this week to discuss “concrete proposals” and to listen to protesters’ demands — but many of them remain skeptical.

How did this begin?

It started in September with a strike by students and teachers at a high school in the Parisian suburbs, who demanded more staff and resources. Their demands were met and the strike ended – but it lit a spark that soon caught nationwide.

Students around the country, long frustrated with an understaffed and overcrowded education system, launched protests that at times turned violent. A heavy-handed police response fueled public anger and pushed hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets, especially after videos of a police officer using a banned headlock on a girl.

Students gather in front of barricaded gates at the Lycee Paul-Eluard high school in the northern Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, France, on September 29. Luc Auffret/Anadolu/Getty Images

Within a few weeks, the protests swelled to become a broader movement beyond students, capturing widespread discontent over affordability, perceived government inaction, a growing wealth divide, and a deep desire for social and political change.

“This can’t go on,” said 57-year-old Maria Pallas, a member of a major French trade union, speaking to CNN at Saturday’s protest in Paris. “There’s the cost of living. There’s unemployment. There’s a bunch of things. A young person will go looking for work, we’ll promise him a lot, and he’ll end up with nothing.”

What happened this weekend?

Over half a million people demonstrated across France on Saturday. For the most part, things were peaceful.

But in several locations the protests spilled into violence, especially as night fell. In Paris, groups of masked young people looted shops and started fires; in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office; in the central city of Limoges, the spire of a 143-year-old town hall collapsed in flames, reviving painful memories for some of the Notre Dame Cathedral fire. Around 3,000 shops were looted across the country, justice minister Gérald Darmanin said Tuesday. Small pockets of protests flared on Sunday too.

By the end of the weekend, Paris looked like a “war zone,” one visitor to the city told Reuters. Residents in Paris and other French cities were stunned, with some condemning the looters and rioters, and others placing blame with authorities who failed to address the crisis earlier.

French firefighters on Saturday work to extinguish a blaze in a building amid protests in Marseille. Manon Cruz/Reuters

“It’s heartbreaking, heartbreaking seeing our city like this,” said 59-year-old Marseille resident Farida, who did not give a last name, according to Reuters. “If every protest ends with all the shop windows smashed and stores trashed, this simply cannot go on — it cannot go on.”

One Paris resident, 56-year-old Paola Formenti, voiced support for the protesters’ “legitimate” anger, even as she condemned the violence.

What comes next and will it spread?

The protests and fallout could shape France’s upcoming election next spring. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, claimed this weekend that “legitimate social grievances have, yet again, been held hostage by the far left.” Her hard-left rival, Jean-Luc Mélenchon has repeatedly defended the students’ right to protest.

Demonstrations took place elsewhere in Europe last weekend, too.

In Belgium, students demonstrated against the state of their education system. In Portugal, tens of thousands of people marched in Lisbon on Saturday to protest rising costs of living and the country’s housing crisis.

In Italy, Milan also saw two consecutive nights of unrest this weekend that led to about €1 million in damages, according to officials. Protesters threw stones and looted supermarkets, while police responded with tear gas, and water cannons, and arrested 32 people.

Shops only reopened on Tuesday as the government announced a series of measures to deal with the violent protests.

Among them is a new, punishable criminal offense: “violent participation in a demonstration.” Offenders can face up to five years in prison and up to a €20,000 fine.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said if the protester’s face is covered or if they injure someone, or if a group of protesters vandalize property, the penalty increases.

Protesters or the parents of protesters who are minors will now have to pay for any damages they are responsible for, as part of the new measures.

And minors can now be subject to preventative detention, a measure previously reserved for adults. The prime minister said that an 11-year-old was among the youngest protesters identified in Milan.

Italian Justice Minister Carlo Nordio said those who use social media to organize violent protests could face up to 12 years in prison.

Meloni also said 500 additional military personnel will be deployed to Milan through the end of the year to support law enforcement officials. Additional spaces in juvenile detention centers will be opened to accommodate even more young detainees.

Police officers stand inside a looted Decathlon sporting goods store behind shattered glass in Milan, Italy, on Sunday. Stringer/Reuters

Meanwhile in Albania, students have been taking to the streets for months, protesting perceived government corruption. Demonstrations in the capital Tirana turned violent this weekend, with one person photographed throwing a Molotov cocktail at riot police.

Authorities in many of these countries have condemned the violence and called for calm. The protests have caught the attention of the White House, with Vice President JD Vance posting a video of the burning Limoges town hall on X and blaming the unrest on failed immigration policy.

US President Donald Trump also mentioned the protests during a rally in Georgia this weekend, joking: “Let’s go to France and join the revolution and spend our $5,000 there,” referring to the dividend promised if the Republicans win the midterm elections.

World.title: US warns of potential attacks and travel disruptions across 12 Middle Eastern countries
World.content:
In a rare move, Washington has issued a high-level security warning for US citizens across 12 Middle Eastern nations, citing heightened risks of potential attacks targeting American interests.

US embassies across the region released synchronized security alerts advising citizens in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, the United Arab Emirates, Yemen, and Iran to exercise extreme caution.

The notices warned of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and severe travel disruptions stemming from escalating military tensions linked to Iran and the Houthi movement in Yemen.

The advisory, covering all twelve countries, cautioned that hostilities could swiftly expand beyond their immediate theater and strongly recommended establishing advance contingency plans.

According to the statement, Iran and its affiliated groups might target US assets, affiliated sites, and American citizens worldwide, including corporate entities and foreign-based institutions.

Strikes in Saudi Arabia

In Saudi Arabia, the US Embassy highlighted a complex security environment, noting that Iranian-backed Houthis have carried out hostilities against the Kingdom.

These include strikes on civilian airports and vital infrastructure, resulting in civilian casualties and major transport disruptions.

The advisory reiterated concerns regarding potential threats to American businesses and institutions globally.

The US Embassy in Qatar urged citizens to closely monitor official updates and local news, stay clear of demonstrations and large gatherings, and adhere to local security guidelines.

Qatar Airways announced the suspension of its flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam until October 24, alongside scaling back its daily services to Jeddah from seven flights to four.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Egypt reveals what happened behind closed doors with GERD negotiations
World.content:
Egyptian Minister of Water Resources and Irrigation Hani Sewilam stated that Cairo has exhausted all negotiation paths in the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) dispute.

He emphasized that Egypt’s policy exercised patience and endurance, but found no response from Ethiopia that would lead to an agreement.

Speaking during a session titled “National and Citizen Security” on the third day of the Egypt Forum—in the presence of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi—the minister added that Egypt did everything in its power to address the crisis.

This included participating in negotiations and signing the 2015 Declaration of Principles agreement, which Cairo viewed as a step to demonstrate good intentions toward Ethiopia and offer an opportunity to reach a formula for peaceful coexistence and shared interests.

Sewilam explained that Cairo hoped the Declaration of Principles would help correct the trajectory that began when the GERD project launched in 2011.

According to Sewilam, Addis Ababa failed to implement what was agreed upon in the declaration, leading to ongoing disputes over the rules for filling and operating the dam, as well as handling periods of drought and prolonged drought.

Reviewing the timeline of negotiations, Sewilam noted that Washington-hosted talks reached a balanced draft agreement approved by all three countries, designed to protect the water rights and interests of all parties, including future generations.

Ethiopia’s evasiveness

He accused Ethiopia of evading the signature before shifting the issue to other negotiation tracks that yielded no results, ultimately prompting Egypt to step away from negotiations that failed to reach a conclusion.

The US-sponsored talks, held with World Bank participation, had seen progress in drafting operational and filling rules, but did not result in a final, signed agreement among the three nations.

The primary point of contention remains the lack of a binding agreement governing dam management during drought periods, along with mechanisms for data sharing and operational coordination to ensure no significant harm is caused to downstream countries Egypt and Sudan.

The dispute dates back to 2011 when Ethiopia began constructing the GERD on the Blue Nile to generate electricity and boost domestic development.

Cairo emphasizes that it does not oppose Ethiopia’s right to development and power generation, but demands a legally binding agreement detailing filling and operation rules to safeguard its water security.

Addis Ababa maintains its right to utilize its water resources for national development.

Sewilam further noted that addressing the Nile issue should not be limited solely to the dispute with Ethiopia.

He highlighted that the Nile Basin includes 11 nations, and that Egypt’s relations with other basin countries have seen significant progress during President Sisi’s tenure.

Nile Basin Cooperative Framework Agreement

Sewilam addressed the Nile Basin Cooperative Framework Agreement (known as the Entebbe Agreement), stating that all basin countries except one agreed to reopen and discuss the agreement, asserting that solutions are attainable if political will and sincere intentions are present.

The Entebbe Agreement stems from regional efforts to create a new legal framework for cooperation and benefit-sharing among basin states.

Controversy remains over Egypt and Sudan’s position on certain provisions—particularly those concerning existing water rights and uses—making comprehensive consensus among basin countries an ongoing challenge.

Sewilam concluded by emphasizing that other Nile Basin countries do not face a water crisis as severe as Egypt’s.

Cairo suffers from acute water scarcity due to limited resources relative to growing needs, relying heavily on the Nile River for its core water security amid rising pressures from population growth, agricultural expansion, and climate change.

World.title: Egypt condemns attack on King Fahd Airport in Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Egypt strongly condemned the Wednesday evening attack on the King Fahd Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia.

In an official statement published on its Facebook page, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated: “The Arab Republic of Egypt expresses its strongest condemnation and denunciation of the attack that targeted King Fahd Airport in the city of Dammam in the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The attack resulted in two civilian casualties and several injuries, in a continued violation of international law and a indiscriminate, irresponsible targeting of air navigation, facilities, and civilians.”

“Egypt stresses its absolute rejection of such practices that inflame the crisis, escalate tension, and destabilize the region. Egypt reaffirms its full solidarity and stand alongside the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its leadership in defending its territory and citizens, as the Kingdom’s security is an integral part of Arab and Egyptian national security,” the statement added.

Death toll at 2, 8 injured

The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) announced on Thursday that the death toll from the attack rose to two following a confirmed additional fatality, while the number of injured remains at eight people.

According to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA), quoting the authority’s statement: “Further to the statement issued by the General Authority of Civil Aviation regarding the brutal attack that targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday evening, Jumada Al-Awwal 10, 1448 AH (corresponding to October 21, 2026); the Authority reports that the death toll from the attack has risen to two following a confirmed additional fatality.”

The authority stated that the deceased were a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident.

The list of injured includes a Saudi citizen, two Indian residents, two Yemeni residents, two Bangladeshi residents, and a Nepalese resident.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Egypt to see falling temperatures and heavier autumn rains
World.content:
Meteorological authorities have issued a warning regarding weather conditions during late-night and early-morning hours, as lower minimum temperatures are expected across all regions, alongside winds that will heighten the coldness.

Authorities advised taking a jacket when going out during this time of the year —especially for the elderly and children— in order to prevent catching colds.

El Niño strikes Egypt

According to meteorologists, Egypt is currently being affected this year by the El Niño phenomenon, which impacts countries surrounding oceans, particularly the central and eastern areas of the Pacific Ocean, leading to altered weather patterns.

El Niño leads to a rise in global average temperatures, and the overall warming of the Earth contributes to increased climate shifts.

Meteorologists forecast that the phenomenon’s impact will intensify during November and December, causing a clear climatic shift during the autumn season.

They explained that Egypt is among the countries indirectly affected by this phenomenon, noting that the Meteorological Authority announced autumn rainfall rates this year will be higher than average due to rising sea surface temperatures in the Mediterranean Sea and the impact of climate change.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court Reserves Ruling in Kolubah–House Leadership Dispute
World.content:
Massaquoi Cites Civil Procedure Law in Challenging Service of Court Order

MONROVIA — The Supreme Court of Liberia has reserved ruling in a contentious legal dispute involving expelled Montserrado County District #10 Representative Yekeh Kolubah and the leadership of the House of Representatives, leaving unresolved questions about the service of court orders, compliance with judicial directives, and the limits of legislative authority.

By Victoria G. Wesseh



At the center of the dispute is whether the House leadership was properly served with a Supreme Court order directing it to suspend further action pending the outcome of proceedings before the Court.

During arguments, Cllr. Jonathan Massaquoi, head of the petitioners’ legal team, challenged claims that the Court’s precept had not been properly served. He argued that Liberia’s Civil Procedure Law, rather than the legislature’s internal administrative procedures, provides the relevant legal framework for determining the validity of service.

The dispute places before the Supreme Court a fundamental question: whether the House leadership proceeded with the contested action despite an effective judicial directive intended to preserve the status quo.

Massaquoi Invokes Civil Procedure Law

In advancing his argument, Massaquoi cited Section 3.38 of Liberia’s Civil Procedure Law, particularly subsection (9), which addresses service upon a government subdivision subject to suit or a municipal corporation.

The provision states:

“Personal service upon a subdivision of the government subject to suit or upon a municipal corporation shall be made by reading and delivering the summons to the chief executive thereof.”

The provision appears in Title 1, Chapter 3, of the Civil Procedure Law, which governs the commencement of civil actions and service of process.

“Read the Civil Procedure Law” (https://www.lla.gov.lr/index.php/downloadable-resources/policies-laws-regulations-repository?download=41%3Acivil-procedure-law).

Relying on this provision, Massaquoi argued that the validity of service should be assessed under the applicable statutory framework rather than determined solely by the House of Representatives’ internal rules for receiving and processing official communications.

His argument focused on the delivery of the Court’s precept to the office of the Speaker of the House of Representatives. The petitioners maintained that the Speaker was the appropriate official through whom the relevant court process could be received.

However, whether Section 3.38(9) directly applies to the House of Representatives and the specific process involved in this case remains a question for the Supreme Court to resolve. The provision expressly refers to a government subdivision subject to suit or a municipal corporation, and its application to the legislature cannot be presumed.

Dispute Centers on Service and Marshal’s Return

The proceedings also examined the role of the Supreme Court Marshal in serving the precept.

According to the arguments presented during the hearing, a court officer identified as Joshua B. was assigned to deliver the document to the Speaker’s office. The petitioners maintained that the document was received there, with a receptionist reportedly acknowledging receipt and signing for a copy.

Massaquoi argued that the legal effect of the service should be determined by the applicable law and the circumstances documented by the court officer, rather than solely by the House’s internal procedures for handling official correspondence.

The issue is consequential because the validity of service could determine whether the House leadership was legally placed on notice of the Court’s directive and whether its subsequent actions amounted to noncompliance.

The Supreme Court will have to consider the terms of the precept, the Marshal’s return, the reported acknowledgment of receipt, and the legal status of the office or official that received the document.

World.title: Liberia: Samuel Jackson Begs Court for Medical Leave Amid Health Concerns
World.content:
Jackson (center), who is seeking court permission to travel abroad for medical treatment, remains barred from leaving Liberia. He was seen being assisted by two men at the courthouse.

Monrovia – Liberian economist Samuel Jackson has appealed to Criminal Court “A” Judge, Onesimus Barwon, to grant him medical leave to travel abroad for specialized medical treatment amid concerns about his deteriorating health.

By Victoria G Wesseh

On Thursday, October 22, 2026, Jackson was seen struggling to walk on the grounds of the Temple of Justice in Monrovia, reportedly due to his poor health condition.



Jackson is seeking permission to travel abroad for medical attention but is currently barred from leaving the country.

The economist is also facing charges in connection with the death of his wife, who was found dead in their bedroom in March 2026.

The case remains a significant legal matter, with Jackson seeking medical relief as his legal proceedings continue.

It can be re-called that Mr. Jackson told authorities he found his wife semi-conscious in their bedroom after returning home.

South African attorney Ntombi Khumalo Jackson has been found dead in her home in Monrovia, Liberia, and her husband, economist and political commentator Samuel Jackson, has been detained as a suspect.

Samuel Jackson told authorities he found his wife semi-conscious in their bedroom after returning home from a television talk show engagement.

Ntombi Khumalo Jackson, a Gauteng-born attorney and founder of NK Attorneys, has died in Liberia.

The case has drawn widespread attention after graphic images allegedly showing Khumalo Jackson bruised and battered circulated on social media.

Khumalo Jackson died after suffering severe head injuries that required emergency brain surgery.

World.title: Gonet Academy Taps Youth Minister Kruah to Challenge Graduates on Skills, Innovation and Service
World.content:
Her “Paradigm Shift” agenda offers a framework for connecting professional training with entrepreneurship, employment and national development.

Youth and Sports Minister Atty. Cornelia Wonkerleh Kruah

Gonet Academy has named Youth and Sports Minister Atty. Cornelia Wonkerleh Kruah as keynote speaker for its Cohort 15 graduation, bringing the government’s youth empowerment agenda into an event focused on professional development, leadership and practical skills.



The ceremony is scheduled for Saturday, October 31, 2026, at 10 a.m. at Harvest Intercontinental Cathedral in Congo Town, Monrovia.

Kruah’s selection comes as Liberia continues to confront the challenge of translating its youthful population into a productive workforce through skills development, entrepreneurship and employment opportunities.

The upcoming occasion, for Gonet Academy, reinforces a central principle of professional training that emphasizes that education must extend beyond certificates to equip graduates with the competence, discipline and leadership capacity to contribute meaningfully to their workplaces and communities.

The minister’s “Paradigm Shift” approach to youth development similarly emphasizes moving beyond short-term interventions toward programs that provide practical support, build capacity and deliver measurable results.

The significance of her appearance, however, will ultimately depend on the substance of her message and whether the occasion encourages stronger connections between training institutions, government and employment opportunities.

Gonet Academy Chief Empowerment Officer (CEO), Mohamed Kerkulah, welcomed Minister Kruah’s acceptance to serve as keynote speaker.

Kerkulah said the minister’s acceptance underscores the importance of recognizing efforts to develop professional skills and build the capacity of young Liberians.

“We are deeply honored and grateful to Minister Cornelia Kruah, for graciously accepting our invitation,” he said, adding that the Academy looks forward to welcoming the minister and benefiting from her perspectives on “youth empowerment, leadership, innovation, and national development.”

Minister Kruah has emphasized the need to strengthen youth development through institutional reform, technical and vocational education, entrepreneurship, sports and the creative economy. She has also outlined plans for youth resource centers across the 15 counties and greater use of data to inform policy and programming.

Her approach recognizes that providing assistance is only the first step; beneficiaries also need the skills, guidance and follow-up required to turn opportunities into lasting progress.

At the launch of a small-scale grant initiative for market vendors under the National Youth Pathway Program, Kruah said the government wanted to move beyond providing grants without sustained follow-up.

“We want to shift the paradigm that government grants are simply given and forgotten,” she said.

The initiative announced plans to support 2,000 vendors across all 15 counties, with training in financial literacy, customer service, business management and record-keeping.

The government’s National Cadet Program has also expanded, with reported participation increasing from 235 cadets in the first cohort to 1,100 in the second. Its coverage grew from eight counties to all 15, while the service period increased from three to six months.

These initiatives reflect an emphasis on linking youth interventions with practical experience, accountability and broader access to opportunities. Their long-term impact will depend on implementation, sustained support and evidence of improved outcomes for participants.

Gonet Academy’s professional development model complements this agenda by seeking to equip learners with industry-relevant skills, workplace competence and leadership abilities.

The transition from training to employment or entrepreneurship, however, often requires more than technical knowledge. Graduates may also need mentorship, professional networks, workplace exposure and access to financing or business support.

Training institutions can help prepare young people for these demands, while government agencies and private-sector employers can help create pathways through internships, recruitment, enterprise development and other opportunities.

Neither side can achieve this alone. Training providers must remain responsive to workplace needs, while public policy must support an environment in which acquired skills can translate into productive work and economic participation.

Kruah’s keynote therefore offers an opportunity to connect the achievements of Gonet Academy’s graduating professionals with the wider national conversation about employment, entrepreneurship and youth development.

The country’s youth challenge is not simply demographic; it is also about whether young people can access the education, skills and institutional support needed to participate meaningfully in the economy.

The 2022 Liberia Population and Housing Census thematic report on children, adolescents and youth highlights the importance of understanding young people’s circumstances and development needs. Persistent concerns about unemployment, underemployment and vulnerable work further underscore the need to connect education with practical opportunities.

Kerkulah emphasized that academy’s graduation ceremonies represent more than the awarding of certificates and diplomas, noting that each graduating cohort reflects months of commitment, sacrifice, learning and personal growth.

“Every graduation at Gonet Academy represents more than the awarding of professional certificates and diplomas. It represents months of dedication, sacrifice, learning, and personal transformation,” he said.

He described October 31 as an opportunity to celebrate Cohort 15’s accomplishments while reminding graduates that the real value of education lies in how they apply their knowledge and skills beyond the classroom.

“For Cohort 15, October 31 will be a celebration of professional achievement and a reminder that the true value of education lies not merely in the qualifications we acquire, but in how effectively we apply our knowledge and skills to solve problems, create opportunities, and contribute to society,” Kerkulah stated.

His remarks reflect the Academy’s emphasis on practical learning and the application of professional competencies to workplace challenges, entrepreneurship and community development.

The CEO also stressed that the country’s development depends on deliberate investment in its people, particularly its young population.

“Liberia’s greatest resource is its people, particularly its young population. However, potential alone does not guarantee progress,” Kerkula said.

He called for sustained investment in relevant skills, mentorship, practical experience and entrepreneurship to help young people become productive contributors to the economy.

The next test, for Cohort 15 graduates, will be how effectively they apply their training in workplaces, businesses, public institutions and their communities.

Kruah’s public agenda could reinforce that responsibility by challenging graduates to remain adaptable, demonstrate integrity, solve practical problems and use their professional capabilities to create value for others.

Her selection should not, by itself, be interpreted as evidence of a formal partnership between Gonet Academy and the Ministry of Youth and Sports. Any such collaboration would require deliberate engagement, defined priorities and measurable commitments.

Nevertheless, the graduation provides a platform for exploring how professional training can complement national youth development efforts.

The challenge, for Gonet Academy, is to ensure its graduates translate their qualifications into professional growth and meaningful contributions to society. For the government, the task is to turn youth empowerment priorities into accessible programs and demonstrable results.

As Cohort 15 prepares to graduate on October 31, the shared message is clear that certificates are milestones, but the greater measure of success lies in the skills graduates apply, the opportunities they create and the contributions they make to Liberia’s development.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court Hears Kolubah’s Appeal Against Expulsion Today; Five Other Cases on Docket
World.content:
Monrovia – The full bench of the Supreme Court of Liberia is scheduled to hear arguments today, Thursday, October 22, 2026, in former Montserrado County District #10 Representative Yekeh Y. Kolubah’s appeal against his expulsion from the House of Representatives. The case is one of six on the Court’s 5th Day’s Session assignment for the October Term.

Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay, Sr. and Associate Justices Jamesetta H. Wolokolie, Yussif D. Kaba, Ceaineh D. Clinton Johnson and Boakai N. Kanneh were listed to sit for the 11:00 a.m. session. The assignment was signed by the Clerk of the Supreme Court, Cllr. Sam Mamulu.

Kolubah vs. the House



Kolubah’s case, listed as an appeal from a ruling on a Bill of Information, names the House of Representatives, Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, Deputy Speaker Thomas Fallah, the Chief Clerk and the Sergeant-at-Arms as appellees.

The dispute dates to April. The expulsion process began on April 9, 2026, when Kolubah was accused of gross misconduct, violating his oath of office, repeatedly breaching House rules and damaging the Legislature’s reputation. The House said he violated its rules and undermined Liberia’s national interest through comments on the Liberia-Guinea border dispute.

Justice Kaba, then presiding in Chambers, granted Kolubah’s petition for a writ of prohibition on April 16, 2026, summoning the House leadership to a conference on April 20 and ordering a stay of all further proceedings. The House went ahead anyway. The expulsion was supported by 49 lawmakers who signed a resolution from the Committee on Rules, Order and Administration, but the House Clerk’s Office said it had not received any Supreme Court communication to stop the proceedings.

On May 20, Justice Kaba ruled against Kolubah. He held that the House was not properly served with the writ and stay order, noting that under House procedure only the Sergeant-at-Arms is authorized to accept court documents, and that because the House was not lawfully served it could not be held in contempt. Court records showed the Supreme Court’s Marshal had served the papers on a receptionist and a computer operator in the offices of the Speaker and the Chief Clerk. Kolubah’s lawyer, Cllr. Jonathan Massaquoi, said they had appealed to the full bench.

It is not Kolubah’s first clash with his colleagues in court. In 2021, he twice took the House to the Supreme Court over suspensions, and then-Justice Joseph Nagbe reversed one of those suspensions.

Srimex vs. Eco Fuel

Also on the docket is a Bill of Information filed by Srimex Oil and Gas Company, through its Chairman Musa Hassan Bility and CEO Wadei H. Powell, against Civil Law Court Judge Nelson B. Chineh, Eco Fuel Trading of Geneva, Switzerland, and Srimex Eco Fuel FZE, Inc.

The two companies have fought in court for years. In November 2018, Srimex sued the National Port Authority, LPRC and Eco Fuel at the Civil Law Court seeking a declaratory judgment, and obtained an injunction barring Eco Fuel from the Petroleum Storage Terminal. Eco Fuel claimed it invested about US$25 million to build the terminal, which it accused Srimex of hijacking, and argued Srimex had transferred its NPA lease to Eco Fuel through a novation agreement. Eco Fuel separately filed a debt action against Srimex at the Commercial Court in 2018 over unpaid oil products.

Land and labor cases

The Intestate Estate of Daniel Webster Urey, through administrators Edwin M. Urey and Evan Urey, has filed a Bill of Information against the Intestate Estate of Karboyah of Tartee Town, Careysburg District. The Supreme Court earlier upheld a trial court ruling in favor of the Karboyah Estate, relying on a survey showing the estate’s deed predates the Ureys’ and that the Urey claim of 1,337.4 acres far exceeded what their deeds specified.

Edwin Urey, the Careysburg City Mayor, has accused the courts of bias and said the land has belonged to his family for over a century.

ABC Children’s Aid Liberia, Inc. returns to court in a Bill of Information and Appeal in an ejectment action against Augustine Moore, Aruna Bangura, James F. Kolangbanyan and others of Gbengbah’s Town on the RIA Highway. The Court previously ordered the eviction of more than 100 occupants who built about 70 homes on the organization’s 72.76 acres, purchased in 2005 and 2006 from the administrators of the town.

In a labor matter, Ministry of Labor Hearing Officer H. Nyeswa Davis, Sr. and Kou Dolo are seeking to dismiss an appeal by the management of RLJ Kendeja Resort and Villas, through Managing Director Raderick John Peck. The hotel has previously faced accusations of bad labor practices, with more than 300 staff made redundant after management moved from an American to a Ghanaian team.

The sixth case is a Bill of Information by Samuel B. Borley against Circuit Judge J. Boima Kontoe and the family of the late David C. Wilson, represented by Rachael Nyemah.

World.title: Liberians in Rwanda Back Push for Direct Kigali–Monrovia Flights
World.content:
LIBCOR leaders meet travel agency, RwandAir representatives

KIGALI, Rwanda – Leaders of the Liberian Community in Rwanda (LIBCOR) have pledged to support an initiative to establish a direct air link between Kigali and Monrovia. They gave the pledge after meeting a Liberian travel agency working on the effort with Rwanda’s national carrier, RwandAir.

The LIBCOR delegation met Tuesday evening with Gbomai Bestman, chief executive officer of Easy Continental Travel Agency, and two senior members of her team. Bestman is in Rwanda on a working visit.



According to a statement from LIBCOR, the talks focused on the agency’s ongoing initiative with RwandAir, its objectives, and what it could mean for Liberians living in Rwanda.

Seleke Kromah, LIBCOR’s Vice Chairman for Administration, led the delegation. Other members of the community’s National Administrative Council attended, including the Vice Chairman for International Affairs, the Financial Secretary and the Treasurer.

The statement said the council took part on the instructions of LIBCOR Chairman James Edgar Denia. Members discussed how the community’s leadership could support the initiative.

Speaking for the delegation, Kromah thanked Bestman for what he called her continued cooperation, partnership and support for Liberians in Rwanda. He said LIBCOR would work with her team to explain the initiative’s goals and benefits to community members.

LIBCOR said it would share details of a planned engagement with the wider Liberian community in Rwanda beginning Thursday.

“LIBCOR remains committed to building meaningful partnerships that promote connectivity, strengthen relationships, and create opportunities for Liberians in Rwanda and back home,” the statement said.

The statement did not say when direct flights might begin, what routes or schedules are being considered, or what role RwandAir has formally committed to.

World.title: Liberia: Final Arguments Set in Peter Bon Jallah Case
World.content:
After months of contested proceedings, prosecution and defense are expected to present their closing arguments as Criminal Court ‘E’ prepares to conclude the trial phase.

By Victoria G. Wesseh

MONROVIA — Criminal Court “E” is scheduled to hear final arguments on Thursday, October 22, in the high-profile case involving Peter Bon Jallah, who is facing multiple felony charges, including gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping.



The case has reached a critical stage following months of evidentiary proceedings in which the prosecution and defense presented witnesses and sought to establish their respective positions.

The closing arguments will give both sides an opportunity to summarize the evidence, address disputed facts and advance their legal interpretations before the court determines the next steps toward a verdict.

Prosecution and Defense Rest Cases

According to court records, the trial has been vigorously contested, with both sides presenting witnesses in support of their respective cases.

The Government of Liberia, represented by prosecutors from the Ministry of Justice, presented 13 general witnesses and six rebuttal witnesses before resting its case.

The defense, representing Jallah, called eight general witnesses and three subpoenaed witnesses to challenge the prosecution’s allegations and advance its position.

The testimony presented by both sides is expected to feature prominently in their closing arguments as they seek to persuade the court on the strength of the evidence and the applicable law.

Trial Reaches Critical Stage

The case is being heard under Liberia’s legal framework governing rape and other serious criminal offenses. The charges against Jallah include gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping, each of which carries significant legal consequences if established in accordance with the law.

The final arguments are an important stage of the proceedings, allowing prosecutors to explain why they believe the evidence supports a conviction and enabling the defense to challenge the prosecution’s case.

Presiding Judge Wesseh A. Wesseh will be responsible for considering the evidence and legal arguments presented before the court.

The outcome will depend on the evidence admitted during the trial and the court’s application of the relevant legal standards.

Public Scrutiny and the Fight Against Sexual Violence

The proceedings come amid continued public concern over sexual and gender-based violence in Liberia and calls from civil society organizations and women’s rights advocates for accountability in cases involving sexual offenses.

The administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has pledged to uphold the rule of law and strengthen protections for vulnerable people, including minors.

The handling of high-profile cases such as the one involving Jallah is likely to draw continued public attention to the justice system’s response to allegations of sexual violence and the importance of ensuring that criminal proceedings are conducted fairly and without undue delay.

As the court prepares to hear the final arguments, the prosecution and defense will have the opportunity to make their closing submissions before the matter advances toward a determination.

The defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court to Hear Final Appeal in Dennis Estate’s 200-Acre Property Case
World.content:
After earlier rulings affirmed the estate’s ownership, the Supreme Court is set to review a fresh appeal challenging lower court judgments over land in Paynesville’s 72nd Community, with the timeliness of the appeal emerging as a key issue.

By Victoria G. Wesseh

MONROVIA — The Supreme Court of Liberia is set to hear arguments in a decades-long dispute over approximately 200 acres of land in Paynesville’s 72nd Community, as it considers an appeal challenging judgments affirming ownership by the Estate of the late Wilmot F. Dennis.



The appeal was filed by Mark Dennis, also known as Mack Dennis, and Henry Dennis, who are challenging lower court rulings in favor of Madam Estella Dennis-Turay, administratrix of her late father’s intestate estate.

The dispute dates back to 1963 and has passed through multiple judicial proceedings, including earlier appeals to the Supreme Court. The latest proceedings could determine whether the challenged lower court judgments will stand, although the outcome remains in the hands of the justices.

A Dispute Dating to 1963

According to court records, the dispute began in 1963 when four children of Wilmot F. Dennis—Estella Dennis-Turay, Sam Ford Dennis, Mabel Dennis Mann and Jeannette Dennis-Pratt—filed an action before the Sixth Judicial Circuit seeking to cancel deeds they alleged had been improperly obtained by distant relatives to properties belonging to their father, who died before 1954.

After 16 years of litigation, the Civil Law Court ruled in 1979 in favor of the siblings, voiding the disputed deeds and ordering the approximately 200-acre property restored to them.

Subsequent disputes involving boundaries and alleged encroachment by adjoining landowners led to two separate appeals before the Supreme Court.

In 1988 and 1989, the Supreme Court affirmed the 1979 judgment, according to the case history presented in the court records.

Those rulings form a central part of the estate’s position in the latest proceedings.

Dispute Resurfaces After Civil War

The dispute resurfaced during the period surrounding Liberia’s civil conflicts, when Dennis-Turay was reportedly outside the country.

According to subsequent court findings, the defendants began asserting ownership claims over the property during her absence.

On August 30, 2005, then-Civil Law Court Judge Emery Paye issued a writ of possession placing the defendants in possession of the land. The estate later challenged the writ, arguing that it had been issued without notice to the parties previously adjudged to be the rightful owners.

In a ruling dated August 26, 2025, Judge George W. Smith of the Civil Law Court revisited the matter. The decision was subsequently reaffirmed by then-presiding Judge Boima Kontoe on February 25, 2026.

According to the rulings described in the court records, the lower court found that the defendants had misrepresented their status in the proceedings that led to the 2005 writ.

The court characterized their conduct as involving alleged deception, fraud, perjury and contempt, and described them as impostors in relation to the ownership claims.

Those findings form part of the judicial history now before the Supreme Court.

Estate Relies on Probate and Earlier Judgments

Probate records cited by the estate indicate that between 2005 and 2012, Dennis-Turay petitioned the Probate Court to administer her late father’s estate.

The records reportedly included original deeds and certified copies of the 1979 Civil Law Court judgment and the Supreme Court’s 1988 and 1989 decisions.

In 2012, Dennis-Turay was reportedly deeded the property as the sole surviving heir. The deed was subsequently probated and registered.

The estate is relying on these records, together with the earlier judgments, to support its position that ownership of the property has already been judicially determined.

The defendants’ latest appeal has nevertheless brought the matter back before the country’s highest court.

Timeliness of Appeal Becomes a Key Issue

Following Judge Kontoe’s February 25, 2026 ruling, the defendants filed a Bill of Exceptions on March 23, 2026, challenging the judgment.

The estate contends that the filing was made outside the statutory deadline and has asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the appeal on procedural grounds.

According to the estate’s filing, the Bill of Exceptions was submitted 28 days after the judgment, rather than within the 10-day period it says the law requires.

On March 31, 2026, the estate filed a motion seeking dismissal of the appeal for untimely filing.

The case record has since been transmitted to the Supreme Court for consideration.

The justices will have to determine the procedural issues raised by the parties and consider any substantive questions properly before them. Whether the appeal can proceed will depend on the court’s assessment of the applicable legal requirements and the arguments presented.

Earlier Supreme Court Rulings at the Center of the Case

The estate’s position rests substantially on the Supreme Court’s 1988 and 1989 decisions affirming the 1979 judgment.

The doctrines of res judicata and stare decisis may be relevant to the dispute. Res judicata generally concerns the finality of matters already adjudicated between parties, while stare decisis addresses the authority of judicial precedents.

However, the application of these doctrines depends on the specific facts, parties, issues and procedural circumstances before the court.

The Supreme Court’s earlier decisions and the subsequent probate proceedings are therefore likely to feature prominently in the estate’s arguments as it seeks to preserve the lower court judgments.

The defendants’ appeal, meanwhile, will give the justices an opportunity to consider the challenges raised against the latest ruling.

For Dennis-Turay and the estate, a dismissal of the appeal or a decision affirming the lower court judgment would reinforce the existing rulings in their favor.

After more than six decades of litigation, the Supreme Court’s determination could mark a significant development in the long-running dispute over the 200-acre property in Paynesville’s 72nd Community.

The final outcome, however, will depend on the court’s ruling.
