World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: Trump won’t betray Britain over the Falklands
World.content:
Trump won’t betray Britain over the Falklands

22nd Thursday, October 2026 - 14:40 UTC Full article

The King’s visit to US in April was a stunning success: even “No Kings” Democrat Members of Congress giving King Charles a series of standing ovations

By Nile Gardiner (*) - In his second term, Donald Trump has aggressively pursued an America First foreign policy. And rightly so. The U.S. president represents the American people, and every policy he advances should be in his nation’s interest. But backing British sovereignty over the Falkland Islands fits firmly within this vision, and his administration should stand shoulder to shoulder with the UK on an issue of huge importance to the British people.

Last month, in response to questions from British media, President Trump declared that the U.S. would review its long-standing policy of neutrality on the Falklands issue. This was immediately seized upon by Argentina’s president Javier Milei, a close ally of Trump, who announced tougher sanctions against foreign companies with plans to drill for oil around the Falkland Islands, as well as a renewed push to end British sovereignty.

The U.S. president has also seemed to equivocate over the question of whether the U.S. would come to Britain’s aid in the event of a future war between London and Buenos Aires. Trump made it clear he was hugely disappointed in the refusal of the British Government to back U.S. military action against Iran.

Trump Will Never Forgive Burnham if the Chagos Deal Is Resurrected Having worked closely with the U.S. administration in opposition to Labor’s disastrous Chagos surrender deal, I have witnessed first-hand the White House’s immense frustration with Britain’s socialist government, which has frequently been at odds with Trump’s team, from the Iran war and Israel to net zero, mass migration and freedom of speech. The Trump administration has been particularly unhappy over Labour dragging its feet on a firm commitment to swiftly increase defence spending in line with Nato commitments made at the Hague summit last year.

This is the tensest relationship that I have seen between London and Washington in nearly a quarter of a century in the D.C. policy world. The reality is that Labour simply isn’t trusted, and the renewed push on Chagos by No 10 under Andy Burnham on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly further underscored this. The British Government has been acting as its own worst enemy.

But I do not believe the Trump presidency will ultimately shift the U.S. position on the Falklands, despite all the stupid actions of the Labour Government. Here’s why.

The Anglo-American special relationship still matters inside the Washington Beltway, in both the executive branch and on Capitol Hill. The King’s visit to the U.S. in April was a stunning success, with even “No Kings” Democrat Members of Congress giving King Charles a series of standing ovations when he spoke to a joint session of Congress.

President Trump’s extremely warm reception for the King at the White House and his speech welcoming the King at the arrival ceremony, which I attended, were a glowing tribute to the enduring strength of our two great nations. The bottom line is that President Trump loves Britain, the British people and his British heritage through his Scottish mother. And like Trump, nearly 60 million Americans have British ancestry according to the 2020 census, including much of America’s political and economic leadership.

How the U.S.-Europe Rift Got Balkanized Throw into the mix the massive levels of trade and investment between the two countries, the vital strategic importance of the U.S./UK base at Diego Garcia, the key role played by RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire (despite the decision to temporarily remove U.S. stealth strategic bombers in the wake of an Iranian terror plot), and the extremely close intelligence ties between the CIA and MI6, and the special relationship remains very real.

Not a single American official I have spoken with in the last few months has told me they support a change in U.S. policy over the Falklands. They understand the huge importance this issue has to the British people, and all of them speak of their admiration for Margaret Thatcher who ordered the liberation of the islands from Argentina following the brutal invasion by its military junta in 1982.

U.S. officials also acknowledge that the Argentine position over the Falklands was viewed sympathetically by the Obama administration when Hillary Clinton was Secretary of State and far-Left Cristina Kirchner was Argentina’s president. Republicans are reluctant to take a stance that Democrats have traditionally favored in Washington, and which would be championed by the American Left.

There remains immense goodwill in the United States towards Great Britain and the British people, and very little desire to throw America’s closest ally under the bus over the Falklands. It is firmly in the U.S. national interest to defend the vital principles of sovereignty and self-determination the American people cherish. This piece originally appeared in The Telegraph.

(*) Nile Gardiner is Director of The Heritage Foundation’s Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom and Bernard and Barbara Lomas Fellow.

World.title: Milei hopes to exploit the Falklands’ oil dispute in next year’s election
World.content:
Milei hopes to exploit the Falklands’ oil dispute in next year’s election

22nd Thursday, October 2026 - 13:35 UTC Full article

By Vicky Kapogianni Associate Professor of International and Environmental Law, University of Reading - Argentina is trying to stop a planned oil project near the Falkland Islands. On October 13, the government asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Seas (Itlos), a court in Hamburg that deals with disputes over the sea, to halt the project. Argentina says the UK approved the drilling without its agreement and in breach of Argentina’s rights to the seabed.

The project, called Sea Lion, is a joint venture between UK and Israeli companies, and has been licensed to produce oil by the Falkland Islands government. The Sea Lion field holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil, 500 million barrels of which is assessed as recoverable.

Argentina began arbitration proceedings against the UK on September 28 and gave London 14 days to stop the project. That deadline expired on October 12. The Argentine government has now called on Itlos to issue “provisional measures” – emergency orders to protect each side’s rights, or prevent serious harm to the marine environment.

The UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has rejected Argentina’s claims, insisting the UK will “vigorously” contest jurisdiction.

Itlos applies the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which governs the sea – not land. Yet rights at sea flow from owning the coast, which means that whoever holds the Falklands holds the seabed – and the oil – around the Islands. Tribunals under the convention have no power to decide who owns land, and can’t settle sovereignty disputes.

Because rights at sea flow from land, every question about the oil in the dispute between Argentina and the UK has been dragged back into a near two-century argument over who owns the Islands.

We proposed settling boundaries, resources and environmental protection on the basis of fairness, as Australia and Timor-Leste agreed in 2018 to share revenue from oil and gas in the Timor Sea.

What Argentina is asking

Argentina’s request asks Itlos to order the UK to prevent Sea Lion from starting production while the arbitration is under way. The Argentine government warns that commencing extraction would create an “irreversible fait accompli”.

To back its argument, Argentina is relying on a 2015 order in a sea-border dispute between Ghana and Ivory Coast. There, the tribunal allowed Ghana’s existing oil operations to continue but banned new drilling. So the question is whether – with Sea Lion’s development due to begin in early 2027 – the project could be halted in the same way.

The tribunal must also accept that the rights at stake are “plausible” – meaning there is a credible legal basis for them, even though the full case has yet to be heard. For Ivory Coast, this was simple. Nobody disputed that both countries had coastlines over which they had sovereignty. The only argument was over where the sea border between them should run.

For Argentina, it is an uphill battle. It insists it is not seeking a ruling on sovereignty, yet its request rests on “sovereign rights” over the continental shelf. It is hard to judge that this is a plausible claim without asking who owns the Islands.

A bridge from Crimea?

In April, a tribunal hearing a dispute between Ukraine and Russian over coastal rights in the Black Sea close to the occupied Ukrainian province of Crimea found that Russia had breached the convention over the Kerch Strait bridge, which connects Russia with Crimea along with associated power cables and gas pipelines. Ukraine had brought the case in 2016, two years after Russia annexed Crimea, accusing it of usurping Ukraine’s rights in the surrounding waters – from drilling rigs to shipping lanes – and seeking compensation.

The tribunal found that Russia’s environmental assessments were inadequate and unpublished, and that it failed to cooperate in protecting the marine environment.

How could the tribunal say all this without deciding who owns Crimea? Because duties such as assessing environmental impact apply to activities under a state’s “jurisdiction or control”. What mattered was that Russia controlled the bridge, cables and gas pipelines. Who owns Crimea could be left for another day.

Could the same reasoning apply to Sea Lion? The UK answers for the Islands internationally, and the convention requires states to ensure that activities under their jurisdiction or control do not cause pollution damage to other states. Argentina’s request cites a spill contingency plan by Premier Oil, Sea Lion’s former operator, which put the chance that oil from a blowout would cross into Argentine waters after 30 days at 30%. A tribunal could, without having to determine who owns the oil, consider whether the UK has assessed and shared such risks.

Should Argentina keep its hopes up?

The tribunal relating to Crimea held that the award was “appropriate declaratory relief”. This meant its formal, binding finding that Russia had broken the law was the sole remedy. Russia was not ordered to change its conduct or pay reparation for its environmental breaches.

So what are Argentina’s chances of success if it pursues an argument about the project’s environmental risk? Real, but the victory, if it comes, may not stop Sea Lion going ahead, and it won’t determine Argentina’s ownership of the Falkland Islands.

Even an interim order requiring the UK to assess and share the project’s environmental risks with Argentina would represent a win of sorts.

And with an election next year in which the incumbent president, Javier Milei, is struggling, and given how strongly most Argentines feel about the issued, even a modest win could help the president.

Any order for Argentina and the UK to cooperate would bring London and Buenos Aires back to the same table over Sea Lion. A conversation about shared risks could be the first step towards sharing the resources.

World.title: A partial win in Hamburg could help Milei in 2027, an analysis suggests
World.content:
A partial win in Hamburg could help Milei in 2027, an analysis suggests

22nd Thursday, October 2026 - 02:24 UTC Full article

The tribunal will hold its hearing on November 10 and 11

Argentina has slim chances of persuading the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to halt the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands by invoking its sovereign rights, but it could secure a partial victory on environmental grounds that would help President Javier Milei ahead of the 2027 election, according to an analysis by an international law academic published on The Conversation.

The author notes that rights at sea derive from sovereignty over the coast and that tribunals under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea cannot decide who owns territory. To prescribe provisional measures, the tribunal must consider the rights invoked “plausible”. Argentina says it is not seeking a ruling on sovereignty, but its request rests on its “sovereign rights” over the continental shelf, which is hard to assess without asking who owns the islands, the author argues. For that reason, the precedent Argentina cites — the 2015 order barring new drilling by Ghana in waters disputed with Ivory Coast — is not comparable: there, nobody disputed sovereignty over the coasts, only where the maritime border should run.

The more promising route, according to the analysis, is environmental. In April, an arbitral tribunal found that Russia had breached the Convention over the Kerch Strait bridge by inadequately assessing its environmental impact, without ruling on sovereignty over Crimea, because such duties apply to activities under a state’s “jurisdiction or control”. The same reasoning could apply to Sea Lion: Argentina’s request cites a contingency plan by the project’s former operator, Premier Oil, that put at 30% the chance of a spill reaching Argentine waters within 30 days.

Even so, the author warns that in the Crimea case the tribunal limited itself to declaring the breach, without ordering Russia to change its conduct or make reparation. An Argentine victory “may not stop Sea Lion going ahead” or resolve sovereignty, but even an order requiring the UK to assess and share environmental risks would be “a win of sorts” that, given how strongly Argentines feel about the issue, could help Milei. And an order to cooperate would bring the two countries back to the same table, the author adds.

The tribunal will hold its hearing on November 10 and 11. The United Kingdom has said it will take part and challenge any attempt to use the proceedings to settle sovereignty.

World.title: Global alert over two critical PHP flaws forces government websites offline
World.content:
Global alert over two critical PHP flaws forces government websites offline

22nd Thursday, October 2026 - 02:14 UTC Full article

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, carry a severity score of 9.2 out of 10 and affect all PHP installations serving web requests

Governments and companies in several countries temporarily took websites offline this week over two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers much of the internet, which allow an attacker to run code remotely on servers without authenticating. PHP’s development team released fixes on Wednesday and urged users to update immediately.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, carry a severity score of 9.2 out of 10 and affect all PHP installations serving web requests, including platforms such as WordPress, Drupal and Joomla. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has dubbed them “php2shell”. The fixes are available in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35.

The European Union’s computer emergency response team advised organisations unable to patch immediately to isolate exposed applications from the internet. According to its latest advisory, proofs of concept are already circulating publicly, raising the likelihood that the flaws are being exploited. Security firms report attack attempts, so far without confirmed success. The US National Security Agency (NSA) urged organisations to prepare to update, and CISA and the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre called for patches to be applied as soon as possible.

As a precaution, the Netherlands took offline portals including the DigiD digital identity system and parliamentary websites; Finland, several public services; and France, its prefecture websites, according to the specialist press. Sites were also taken down in Denmark and Australia, and on major platforms in Japan, whose Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged checks on public websites using PHP and preparation to apply the fix.

World.title: Milei says Argentina will pursue the Falklands diplomatically: “We do not believe in military solutions”
World.content:
Milei says Argentina will pursue the Falklands diplomatically: “We do not believe in military solutions”

22nd Thursday, October 2026 - 00:07 UTC Full article

At the same event, Milei defended his alliance with the United States and Israel

Argentine President Javier Milei said in Madrid on Wednesday that he is confident of recovering the Falklands through diplomacy and repeated three times that his government “does not believe in military solutions”, amid an escalating dispute with the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project.

“The Malvinas are Argentine. In fact, Spain had bought them and when we took over the territory they became ours. The original population was Argentine and was expelled by the English,” he said at a breakfast organised by the Nueva Economía Forum. “We will keep negotiating until they return the islands, because we are the legitimate owners,” he added. Milei also said that “the geopolitical and demographic problems” the United Kingdom is facing represent “a risk for the region”, without specifying what he meant.

The United Kingdom maintains that the islands are British and that their inhabitants have the right to decide their own future. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

The remarks come less than three weeks before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea holds hearings in Hamburg on November 10 and 11 on Argentina’s request to halt Sea Lion. London has said it will take part in the proceedings and has approved measures to protect its companies from Argentine sanctions, while the sovereignty bill promoted by Milei, which toughens those sanctions, remains stalled in the Chamber of Deputies.

At the same event, Milei defended his alliance with the United States and Israel while championing trade with China: “The United States trades with China. So why can’t we trade too?”

World.title: Paraguay’s president travels to Washington and will meet the CIA director
World.content:
Paraguay’s president travels to Washington and will meet the CIA director

21st Wednesday, October 2026 - 19:14 UTC Full article

Peña has declared himself an ally of the White House on foreign policy

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña travelled to Washington on Wednesday for a brief visit that includes a meeting with US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) Director John Ratcliffe and a keynote address at the annual gala of the Inter-American Dialogue think tank.

Peña will be away until Friday, accompanied by Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez and the head of the presidential Civil Cabinet, Javier Giménez, according to the Senate. The president confirmed he will be “meeting the CIA director”, without giving further details. He will also take up an invitation from George Washington University, and the Inter-American Dialogue gala will be held at the headquarters of the Organization of American States.

Before leaving, Peña accompanied US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in the Alto Paraná department on the final day of his official visit to Paraguay. The two toured a new military unit created to fight terrorism and organised crime in the Triple Frontier area with Brazil and Argentina, and the binational Itaipú dam. Landau is now continuing his tour in Buenos Aires.

Peña has declared himself an ally of the White House on foreign policy. In January he signed in Davos, together with Argentine President Javier Milei, the founding charter of the Board of Peace promoted by Donald Trump to oversee the Gaza peace plan, and Paraguay is a member of the Shield of the Americas, the regional security alliance promoted by Washington.

World.title: An unusual die-off of southern right whales in Argentine Patagonia alarms scientists
World.content:
An unusual die-off of southern right whales in Argentine Patagonia alarms scientists

21st Wednesday, October 2026 - 14:44 UTC Full article

Neither researchers nor the provincial government will give an official figure until the season ends; unofficially, more than 300 dead whales are being mentioned

Scientists monitoring the southern right whale population at Península Valdés, in Argentina’s Chubut province, have recorded since July an unusual number of deaths among calves and adults which, they expect, could make this the worst year on record. They are investigating the role of a bacterium and of a toxic algal bloom known as “red tide”.

Neither researchers nor the provincial government will give an official figure until the season ends; unofficially, more than 300 dead whales are being mentioned. Until now, the highest figures recorded by the health monitoring programme run by the Whale Conservation Institute since 2003 were 113 dead calves in 2012 and 28 adults in 2022.

In calves, the deaths have been linked to the bacterium Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, which causes erysipelas and can enter through wounds, such as gull bites, or through feeding, explained Mariano Coscarella of the Centre for the Study of Marine Systems at the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (Conicet). In adults, the cause is still under study, although red tide, which caused the 2022 peak, is suspected. According to Coscarella, no evidence has been found that direct human activity caused the deaths, although climate change or El Niño may have influenced ocean conditions.

The health monitoring programme, led by veterinarian Marcela Uhart of the University of California, Davis, is carrying out necropsies and analyses and will add sampling of water and shellfish in the Nuevo and San José gulfs.

Península Valdés is South America’s largest sanctuary for southern right whales. The population visiting it grew from about 500 whales in the late 1990s to a peak of 2,110 in 2025; this year 1,375 were recorded, including 409 calves. The Whale Conservation Institute warned that, as this is a long-lived species, the consequences of a die-off “are not immediate and cannot be measured from isolated figures”.

World.title: Milei calls Sánchez an “unpresentable dictator” in Madrid in the middle of Spain’s election campaign
World.content:
Milei calls Sánchez an “unpresentable dictator” in Madrid in the middle of Spain’s election campaign

21st Wednesday, October 2026 - 14:31 UTC Full article

Milei explained why he has not met Sánchez on any of his seven visits to Spain as head of state: “I’m not going to see a criminal thief like Pedro Sánchez”

Argentine President Javier Milei on Wednesday called Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez an “unpresentable dictator”, “corrupt” and “authoritarian”, and urged Spaniards to “kick the socialists out” of power, at his first public event in Madrid, just over a month before the snap general election on November 29.

At a breakfast organised by the Nueva Economía Forum, Milei explained why he has not met Sánchez on any of his seven visits to Spain as head of state: “I’m not going to see a criminal thief like Pedro Sánchez because I’m not willing to have to sew my pockets shut so I don’t get robbed.” He added: “Wherever there is an enemy of freedom, I will go and confront him.” Of Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso, whom he will meet in the afternoon, and Vox leader Santiago Abascal, he said they “have healthy and positive ideas to lift Spain out of decline”.

The Socialist Party greeted him with a banner on the façade of its headquarters: “Hello Milei, we lefties welcome you to Spain, the fastest-growing country in Europe.” Sánchez released a video in which he says “I am a leftie”, in a reference to the term Milei uses to insult his left-wing opponents. In May 2024, Spain withdrew its ambassador from Buenos Aires after remarks by Milei about Sánchez’s wife.

The Argentine president linked his trip to his campaign for re-election in 2027. “If we are re-elected, the following four years will be unforgettable,” he said, inviting Spaniards to invest and settle in Argentina, which he said would become “the promised land where good business flows”. He also called the Argentine newspaper Clarín “corrupt” and its journalists “serial liars”.

Milei attributed not being received by King Felipe VI to scheduling problems. According to Royal Household sources quoted by El País, a meeting with the monarch must necessarily be accompanied by one with the prime minister. The Argentine president did not say whether he will attend the Ibero-American Summit, to be held in Madrid on November 4 and 5.

World.title: Baja man takes his blender to the CFE offices and uses their electricity as a protest
World.content:
A man who said he’d been without electricity for three weeks despite paying his bill staged a personal protest this week — taking a blender to a Federal Electricity Commission office and preparing salsa right there in the hallway.

The man, identified as a resident of La Paz, the state capital of Baja California Sur, also threatened to bring his washing machine to the office the next day and do his laundry there if the federally owned utility (CFE) did not promptly restore service.

“They’re good at cutting off the power,” he said, “but when it comes to turning it back on …”

The man, whose name was not reported, said he had submitted proof of payment and filed complaints without getting his electricity restored. Media reports did not identify his community or establish why his service had been interrupted.

“I don’t want to bother anyone,” said the man, a taco vendor according to some reports. “Listen, there’s just two things I don’t have: I have no shame and I have no electricity.”

A similar protest occurred recently in the neighboring state of Baja California. On Oct. 6, residents of Tijuana took spoiled food to a CFE office and left it inside the customer service area after reporting three to five days without electricity, El Mexicano reported.

Some said they had repeatedly called CFE, only to be told when they visited the office that there was no record of their complaints, the newspaper added.

The blender incident in La Paz — observed by bemused customers and CFE employees — was circulating Tuesday on social media, but there was no followup on whether he returned with the washing machine.

The one-man protest followed at least two recent outages in the La Paz municipality, which had about 292,200 residents in the 2020 census.

On Oct. 13, a substation-related failure cut electricity to more than 13,120 customers in communities including El Triunfo, San Antonio, Los Planes and El Sargento, the news website Peninsular Digital reported. It followed a previous outage that reportedly lasted five days.

The outages followed Hurricane Polo’s passage through Baja California Sur in late September, but reports did not establish whether storm damage caused the substation failure. Local officials had reported no damage in the municipality.

In any regard, electrical problems in La Paz predate any recent storm. There are multiple reports over the years of documented interruptions lasting from several hours to multiple days.

In August, for example, residents issued a manifesto demanding action from CFE, the federal government and Congress after repeated outages, some exceeding 24 hours, Radio Fórmula reported. They also complained about voltage fluctuations and interruptions during hot weather.

As for the unnamed Man With the Blender, reports did not establish if his loss of power was connected to any particular outage. No official CFE explanation or expected reconnection date was reported, and whether his electricity has been restored remains unclear.

With reports from Milenio, El Debate, El Imparcial, El Sudcaliforniano and Peninsular.Digital

World.title: Sheinbaum: 59 million liters seized in Guanajuato fuel bust were not stolen
World.content:
The confiscation of 59 million liters of allegedly stolen fuel from a storage terminal in the state of Guanajuato last month was initially described by federal authorities as the largest single-site seizure in Mexico’s history.

But the seized fuel was not in fact huachicol (stolen or illegally imported fuel), President Claudia Sheinbaum said Wednesday, confirming suspicions that emerged shortly after the so-called megadecomiso (mega-bust) was announced.

Las indagatorias para combatir a redes delictivas vinculadas al contrabando de combustible llevaron a la #FGR a cumplimentar diversas órdenes de cateo que derivaron en el hallazgo de más de 59 millones de litros de hidrocarburo en #Guanajuato, de los cuales no se ha acreditado su origen. La FGR continúa las investigaciones tendientes a acreditar la posible comisión de delitos previstos en la Ley Federal para Prevenir y Sancionar los Delitos Cometidos en Materia de Hidrocarburos, así como los diversos previstos en el Código Fiscal de la Federación, en caso de que no se acredite la propiedad y trazabilidad de la totalidad del hidrocarburo localizado. Más información ▶️ https://t.co/ZiONwhxM56 — FGR México (@FGRMexico) September 18, 2026

Asked at her morning press conference whether the seized fuel was huachicol or not, Sheinbaum gave an unequivocal response — “No.”

She said the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) had conducted an investigation, and told reporters that “the knowledge we have is that … there were some illegal matters” related to the entry of tanker trucks to the fuel storage terminal, located in the municipality of San José Iturbide.

“The company resolved that issue,” Sheinbaum said, referring to Grupo SIMSA, the owner of the storage facility.

“… In general, the entire facility was a facility that had its permits. There was an illegal action, but the company resolved it,” she said.

Sheinbaum said the FGR would report on the findings of its investigation. As of Thursday morning, it hadn’t done so.

On Sept. 17 — the date the fuel bust was first announced — Grupo SIMSA issued a statement declaring its storage terminal was operating legally and was duly registered with state, local and federal authorities.

Acknowledging the legitimacy of the documents, the FGR quietly modified its proceedings, shifting the terms of the case from a seizure to an embargo while it investigated the source and traceability of the 59 million liters of fuel in question.

The FGR’s delegate in Guanajuato, Juan Francisco Vera, was fired after irregularities were detected in the fuel-seizure operation and is currently under investigation.

The operation to seize the fuel — carried out two weeks before the confiscation was announced — was triggered after a July 3 arrest involving a tanker truck loaded with allegedly stolen fuel. On the day of the operation, state and federal agents seized 10 tanks containing fuel, three tanker trucks, containers used to transport fuel, and documentation.

However, no arrests were ever made in connection with the case.

The federal government has made significant progress in the fight against fuel theft and a fuel smuggling/tax evasion scheme known as huachicol fiscal. More than 2,500 people have been detained on fuel theft or fuel smuggling charges since Sheinbaum took office in October 2024, and the president declared in August that her administration had “practically” put an end to huachicol fiscal.

Despite authorities’ initial claims, the seizure of 59 million liters of fuel in Guanajuato — a state known as a fuel theft hotspot — cannot be counted among the government’s successes in combating fuel-related crime, based on Sheinbaum’s remarks on Wednesday.

With reports from Reforma, El Universal and El País

World.title: Quintana Roo’s inland region of Maya Ka’an ranks in National Geographic’s top 25 world travel destinations
World.content:
Maya Ka’an in Quintana Roo has been included in National Geographic’s “Best of the World 2027” selection, which features 25 destinations across six continents recommended for travel in the coming year.

The recognition goes beyond the state’s well-known coastal resorts to spotlight a region south of the Riviera Maya that offers more than beautiful beaches and archaeological sites.

The publication highlights the presence of 78 indigenous Maya communities and their deep connection to the jungles, lagoons and the rest of the natural landscape, as well as to the traditions of the region.

“In a place often defined by mass tourism, Maya Ka’an unites wilderness and living Indigenous culture,” National Geographic said.

What stands out about Maya Ka’an is its community-based tourism, the publication said, offering a way to explore the region through activities involving its local residents. The magazine highlights encounters with Maya families, shared meals, and tours that link the landscape with the local knowledge.

Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez Zamora said the international recognition reflects the value of a model promoted by the Mexican government — one designed to extend the benefits of tourism to more communities across the country, strengthen local economies, and preserve Mexico’s biocultural wealth.

“Maya Ka’an demonstrates that it is possible to offer authentic experiences, conserve our natural and cultural heritage, and create opportunities for families,” she noted. “We want this model to be strengthened and expanded to more regions of the country, because tourism should translate into well-being and shared prosperity.”

Activities recommended by the travel magazine include embroidery workshops in X-Pichil, explorations of traditional cuisine in Señor, and cultural activities in Tihosuco and Chunhuhub, offering travelers a way to engage with Maya culture through its contemporary practices, as well as its historical heritage.

Also mentioned are kayaking in the turquoise waters of the Muyil lagoon, snorkeling and a marine safari to spot dolphins and sea turtles.

Accessing this once secluded region is now easier through upgraded roads and connections from the Maya Train to the international gateways of Cancún and Tulum.

With reports from Hoja de Ruta Digital

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: How common are Indigenous languages in your state?
World.content:
Mexico is one of the world’s most biodiverse countries, hosting more than 10% of the world’s known species on just 1.5% of the planet’s territory, as Mexico News Daily reported in August.

There is also ample linguistic diversity in Mexico, a country with 68 surviving Indigenous languages, according to the national statistics agency INEGI.

Which of those Indigenous languages have the highest numbers of speakers? Which states have the highest proportion of speakers of Indigenous languages among their residents?

You’ll find the answers to both those questions in this “Mexico in Numbers” article, whose data is derived from INEGI’s report on the results of the 2025 Intercensal Survey.

Mexico’s most-spoken Indigenous languages

The 10 Indigenous languages listed below have the highest number of speakers in Mexico.

INEGI counted speakers of these languages age three and above. The area or areas of Mexico where each language is mainly spoken appears in parentheses.

Náhuatl (central and eastern Mexico): 1,628,286 speakers

Yucatec Maya (the Yucatán Peninsula): 778,898 speakers

Tzeltal (Chiapas) 663,799 speakers

Tsotzil (Chiapas): 596,814 speakers

Mixtec (Oaxaca, Guerrero, Puebla): 505,599 speakers

Zapotec (Oaxaca, Veracruz): 464,481 speakers

Ch’ol (Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche): 298,885 speakers

Otomi (central Mexico): 288,875 speakers

Totonac (Veracruz, Puebla): 251,654 speakers

Mazatec (Oaxaca, Puebla, Veracruz): 234,243 speakers

All told, there were 7.42 million Indigenous language speakers in Mexico in 2025, according to INEGI. That figure accounts for 5.9% of the national population age three and over.

About nine in 10 Indigenous language speakers also speak Spanish, according to the results of the 2020 census.

In 2025, speakers of the 10 most-spoken Indigenous languages accounted for 77% of all Indigenous language speakers in Mexico. Speakers of the five most-spoken Indigenous languages accounted for 56.2% of all Indigenous language speakers in Mexico.

Almost 22% of all Indigenous language speakers speak Náhuatl, the language spoken by the Mexica inhabitants of Tenochtitlán.

Chiapas and Oaxaca have the highest proportion of Indigenous language speakers

According to the 2025 Intercensal Survey results, 29% of residents of both Chiapas and Oaxaca speak an Indigenous language.

Yucatán, where 21.4% of residents speak an Indigenous language, was the only other state with a share above 20%.

Rounding out the top ten states with the highest shares of speakers of Indigenous languages were:

Guerrero: 15.4%

Hidalgo: 11.2%

Quintana Roo: 11%

Campeche: 9.8%

Puebla: 9.2%

Veracruz: 8.3%

San Luis Potosí: 8.3%

Speakers of Indigenous languages accounted for less than 1% of the population in eight states:

Aguascalientes: 0.2%

Coahuila: 0.2%

Guanajuato: 0.2%

Zacatecas: 0.4%

Jalisco: 0.6%

Colima: 0.7%

Sinaloa: 0.8%

Tamaulipas: 0.9%

More than 24 million people in Mexico consider themselves Indigenous

According to INEGI’s Intercensal Survey result, just over 24.2 million people in Mexico consider themselves Indigenous. That number represents 18.6% of Mexico’s total population in 2025, which was just over 130.9 million.

Among people age three and over who consider themselves Indigenous, 29.5% speak an Indigenous language, according to INEGI.

“The remainder identified as Indigenous based on their identity, cultural belonging, history, or traditions, even though they did not speak any Indigenous language,” INEGI said.

In its 2025 Intercensal Survey report, the statistics agency also said that 2.1 million people in Mexico consider themselves afromexicanos (Afro-Mexicans) or afrodescendientes (people of African descent). That number accounted for 1.6% of Mexico’s total population in 2025.

Among Afro-Mexicans age three and above, 8.7% speak an Indigenous language, according to INEGI.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: MND Local CDMX: World-class coffee, cool jazz and kids’ workshops
World.content:
Mexico City finally seems to be inching its way out of the rainy season, which means fall is upon us and winter’s right around the corner. Lucky for us, neither should be particularly frigid.

From a world-class coffee showdown to an open-air jazz festival and a creative workshop for the little ones, there’s plenty to look forward to in the weeks ahead. Here’s what’s brewing, swinging and sparking imaginations around the capital.

Let’s get into it.

The battle for the world’s best coffee is brewing in CDMX

Two weeks ago, we filled you in on a craft beer festival slated to take place Oct. 23 and 24, as well as the Mexico City Food and Wine Festival, scheduled for Nov. 7 and 8. Now, it’s the coffee connoisseurs’ turn.

The 2026 World AeroPress Championship will take over Frontón Bucareli in Mexico City’s Colonia Centro from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Sunday, Dec. 6. It’s the culmination of a year-long series that saw roughly 8,000 people competing in more than 230 events across nearly 70 countries.

On Dec. 6, however, a panel of judges will finally determine who can brew the best cup of coffee using a rather rudimentary piece of equipment, the humble AeroPress.

Throughout the day, there will not only be several heats to crown the world champion, but also live demonstrations, hands-on workshops, DJs, local food and more. There’s also a Roasters Village featuring 13 “hand-selected roasters pouring coffees you won’t find anywhere else,” according to the organizers, and competing for the coveted attendees’ choice award.

Now in its 18th year, the World AeroPress Championships began with three people in Oslo, Norway, in 2008. It has since become the world’s largest coffee-making championship, drawing tens of thousands of spectators in-person and online throughout the year. This is the first time the championship is being held in Mexico City.

Date: Sunday, Dec. 6, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Location: Bucareli 118, Colonia Centro, Cuauhtémoc, 06000

Cost: 350 pesos

For more information and to purchase tickets, visit the World AeroPress Championship website.

Polanco swings into winter with a jazzy double bill

What better way to usher in the winter season — at least with Mexico City’s relatively temperate year-round weather — than with a cozy outdoor jazz festival? Polanco Jazz Festival returns to Lincoln Park’s Ángela Peralta Theater Dec. 5 and 6 for its 13th year and 22nd edition.

Day one of the event will feature Mexico’s Luis MTZ Jazz Project, followed by Louise Phelan Blues Band, hailing all the way from Ireland. It’s anyone’s guess where the headliner comes from, but its billing — Extravaganza The Show — is more than enough to pique our interest.

Meanwhile, day two includes Erik Deutsch Band, who are making the trip down from the States, and two more acts out of Mexico, Polanco Jazz Quintet Starring Sunset and Hector Infanzón Trio.

Ángela Peralta Theater is described as “the only theater where the sunset is part of the show,” making for a unique celestial backdrop to your sonic explorations.

Date: Dec. 5 and 6, 4 p.m. to 8 p.m.

Location: Aristóteles s/n, Polanco, Polanco IV Secc, Miguel Hidalgo, 11560

Aristóteles s/n, Polanco, Polanco IV Secc, Miguel Hidalgo, 11560 Cost: Single-day tickets range from 550 pesos to 1,200 pesos. Two-day passes start at 940 pesos.

For more information, visit Polanco Jazz Festival’s official website or head over to Boletia to purchase tickets.

Playtime with a purpose: Imagining a better world together

Unless you have a particularly precocious child, chances are you’re feeling a bit left out with these events. Well, fear not — we’ve got all of our lovely families covered as well.

Colegio de San Ildefonso is hosting a creative laboratory experience dubbed “Un Mundo,” or “One World,” throughout November and into early December.

According to the organizers, children are invited to “imagine and collectively build a place where anything is possible,” using cardboard, fabric and other art materials. Workshop themes include imagining new ways of living and caring for one another.

To be honest, we think some of our adult readers, not to mention our own staff, could benefit from imagining new worlds too. But we digress …

“Un Mundo is a laboratory for play, imagination, and shared, collective creation, where they will discover that other worlds can also be built together,” the organizers state.

The workshops are split into two age groups — noon to 1 p.m. for children ages 3 months to 3 years, and 1 p.m. to 2 p.m. for children ages 4 to 10. Likewise, the organizers note that the event is suitable for children with disabilities and neurodivergence. However, we cannot guarantee bilingual staff will be available.

Date: Nov. 8, Nov. 22 and Dec. 8, noon to 2 p.m. (depending on your child’s age)

Location: Colegio de San Ildefonso, Room 11, Justo Sierra 16, Historic Center, 06020

Cost: Free, but registration is required.

For more information and to register your kid(s), visit Cultura UNAM’s website or email acsiedu@gmail.com.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Lawmakers approve hotly contested bill targeting unauthorized use of official logos
World.content:
After a nearly 10-hour floor debate, the Chamber of Deputies — Mexico’s lower house — approved on Wednesday legislation aimed at digital deception, but roundly criticized as a threat to free speech.

The bill — which had already won passage in the Senate on Sept. 30 — was approved on a 281-83 vote, but only after 177 objections were voiced by 64 different speakers, several of whom expressed concern that the reform could be used to silence political dissent.

Once signed into law by the president, who sponsored the bill, the reform will allow the penalization of the unauthorized, commercial misuse of elements — such as logos or symbols — that officially identify public institutions. Penalties include hefty fines reaching millions of pesos and prison sentences of one to five years.

Opposition lawmakers have referred to the legislation as an “anti-meme bill,” arguing that its scope and language allow for punishing criticism that takes the form of parody and internet memes featuring official symbols.

There was lengthy debate over Article 403 bis, which sanctions anyone who “uses, reproduces, imitates or incorporates — on a commercial scale — the institutional graphic identity, electronic domains or official documents of any public institution … with the intention of inducing error or deception to commit an illegal act based on official origin.”

Critics fear its vague wording — and the ambiguity surrounding the concepts of deception and intent — could be weaponized to censor parody, editorial cartoons and online criticism.

They also worry that internet providers and digital platforms — which will now be required to remove or suspend content upon receiving infringement or identity-misuse claims — will err on the side of caution by deleting controversial posts rather than risk steep fines ranging from 80,000 (US $4,300) to 4 million pesos (US $214,000).

Supporters of the reform argue that memes, satire and criticism are not being targeted. Rather, they insist, the legislation strictly targets commercial piracy, digital fraud and the malicious impersonation of state institutions using artificial intelligence.

Morena party Deputy Elena Edith Segura pointed to the phrase “on a commercial scale” — i.e., “to obtain profits,” she said — as sufficient clarification that the intended target is piracy.

National Action Party Deputy Luis Agustín Rodríguez disagreed, asking how “commercial scale” would be determined and what “institutional graphic identity” actually means, while also questioning the meaning of “’intention to commit illegal acts based on official origin.”

“When a person’s freedom is at stake, these answers must be expressly stated in the law,” he said.

With reports from La Jornada, Publimetro, Yucatán Magazine and Wired

World.title: Sheinbaum lauds 8% raise for healthcare workers as protests continue: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🏥🤝 Sheinbaum acknowledges new pay agreement between IMSS and workers’ union : The president said the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) and the National Social Security Workers Union (SNTSS) agreed to an 8% pay increase for IMSS workers. The raise improves on IMSS’s initial offer but falls short of the 10% base pay increase workers wanted. She praised IMSS for negotiating with the union. Hundreds of IMSS workers still protested in Mexico City on Wednesday, but Sheinbaum said the turnout was much lower than at an Oct. 13 demonstration.

: The president said the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) and the National Social Security Workers Union (SNTSS) agreed to an 8% pay increase for IMSS workers. The raise improves on IMSS’s initial offer but falls short of the 10% base pay increase workers wanted. She praised IMSS for negotiating with the union. Hundreds of IMSS workers still protested in Mexico City on Wednesday, but Sheinbaum said the turnout was much lower than at an Oct. 13 demonstration. 🌎 Sheinbaum backs North American economic integration : Sheinbaum said it is “legitimate” for any country, including the United States under Trump’s re-industrialization agenda, to seek to boost domestic manufacturing. However, she said that because the Mexican, U.S. and Canadian economies have become highly integrated since NAFTA took effect in 1994, the three countries should “work as a region” while respecting each other’s sovereignty. Her comments came as Mexico and the U.S. continue talks on trade differences, with both presidents saying this week that a bilateral deal is “very close.”

: Sheinbaum said it is “legitimate” for any country, including the United States under Trump’s re-industrialization agenda, to seek to boost domestic manufacturing. However, she said that because the Mexican, U.S. and Canadian economies have become highly integrated since NAFTA took effect in 1994, the three countries should “work as a region” while respecting each other’s sovereignty. Her comments came as Mexico and the U.S. continue talks on trade differences, with both presidents saying this week that a bilateral deal is “very close.” 🔥🎓 Tamaulipas student wins gold medal for sound-based fire extinguisher: Sheinbaum highlighted that Ángela Karime Venegas Hernández won a gold medal in the technology category at the International Science and Invention Fair in Indonesia. She said the Ministry of Science, Humanities, Technology and Innovation has contacted Venegas to learn more about her “great invention.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

A new pay agreement for Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) workers and North American economic integration were among the significant issues President Sheinbaum addressed at her Thursday morning press conference.

The wage deal didn’t stop hundreds of IMSS healthcare workers from protesting in Mexico City on Wednesday to demand higher pay, better working conditions, increased funding for healthcare and an end to shortages of medicines and medical supplies. Wednesday’s protest followed a larger demonstration in the capital on Oct. 13.

Mexico City health care workers demand higher wages and better conditions

Watch this video on YouTube

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s acknowledgement of an innovation by a Mexican student who won a gold medal at an international science fair in Indonesia.

Sheinbaum acknowledges new pay agreement between IMSS and workers’ union

Sheinbaum noted that IMSS and the National Social Security Workers Union (SNTSS) reached an agreement to give IMSS workers an 8% pay increase. The raise consists of a 4% increase in base pay and a 4% increase in housing assistance.

The 8% increase is an improvement on an initial offer from IMSS, but falls short of the 10% base pay raise workers were seeking.

Eight days after holding protest marches across Mexico, IMSS workers returned to the streets of Mexico City on Wednesday, but Sheibaum said the turnout was much lower.

She praised IMSS for holding talks with the SNTSS and developing an improved pay offer.

“Tell me, in what other country in the world are things resolved like that?” Sheinbaum asked.

“Authoritarianism prevails a lot of the time — ‘No, I already said that pay increase is 2.9% and that’s it,'” she said, mimicking an official who refuses to budge.

Sheinbaum voices support for North American economic integration

Sheinbaum acknowledged that U.S. President Donald Trump has a re-industrialization agenda and told reporters that it is “legitimate” for any country to seek to increase domestic manufacturing production — as Mexico is doing.

However, given that the economies of Mexico, the United States and Canada have become highly integrated since NAFTA took effect in 1994, “we should see ourselves … [and] work as a region” while maintaining respect for sovereignty and autonomy, she said.

“… It’s a lot better to work together in order to compete with other regions [of the world] than to isolate oneself,” Sheinbaum said.

“That has always been our vision and we’ve set it out on various occasions,” she said.

“… [Economic] integration is very important for the three countries and it creates a very competitive region,” Sheinbaum said.

Her remarks came amid ongoing talks between Mexico and the United States. The talks are aimed at resolving trade differences that contributed to the Trump administration’s decision not to extend the USMCA free trade pact until 2042. Both Sheinbaum and Trump said this week that a bilateral deal is “very close.”

The Trump administration has significantly undermined the USMCA by imposing tariffs on various goods from both Mexico and Canada. Mexico’s main aim in its trade talks with the U.S. is to secure a reduction in the tariffs they currently apply to steel, aluminum and vehicles.

Tamaulipas student wins a gold medal for her sound-based fire extinguisher

Early in her press conference, Sheinbaum highlighted that a lot of young Mexicans have won prizes at mathematics and physics olympiads.

She subsequently noted that a teenage girl from Tamaulipas, Ángela Karime Venegas Hernández, won a gold medal at the International Science and Invention Fair, held last week at the University of Indonesia in Depok, near Jakarta.

🥇Con gran orgullo reconocemos a Ángela Karime Hernández Venegas, alumna del #CETIS78 #Altamira al obtener medalla de oro en Competencia Internacional de Ciencia y Tecnología ISIF 2026 en #Indonesia, en la categoría de Tecnología, nivel secundaria, al participar con su prototipo. https://t.co/0sni2iDWlL — SEMSyS Tamaulipas (@VinculacionTam) October 20, 2026

Sheinbaum displayed an article from the news outlet Infobae about Venegas’ win and read out its headline: “Mexican student wins gold medal in Indonesia with her extinguisher that puts out fire using sound waves.”

The 17-year-old student hails from the CETis 78 school in the Gulf of Mexico port city of Altamira. She won her gold medal in the technology category for a “fire suppression system using acoustic waves.”

Sheinbaum said that the Ministry of Science, Humanities, Technology and Innovation contacted Venegas to learn more about her “great invention.”

“She is an example of hundreds and hundreds [of talented young Mexicans],” she said.

Mexico News Daily reported last Thursday that Venegas’ sound-based extinguisher, called Vortex Tech, uses a 12-volt battery, a frequency generator set to 30 hertz, an amplifier and a speaker.

“A modified bucket channels the output toward a flame,” MND reported.

“According to Venegas’ explanation, the sound generates swirling rings of air that disrupt the oxygen supply sustaining combustion, extinguishing small flames within seconds.”

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Mexico and My Money: Investing in Mexico as a foreigner (beyond real estate)
World.content:
In last week’s installment of Mexico and My Money, I wrote about investing in Mexican real estate through the lens of financing a property purchase. But foreigners have many more options for investing extra cash in Mexico, whether it’s to diversify a portfolio or invest funds acquired while living here.

Our recent financial survey found that readers’ top investment in Mexico is real estate, with 85% of respondents saying they had bought property here, either to live in or for other reasons. Besides real estate, MND readers apparently do very little investing in Mexico. About 8% of survey respondents said they have bought stocks or bonds, while roughly 10% said they had invested in a local business.

Below, I’ll look at three investing opportunities for foreign residents in Mexico: CETES, pagarés and stocks.

Earning passive income with Mexican government bonds

Known as CETES, government bonds are one of the simplest, low-risk options expats have to earn passive income while living in Mexico. And who doesn’t need a little extra money these days?

CETES, or Certificados de la Tesorería de la Federación, are Mexican federal treasury certificates and the functional equivalent of U.S. Treasuries. They are auctioned by the Bank of Mexico most Tuesdays and available in various maturities (e.g., one, three, six and 12 months).

Known as “zero coupon” bonds, these securities are sold at a discount, with investors receiving the full face value at maturity, just like a U.S. T-bill. For this reason, you receive no interest payments on CETES until maturity, so holding them for the full term is essential to earn a return.

Yields and requirements for buying CETES

The most obvious benefit of investing in CETES is to help insulate your savings from inflation, which is currently running around 3.5% in Mexico. Besides, CETES are currently leaving U.S. T-bills in the dust on yields.

CETES yields vary based on the holding period, with six-month bonds currently offering 6.79%, while those with a one-month maturity yield 6.25%. In contrast, a six-month T-bill yields about 4.36% and a one-month T-bill yields a little over 4%, which is only slightly above the U.S. 3.7% inflation rate.

While savvy investors know there’s a first time for everything, the Mexican government has never defaulted on interest payments for CETES bonds. Given the stability of Mexico’s economy lately, the odds of a government default on these bonds (especially for short holding periods) are very low.

These bonds can be purchased by Mexican citizens and legal foreign residents, but not by tourists or those living outside Mexico. In addition, foreign residents must meet the following requirements:

Be over 18 years of age.

Show proof of legal residency (e.g., a permanent or temporary residency card).

Have a bank debit card or CLABE number for a Mexican bank account in which the investor is the owner. (Foreign accounts cannot be linked.)

Have a CURP number (found on your residency card) and RFC number (Mexican tax ID).

The Mexican government operates a website to sell CETES directly to the public at cetesdirecto.com. These bonds can also be purchased through Mexican brokers.

Mexican bank promissory notes (pagarés)

Pagarés, short for pagaré con rendimiento liquidable al vencimiento, are a low-risk, term deposit earning a fixed yield.

They work similarly to certificates of deposit in the U.S., where the purchaser lends money to a Mexican bank for a specified period and the bank pays a fixed interest rate upon maturity. Pagarés are funded with cash and fully insured up to the IPAB limit of 400,000 UDIs (3.54 million pesos or about US $193,000) when purchased from regulated banks.

Right now, these investments are yielding anywhere from 3% to 11% annually. Traditional banks like BBVA, Santander and Banamex tend to offer lower yields (3% to 7%), while fintech and digital providers such as Inbursa offer higher yields (8% to 11%).

Key trade-offs of pagaré investments

The primary downside to pagarés is their lack of liquidity. If an investor withdraws funds from a pagaré before it matures — or sells it on the secondary market before maturity — all of the accrued interest is forfeited and the seller incurs a penalty. So, it’s important to commit funds that won’t be needed during the lockup period.

Pagarés are purchased directly from the issuing bank. Unlike CETES, they cannot be bought from brokers. Another key difference between CETES and pagarés is the capital required. Banks typically have a minimum investment of around 5,000 pesos (US $267) for pagarés, while CETES can be purchased for as little as 100 pesos (US $5).

Like CETES, foreigners interested in buying pagarés must hold legal residency in Mexico and maintain a Mexican bank account.

Foreigners can also invest in Mexican stocks

Full confession: I spent six years working as an equity analyst for various investment banks back in the early aughts, so I do not take stock investing lightly.

While some investors may purchase stock after hearing a hot tip from a friend or watching an influencer on TikTok, I don’t endorse it. In contrast to purchasing CETES and pagarés, there is more risk associated with stock investing.

There is no guarantee that your investment will make money, and it’s possible to lose all your principal. For anyone serious about stock investing, due diligence is required.

Stock investing by Mexican households is not common, with an estimated 1% to 5% actively trading stocks. For those who do, one of the best places I’ve found to research Mexican stocks is TradingView Mexico. For market news, another great resource is Mexico Market Chatter from Miranda Intelligence. Mexican brokers such as BBVA, Actinver and Monex also produce equity research for their private clients, as do some foreign brokerage houses.

Navigating Mexican brokerage accounts

Legal foreign residents can trade Mexican stocks through a licensed Mexican brokerage house. Two of the most popular platforms with retail investors today are GBM+ (Grupo Bursátil Mexicano) and Bursanet (by Actinver).

But there are a few unique hurdles for foreign nationals to clear. Chief among them is that foreigners must open a Mexican brokerage account in person rather than online.

When doing so, the following is typically required:

A valid passport.

Proof of legal immigration status (residency card), either temporary or permanent.

CURP and RFC numbers.

Constancia de Situación Fiscal (your official tax status issued by the SAT).

(your official tax status issued by the SAT). Proof of local domicile less than three months old (e.g., a CFE bill).

CLABE number for a Mexican bank account in your name.

If none of these options appeal to you, keep an eye out for my upcoming article examining emerging opportunities across Mexico’s fast-growing fintech sector.

From tipping and working with local contractors to moving money into Mexico from abroad, check out more from MND’s “Mexico and My Money” archive.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.
