World.title: Breaking: Commonwealth makes offer to send Australian of the Year to space
World.content:
The federal government has submitted an offer to the European Space Agency (ESA) to send Australian of the Year Katherine Bennell-Pegg to the International Space Station.

If ESA agrees to Australia's offer, Ms Bennell-Pegg will be required to attend training at the European Space Agency’s astronaut training centre in Cologne, Germany.

"We have submitted a final bid to our friends in the European Space Agency," Science Minister Tim Ayres said on Friday morning.

"We are grateful for the opportunity to apply for this important project. It is an important opportunity. It does require careful fiscal management and making sure that we are balancing the fiscal pressures appropriately."

A spokesperson for the minister said "the government has long held ambition to see an Australian astronaut go to space wearing an Australian flag on their space suit".

"The government has been engaging extensively with the private sector, philanthropists, and other levels of government to raise funding to support a space flight — which is a significant cost," the spokesperson said.

"We are grateful to the philanthropists who have committed over $6 million in cash, plus in-kind support, and some indicative support from some state governments."

South Australia is the only state or territory to have publicly confirmed it would provide financial support to the endeavour.

World.title: Breaking: Amanda Camm to step down as Qld child safety and domestic violence minister
World.content:
Embattled frontbencher Amanda Camm will step down as Queensland's child safety and domestic and family violence minister, the ABC understands.

The Whitsunday MP has faced months of intense scrutiny, including over children in residential care sleeping on the floor of child safety offices, and cuts to the DFV prevention sector in the latest state budget.

The ABC understands Ms Camm's resignation will trigger a mini reshuffle in the Queensland cabinet, the first movement in the frontbench since David Crisafulli came to power in 2024.

The premier will address the media shortly this morning.

Last month, it was revealed the number of Queensland children known to child safety who have died had gone up almost 60 per cent in a year.

It led the opposition to renew calls for Ms Camm to be sacked, labelling the state's child protection system a "crisis".

Minister for Child Safety and the Prevention of Domestic and Family Violence Amanda Camm. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Mr Crisafulli swept to power promising ministerial accountability.

Ms Camm was elected to her Whitsunday seat in 2020, after defeating ousted LNP MP, turned independent, Jason Costigan.

She immediately took up the shadow portfolio for child protection, the prevention of domestic, family and sexual violence and women's economic security before the LNP took power in the 2024 election.

In May this year, Ms Camm was forced to clarify the timeline of her relationship with fellow frontbencher, Tim Mander, after integrity questions arose around whether they had declared their previous relationship when appointed as ministers.

Ms Camm's department is currently engaged in lengthy negotiations with the union representing child safety and youth justice workers.

Bargaining stalled last month, leading to thousands of workers walking off the job for hours.

Amanda Camm has been under scrutiny for months. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The minister has been under scrutiny for months, including after she defied a promise by the premier to provide a progress update during an estimates hearing on the implementation of recommendations from a taskforce set up to combat domestic violence and coercive control.

The Womens Safety and Justice Taskforce made 277 recommendations to the state government across two reports handed down in 2021 and 2022.

World.title: UN sends warning as satellite detects greenhouse gas plumes over Gorgon plant
World.content:
Independent satellite monitoring has detected massive plumes of methane emerging from one of Australia's largest oil and gas complexes.

The persistent clouds above Chevron's Gorgon liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant on Barrow Island off Western Australia's Pilbara coast were picked up by five consecutive passes of the Tanager-1 satellite since November last year.

The most recent, in late August, recorded an average emission rate of about 7.8 tonnes of methane an hour.

That is the equivalent of almost 51 petrol-powered cars driven for one year, or burning more than 110,000 kilograms of coal, calculated using an online tool by the US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA).

Satellite imagery of the alert triggering methane emissions, captured in August. (Supplied: Carbon Mapper)

The repeated detections, the latest far exceeding a "super emitter" event under US EPA guidelines, prompted a United Nations (UN) warning to Chevron.

According to the UN, methane is responsible for about 25 per cent of global warming and is a greenhouse gas 80 times more harmful than carbon dioxide.

Chevron confirmed it had received the alert and was working with the UN Environmental Programme (UNEP) to address it.

However, a UNEP spokesperson told the ABC it had not received formal feedback from Chevron or the Australian government, and would update its publicly available data when it had.

Chevron was similarly notified about methane emissions at Gorgon in July last year.

In a statement, Chevron said satellite monitoring came with "a wide range of uncertainty".

"We are engaging with the UNEP, and we are seeking further clarity on their data," a company spokesperson said.

Non-profit Carbon Mapper operates the satellite as part of UNEP's International Methane Emissions Observatory, of which Australia is listed as a key donor.

The satellites monitor emissions from around the world, with the website showing Chevron's Gorgon project as the highest emitter of methane in WA.

State regulators investigating

Chevron is required to log its emissions through the National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting Scheme, with the numbers published annually.

But ABC enquiries to the National Environmental Protection Agency were referred back to state regulators because methane falls outside Gorgon's federal approval.

The WA government said it was unclear of its role in managing the potential leak.

"The Department of Water and Environmental Regulation is aware of these reports and is investigating them to understand what compliance or regulatory measures may be required," a spokesperson said.

The observations of Chevron's Gorgon project ranged from about 1 to 8 tonnes of methane an hour. (Supplied: Chevron)

Conservation Council WA slammed the lack of action.

"What I would hope is that our levels of government are communicating with each other and checking where the responsibility is," executive director Matthew Roberts said.

"Whatever happens, that is a piece of infrastructure from a private corporation that is profiting off of our resources."

Possible operational issue

The high-volume methane release adds to an already troubled environmental record at Gorgon.

The project's highly touted carbon capture and storage technology has drastically underperformed since operations began in 2016.

Chevron also reported that an unknown amount of gas had seeped into Barrow Island's surface last year.

Chevron did not confirm the cause of the high-volume emissions or whether they had been stopped. (ABC News: Daniel Mercer)

Louis Goddard, head of research at British climate investigative firm Data Desk, said greenhouse gas levels around the facility were "unusual" and consistent, suggesting an operational issue.

"What we're seeing here is a wasting of gas that they've gone to great lengths to extract in the first place," he said.

"[The plumes] are certainly larger than some you would see from individual oil wells and gas wells for one-off incidents."

Mr Goddard and Data Desk pinpointed the emissions as originating from or near Gorgon's acid gas removal units, which strip impurities from natural gas.

Chevron did not respond to specific questions about the cause of the plumes or whether they had been stopped.

Darwin gas leak kept secret from public in 'national scandal' Documents reveal the scale of carbon pollution leaking from a Darwin LNG tank was like adding 8,300 new cars to the road every year. It is about to be filled again.

University of Western Australia chemical engineering program chair Bruce Norris said closer measurements were needed.

He estimated that based on the five satellite observations, a few thousand tonnes of methane could have been leaked over the course of a year.

For comparison, an ABC investigation revealed that a Santos LNG tank at the company's Darwin plant had leaked an average of 832 tonnes every year for more than a decade.

"Any one event is generally not extremely significant, but in aggregate, it's more about how all the different companies and how the government are coming together to try and make these measurements," Dr Norris said.

World.title: 'Pink man' fights for better cancer care in regions
World.content:
Harold Alford, fondly nicknamed the "pink man", is a local legend in Queensland's Kilcoy.

The "true gentleman" is known for his pink Akubra, pink clothes, pink gumboots, pink lawn bowls, pink scooter, and even a pink walking frame.

Cancer has touched the 85-year-old in almost every stage of his life, and his closest loved ones.

Harold Alford has lost his father and wife to cancer. (ABC News: Jessica Ross)

Harold's father died from bone cancer more than 60 years ago.

His daughter has been battling colon and lung cancer for 10 years.

His wife, Gladys Alford, was diagnosed with breast cancer 33 years ago.

She underwent eight years of chemotherapy, multiple operations, and towards the end, 35 consecutive days of radiation.

Harold Alford drove his late wife Gladys to Brisbane hospital for radiation every day. (ABC News: Jessica Ross)

"Every day I drove her to Brisbane for radiation," Harold said.

"They wanted us to stay down there, but she was really old-fashioned, wanted to sleep in her own bed."

Gladys died on their 44th wedding anniversary.

Overcome with grief for his late wife, Harold had an idea that would colour the remainder of his years.

Loading...

Man wears pink to regional pub

"I started wearing pink because I wanted to get the message out there about breast cancer," Harold said.

"And at that time, pink was the colour for breast cancer."

He donned the stereotypically feminine colour to play bowls, to his local golf club, and even at his local watering hole.

Kilcoy is a regional town in Queensland, just over 100 kilometres from Brisbane. (ABC News: Jessica Ross)

"I got called all sorts of names when I first started wearing pink," Harold said.

"When I explained to them why, they changed their attitude."

Two decades ago, it was uncommon for everyday Australians to speak freely about cancer, Harold said.

"Not only that it was a secret, but it was a sort of more or less a taboo subject," Harold said.

"But when I started to turn up in pink, there was a lot of talk about cancer."

Michelle Blogg says everyone in Kilcoy knows Harold. (ABC News: Jessica Ross)

Michelle Blogg, the Pink Up Kilcoy president, met Harold 10 years ago.

"I thought, 'Who's this guy? Why is he wearing pink all the time?' And then I learned the story about his lovely wife," she said.

"He's such a character in the community and he's one of nature's true gentlemen as well. He's just an amazing guy."

'Get out there and live'

Harold was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in December last year.

He was given 12 months to live and has opted out of chemotherapy or any other cancer treatment.

Harold Alford loves lawn bowls and fundraising for better cancer care. (ABC News: Jessica Ross)

"I couldn't see myself making myself sick for three weeks every month. I'm not that sort of person," Harold said.

"I just like to get out there and live."

Regional town turns pink

He has dedicated his later years to raising awareness of cancer and fundraising for further research, care, and treatment options.

What started as one man's mission has united the town of Kilcoy.

Harold Alford is known around Kilcoy for his pink get-up. (ABC News: Jessica Ross)

Through Pink Up Kilcoy, they have raised about $30,000 for cancer care nurses through the McGrath Foundation.

"When you've got cancer, you need help," Harold said.

"I'm trying to get people to think about it, see if they can do something to raise money to any way they can help to get a cure for cancer."

Nearly every Aussie touched by cancer

McGrath Foundation ambassador and director, Tracey Bevan, said nearly one in two Australians were likely to be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime.

"That's 450 people every single day," she said.

Ms Bevan said Harold's mission epitomised what the foundation stood for.

"Wearing pink every single day is so beautiful. But not only that, he's there showing his support and raising funds for other families who've had a cancer diagnosis," she said.

Tracey Bevan says Harold is making a real difference. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

McGrath Foundation cancer care nurses provide free care, without referrals, to those in need.

"They make a difference clinically, physiologically, emotionally. They're there for the patient, not just the patient but their whole family," she said.

Harold said he regularly came across people affected by cancer in some way.

"It has become more or less an everyday subject, cancer, all sorts of cancer," he said.

"I'll keep wearing it [pink] for as long as I can. And anything I can do to support McGrath, anybody that's raising money for cancer, I will support as long as I can."

Harold Alford rides his pink scooter around Kilcoy. (ABC News: Jessica Ross)

'Too late for me'

Harold said he would not stop fighting for better cancer care across regional Australia.

"We need people who can care for people in their homes without them having to drive for hundreds of kilometres," he said.

"People out in the west, they got no facilities out there for cancer.

"It's going to be too late for me, I know that, but I will do everything in my power while I'm alive to help to get cancer care nurses."

World.title: Magnitude-7 earthquake hits China's Tibet region, killing 16 people
World.content:
A magnitude-7 earthquake has struck China's south-western region of Tibet, killing 16 people and injuring 32 others, state news agency Xinhua has reported.

Citing Nagqu City's emergency management bureau, Xinhua reported the earthquake struck about 10:33pm Thursday, local time.

As of 2:25am on Friday, 11 of the injured were in serious condition while 21 sustained minor injuries, Xinhua reported.

At least 339 homes collapsed, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials.

The quake is the strongest to hit China since January 2024.

The epicentre was in a sparsely populated, high-altitude county in Nagqu, northern Tibet, at a shallow depth of 10 kilometres.

The average elevation within 5km of the epicentre is about 4,864 metres, China Earthquake Networks Center (CENC) data showed.

Videos released by local officially run media showed people leaving their homes and seeking shelter outside or in their cars parked on the street.

One resident reported being woken by the strong quake and hearing the house squeaking in the tremor.

The quake was clearly felt in the local area, CENC said. The epicentre was about 400km from the Tibetan capital of Lhasa.

As search and rescue efforts continued, police and emergency crews were building tents to house people displaced by the quake.

CENC data showed that a string of smaller tremors of about magnitude 3 and 4 were recorded in surrounding regions afterwards.

Earthquakes in China are relatively common.

In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in an earthquake in Tibet's rural Tingri county.

In 2010, a magnitude-7.1 tremor struck Yushu, in the Qinghai province, killing at least 2,698 people and leaving nearly 300 people missing.

Reuters/AP/AFP

World.title: Awkward questions linger as creaky Australia receives South African hiding
World.content:
That Australia slowly folded and lost the Gqeberha Test by an innings and 31 runs late on day five was hardly surprising in light of its batting calamities of 24 hours earlier. That Kagiso Rabada and Marco Jansen ran through the tail to finish things off even less so.

But it remains startling to consider the reversal of fortunes this quite disastrous loss represented for Australia. On day two, they were 1-0 up in the series, had South Africa on the ropes at 5-97, on a greenish pitch, and fancied a rout of their own.

Bavuma hides from Smith catch as Boland outdoes batters in loss Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha. Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test.

Instead, in a game that lost 145 overs to rain and associated delays, the annihilation took place in reverse and a series some considered Australia's stepping stone to more difficult engagements ahead is now set for an enticing decider. For Australia, the task ahead is now daunting on multiple levels — not just to find form and the right combination of players to defeat an ascendant and cohesive opponent, but how to do so in Cape Town, with all the extra heat that will entail.

First the few positives. Travis Head, whose role as opener will continue to be endlessly scrutinised, laboured unselfishly for five hours to make 121. Nightwatchman Scott Boland, who was Australia's best all-round performer of the game, absorbed 187 deliveries for his rearguard 40.

Scott Boland's vigil at the crease on day five was one of the few positives for Australia. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

The negatives? Australia's next-best batsman was Mother Nature, who wiped out the first session of play and briefly raised hopes that Australia would force a draw. It didn't, for neither did Boland's patient hand inspire his better credentialed batting partners to hang around and save the day.

It is pointless to analyse the tail. Most culpable this time was Steve Smith, who in his short and strange stay at the crease was given a reprieve by Proteas keeper Ryan Rickelton but failed to make South Africa pay, falling soon after to an objectionably unserious dismissal in a game that was, from Australia's perspective, a little too full of them.

Australia was 5-219 at the time of this pivot point, not entirely written off. Rabada had just taken the second new ball. Boland, batting steadily, had just driven him to the long-off boundary with a beautifully straight bat. Smith? Convention be damned. Rabada sent down a length ball on a fourth-stump line. Smith, for reasons known only to him, decided he should launch over the fence at deep mid-wicket. Instead he skied it and Matthew Breetzke juggled a catch. Therein lay the death of the contest.

Steve Smith's nightmare shot in the second session opened the door to a South African win. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Much has been made of Marnus Labuschagne's battle against morality, but Smith is now a fairly pressing problem too. For a long time, he has been Australia's Mr Dependable — not simply a better batsmen than younger alternatives, but an undroppable ornament, encouraged to play how he likes, to bat where he wants and indulge his obsessions however he sees fit.

Yet that greatness is suddenly fading fast, the numbers dwindling, Smith's insularity intensifying into less pardonable distractions. It is hard to shake the feeling that he and Labuschagne's overall effect on Australia's flaky batting group is a net negative on a psychological level as much as a statistical one.

A subtle but remarkable insight into this dynamic — ignored at the time — was glimpsed during the Bangladesh series in August, when Cameron Green used a post-match interview to explain the genesis of his own breakthrough first Test century on home soil.

South Africa has the momentum going into the final Test, something that seemed inconceivable two days into this match. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

"I was able to go back to Shield cricket … kind of a good little reminder about how I want to go about it," Green told ABC Sport at the time. "I think when you're playing in a pretty good Australian Test team, you bat behind some pretty good players in front of you and I think I probably got caught up in how they go about it. So, I think the beautiful thing about going back to state cricket is to remind myself how I want to go about it."

In other words, Australia's most gifted player of the generation to come was admitting that in order to get himself firing as a middle-order batsmen in this Test side, first he had to get himself far away from the influence of his teammates.

Green, of course, will be pushing his case for selection in Cape Town after injury ruled him out of the first two Tests. Should he be declared fit, the Beau Webster dilemma need not be as emotive as Australian coach Andrew McDonald made it in his press conference on day four.

Beau Webster (right) is likely to make way for Cam Green for the series finale, provided Green is fit to play. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

But it is puzzling to consider the reasoning for even selecting Webster in this match, in which he was never likely to bowl many of his seamers in an attack featuring four frontline quicks, was not asked for his off-spin, nor deemed top-six material with the bat.

McDonald was right to say the issue is not as straightforward as armchair selectors would have it. Like Mitch Marsh before him, Webster is clearly a much-loved team man. Over the English summer just gone, Warwickshire teammate Sam Hain spoke with genuine emotion of the mutual respect and pride Webster had created from the minute he arrived. Warwickshire duly won the championship trophy. But Webster's numbers told a less compelling story: 403 runs at 33, 12 wickets at 40. At Test level, same goes.

The most sensible scenario at the top of the order is that Nic Maddinson, a walking wicket against Rabada, will drop out and Matt Renshaw slide up. Cooper Connolly, who at ODI level recently justified the hype around him, must surely be in line to enter a team crying out for fresh blood.

Australia selector George Bailey's refusal to infuse the Test side with youth is providing diminishing results. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Looking beyond this result and this series, one wonders whether Australian cricket can find a clarity of purpose and be as ruthless as it needs to be to avoid toppling over a cliff when Smith, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon are finally gone.

On that note, here is a quote to consider, from Australia's chairman of selectors: "Part of our charter is obviously to provide for the future," he said. "We are very aware that some of these blokes are getting on in age, and that's why it's very, very important for them to continue to perform."

Unfortunately, that was not George Bailey referring to this current Australian team, average age 34, which in Durban was the oldest XI since the 1920s and the first in Test history to not feature a single player under the age of 30.

No, it was Trevor Hohns, late in 2000, referring to arguably Australia's greatest combination ever. Its average age? Erm, 30.

Time, perhaps, for a new charter.

World.title: US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in Top Gun and Alien, dies aged 93
World.content:
Emmy award-winning actor Tom Skerritt, known for his roles in TV series Picket Fences and films such as Top Gun and Alien, has died aged 93.

Skerritt died on Wednesday, local time, of natural causes, his family said in a statement.

"While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives," the statement read.

" He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices. "

He was twice nominated for an Emmy, both for Picket Fences in 1993, when he won Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series.

In an interview in 1997 with the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, Skerritt said: "A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man's body.

"I've always loved that. It's a nice compliment. I've been able to walk the line between television and features."

Tom Skerritt (left) poses with David E Kelley and Kathy Baker at the Emmys in 1993. (AP: Douglas C Pizac)

Lifelong friendship with Robert Redford

Skerritt grew up in a middle-class Detroit family, his father a small businessman and his mother a housewife. He had two brothers. A sister died as a child.

He spent four years in the air force, attended Wayne State University and then switched to the University of California, Los Angeles, to study filmmaking, inspired by a viewing of Citizen Kane.

His performance in an LA theatre production of The Rainmaker led to his first film role, a supporting role as a sergeant in the 1962 Korean War film War Hunt.

The scrappy independent film marked the debut of Skerritt, Robert Redford, Sydney Pollack and Francis Ford Coppola.

In describing their friendship, Robert Redford said he had shared values with Tom Skerritt. (Reuters: Lilian Wagdy)

Redford, who died last year, became a lifelong friend of Skerritt.

"There was such a deep connection we made with each other that it matured into a level-headed friendship," Redford told The Seattle Times in 2007.

"His values were close to mine, and he kept his integrity."

Skerritt's roles in Alien and Top Gun

One of Skerritt's most well-known roles came in Alien, in which he played the beleaguered and doomed captain of the ship Nostromo.

He told The Seattle Times that what appealed to him in the script was that the lead actor disappeared and "the woman becomes the hero. I really like that idea".

Following his performance in Alien, he was cast as Tom Cruise's instructor in Top Gun.

"Gentlemen, you are the top 1 per cent of all naval aviators. The elite. The best of the best. We'll make you better," he said in the film.

"This school is about combat. There are no points for second place."

Tom Skerritt playing Commander Mike "Viper" Metcalf in Top Gun. (Photo: CBS via Getty Images)

Skerritt initially dreamed of directing and writing but that was overtaken by a career in front of the camera.

But he managed to direct and star in the 1997 television movie Divided by Hate.

"Things happen," he told The Ottawa Citizen in 1992.

"You get hired for a film and the roles kept coming for me. I kept telling myself that if I stuck with acting it would be a really good training for what the problems are in directing. Then the family came along and I had to support them.

"The years flew by and there was a time when I said I would give up acting and really try to get into directing. But it hasn't worked out that way and I have no regrets."

He is survived by his third wife, Julie Tokashiki, and five children.

ABC/wires

World.title: Mother banned from NDIS support job after children removed from her care
World.content:
An NDIS support worker has failed to overturn a decision banning her from working with children and vulnerable adults after she was found to have had children removed from her care.

The Department of Human Services issued a prohibition notice in December 2025 barring the woman — who had been working as a support care worker for five years — from continuing her work.

The woman referred the matter to the South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT) who last month upheld the decision made by the Department of Human Services.

"During the time she has worked in this area, [the woman] has had no complaints concerning any risk posed to the people with disabilities she worked with," the judgement said.

"[She] told the Tribunal she should be able to work with children, as she was not an unsafe person," it said.

"The work was with people with disabilities, and she provided general support care, including driving her clients and taking them on social outings. She told the Tribunal she is a good support worker and well liked."

The judgement said that, although the woman had previously obtained clearances to work with vulnerable adults, she "poses an unacceptable risk to children, and poses a risk of harm to people with disability".

'Issue of neglect' consistent over 16 years

The judgement said that the "crux" of the Department of Human Services decision "was that over a long period of time there had been themes of significant risk associated with [the woman's] care of her children, and this was relevant to her future work both with children and with people with disabilities".

"All of [her] children ... have been removed from her care," it said.

"The matters of concern addressed in the removal of the children have been raised over a period of some years.

"The issue of neglect remained consistent through the concerns raised with investigations by the department across the years, from 2004 to 2020.

"In respect of the elder children, the concerns were the exposure of the children to ongoing domestic violence, neglect, emotional abuse, and a lack of protective capacity by [their mother].

"Later similar concerns were raised in respect of [her] three younger children, although there was not the same level of concern about domestic violence."

The SACAT judgement said that, although they found the mother "poses an unacceptable risk to children, and poses a risk of harm to people with disability", it does not mean she is "likely to, cause harm to children or people with disability".

World.title: ASX slides lower after Wall Street’s tech tumble; oil highest since May
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slides lower after Wall Street’s tech tumble; oil highest since May Stan Choe Updated October 23, 2026 — 10:10am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Australian sharemarket has opened lower after AI stocks tumbled on Wall Street, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 26.9 points, or 0.3 per cent in early trade. The ASX lost 0.4 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US70.19¢. Wall Street again came under pressure from weakness in AI-related stocks. AP The S&P 500 fell 1.2 per cent for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6 per cent. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the market, where the majority of US stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up less than 0.1 per cent. AI-related stocks on Wall Street have been shaky on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that stock prices simply shot too high in their years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.

Elon Musk Sky’s not the limit: $5 trillion sci-fi deal could bring Musk closer to Mars Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8 per cent. It gave a range for its forecast for profit this quarter whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4 per cent surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the already healthy gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment. Other big tech stocks were unsettled following their own quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7 per cent after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.



Tesla slipped 3.1 per cent after flipping between gains and losses in the morning. It reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast. The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4 per cent. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total value, the chip giant was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 9.6 per cent, though it’s swung between wide gains and losses of roughly 4 per cent within each of the last two days. The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5 per cent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7 per cent. Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.9 per cent to $US111.99 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s at the high end of the $US97 to $US112 range it’s been yo-yoing through in October on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal. In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4 per cent. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds. Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt. Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns have pushed yields in the US bond market to their highest levels in decades, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors. But US yields nevertheless fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.



Related Article Renewables ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.98 per cent from 5.13 per cent late Wednesday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country. That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks. Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.



CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 6.6 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

He was taken to Hornsby Police Station, where he was charged with having sex with a child aged between 14 and 16, sexually touching a child aged between 10 and 16, and inciting a child aged between 10 and 16 to perform a sexual act to them. British actress Judi Dench says her eyesight has deteriorated to the point that she can no longer act on stage or in films.

Dench, 91, has had macular degeneration for more than a decade.

World.content:
Breaking NationalCancer ‘Landmark moment’: Sydney scientist’s world-first cancer breakthrough revealed Rachel Rasker and Kate Aubusson October 23, 2026 — 9:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A world-first mRNA cancer vaccine has dramatically cut the risk of melanoma recurrence and death in a landmark large-scale trial that signals a new era in personalised cancer medicine. The Australian-led Phase 3 trial found that adding a tailor-made cancer vaccine reduced the risk of the recurrence of melanoma or death by 42 per cent, compared with patients who were only given the immunotherapy drug, pembrolizumab (sold as Keytruda). Professor Georgina Long’s trial results have attracted widespread international attention. Tim Bauer Principal investigator, Professor Georgina Long, said she almost fell off her chair when she got the phone call relaying the trial results. “I’m not one prone to exaggeration, but this really is a very, very big leap forward in cancer,” said Long, who pioneered immunotherapy treatments that transformed melanoma from a death sentence to a treatable disease.



“It’s all the clichés: landmark moment, moon landing, first flight – it really is a foundational shift,” she said from her apartment in Lisbon, Portugal, on sabbatical from her medical director role at the Melanoma Institute Australia, affiliated with the University of Sydney. Related Article Explainer

Cancer Why is cancer so hard to cure? Trial participants had all previously undergone surgery to remove their melanoma tumours. All 1137 were given pembrolizumab. Two thirds were also given the personalised mRNA therapeutic vaccine designed to enable their immune system to recognise and destroy their distinct cancer cells, while the remaining patients were given a placebo injection. The trial, funded by Merck and Moderna, found that at two years, 82 per cent of trial patients who received both treatments were alive and melanoma-free, compared with 70 per cent of those who received pembrolizumab alone. Australian mRNA Cancer Vaccine Hub Director Associate Professor Seth Cheetham said the combination of immunotherapy and the personalised cancer vaccine was an “incredible breakthrough” that would help usher in a new era in cancer research and treatment.



“This is the first really large trial that’s shown definitively that this technology works, it reduces the risk of recurrence or spread and results in better outcomes compared to standard of care,” Cheetham said. “This is really the gold standard, and it’s what the entire field’s been waiting on,” he said. Professor Georgina Long and Professor Richard Scolyer were named joint Australians of the Year in 2024. Alex Ellinghausen Before checkpoint immunotherapies such as pembrolizumab, advanced melanoma was largely a death sentence, with most patients surviving less than a year. Today, about half of patients with advanced melanoma are alive and effectively cured, but around half still die from the disease. Long has dedicated her career to the mission of zero deaths from melanoma, and to finding a cure for these treatment-resistant patients. She won Australian of the Year in 2024 with her colleague and friend, the late Professor Richard Scolyer.



The new therapeutic vaccine is not for people who have never had cancer – it’s designed to help protect patients against their melanoma recurring once their tumour has been removed. Pembrolizumab helps the body hunt down cancerous cells, which can evade the immune system by mimicking healthy cells. The vaccine goes a step further, by telling immune cells exactly what the cancer cells look like. The personalisation of the vaccine is critical, Long said. Trial researchers sequenced the genome of each person’s tumour and compared it with their healthy cells to pinpoint the unique combination of mutations on the surface of their cancer cells, called neoantigens. They used this information to create tailor-made vaccines that would teach the immune system how to recognise those neoantigens as a threat to be destroyed.



Related Article Cancer Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize Cheetham said: “It really is the antithesis of a one-size-fits-all approach, which has dominated cancer care for a long time.” “It’s pioneering a new kind of medicine, in which we are looking at each tumour individually and crafting a unique treatment for it,” he said. Manufacturing such a personalised drug will be a logistical challenge, Cheetham said, especially for sick patients who will need timely access. The trial’s interim analysis will be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology on Sunday, ahead of publication in the New England Journal of Medicine.



In August, news of the trial’s success saw Moderna’s shares surge more than 170 per cent in a single trading day. But on Friday, after the trial’s results were leaked by an oncology website ahead of embargo, the company’s shares plunged by more than 25 per cent, in a phenomenon stockbrokers call “buy the rumour, sell the fact”. The vaccine was generally well tolerated in patients. Long said she hoped the findings could also help patients with active advanced melanoma or other cancers, but research is ongoing. Cheetham said melanoma cells were among the most promising targets, due to their abundance of mutations that make them appear quite distinct from healthy cells, whereas other cancers may not be as susceptible. But early trials of mRNA vaccines to treat lung and pancreatic cancers have some researchers optimistic, Cheetham said. Queensland MP Amanda Camm has stepped down as a cabinet frontbencher. The member for Whitsunday held two portfolios in the Crisafulli LNP government, standing as Families, Seniors and Disability Services Minister, and Child Safety and the Prevention of Domestic and Family Violence Minister. Amanda Camm says her decision to step down from cabinet was her decision, and she was not pushed. Brisbane Times / Cameron Atfield Camm said she informed Premier David Crisafulli of her resignation late on Thursday and the decision was “mine and mine alone”. She said the attack on Helen Haines also affected her decision, as did her recovery from recent surgery.





She came under more scrutiny in August amid revelations that statements made during estimates might have been flawed. And in September, reports revealed the group said to have taken up the work of a dumped domestic violence reform oversight office had not given Camm any progress update in the 16 months since it was set up. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli confirmed Camm would step down from cabinet. Brisbane Times / Cameron Atfield Later in the month, child safety workers walked off the job alongside employees from the Department of Youth Justice. While she was resigning from cabinet, Camm said she would continue to serve as the member for Whitsunday.



Crisafulli said Camm came in to a broken system. “I constantly saw her put the concerns of vulnerable women and children above all else,” he said. Related Article LNP Crisafulli under fire over ministers’ extramarital affair The minister was also caught in a public grilling when her undeclared romantic relationship with Sport Minister Tim Mander was brought to light earlier this year. Questions centred on whether the pair had fulfilled their obligations to report any conflicts of interest and adhere to the parliamentary code of conduct.



The extramarital affair was again scrutinised when the Australian Federal Police investigated reports Mander had not been living at his declared address – which had been the home he shared with his wife Gayle, before their marriage ended in April 2025. We’ve collected all the chef, front-of-house and restaurant finalists into one handy cheat-sheet ahead of the Good Food Guide Awards on Monday, October 26.

While there has certainly been an increase in fancy potato scallops and shimmering Korean soups in 2026, the biggest restaurant trend of the past 12 months has been previously bold and ambitious operators dialling back risk. We’ve never seen more steakhouses, sandwich shops or generic Italian joints sweep Sydney. If at first it doesn’t work, flip to pizza.

Osteria Luna in the Sydney CBD. Jennifer Soo

And we get it – restaurants have become ferociously expensive to run, and the cost-of-living crunch is real. Whether you’re a restaurant investor or a diner, no one’s overly keen to roll the dice on untested pitches right now.

But.

At the same time, young talent and veteran restaurateurs continue to open personal, singular venues because having a point of view – telling a story or sharing a history – is still more important than the profit margins on farmed kingfish and steak frites. Great restaurants find a way.

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume accused the prime minister of having a “tenuous” relationship with the truth after he denied suggestions yesterday that his office had compiled a “dirt sheet” on Helen Haines.

“There is no doubt that his office circulated this file that didn’t just list the projects that Helen Haines had requested, they also implied that she had some sort of conflict of interest,” she told Sunrise this morning.

“But the prime minister’s tenuous relationship with the truth is becoming a pattern of behaviour … The fact is, the prime minister has denied that there was any problem with this. Just own it. If he can justify its existence, justify it. If he can’t, he should own it and just apologise. But he seems to be unable to do that.”

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume. Dominic Lorrimer

Appearing alongside Hume on a regular panel was Health Minister Mark Butler, who said he had seen dirt sheets during his time in parliament and that this was certainly not one.

“Dirt sheets tend to sort of imply, you know, scandalous behaviour, and say things that people aren’t willing to say in the parliament,” he said.

“There was a list of the projects that Helen was advocating for in the lead-up to the election, like every lower house member … I just don’t think there’s anything remarkable about that.”

World.title: US and Israel are planning to hit Iran again once elections are over
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war US and Israel are planning to hit Iran again once elections are over Julian E. Barnes , Eric Schmitt , Farnaz Fassihi , Natan Odenheimer and Ronen Bergman October 23, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Washington: The US and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the American midterm elections, according to US officials and other people briefed on the deliberations. As planning for a short but intensive operation progresses, the US and Israeli militaries have stepped up exercises, flying planes over Iraq to practice strike manoeuvres. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss new strikes, US officials said. Iran’s regime remains defiant despite the concerted military action undertaken against it by the US and Israel. AP Photo/Vahid Salemi The targets would be likely to include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Some officials say one more big round of attacks could push Iran’s economy over the brink and force the country to make diplomatic concessions after nearly eight months of conflict. Still, there are reasons to be sceptical that a renewed war would be any more successful than the first phase of intense US-Israeli strikes between February and April. Those rounds of fighting drove up energy prices and inflation around the world, eroded security in the Middle East and severely strained the Pentagon’s supply of missile interceptors.



It is also far from certain President Donald Trump will approve fresh strikes. Repeatedly this year he has vetoed plans for a return to major combat operations, including this month when the US and Israeli militaries were nearly ready to attack. Related Article US midterms Long lines, late nights, adulation: What it’s really like inside Trump’s midterm election rallies All of the officials interviewed for this story spoke on condition of anonymity to candidly discuss military planning. Iranian officials have promised to retaliate this time by expanding their targets beyond commercial ships and energy infrastructure in the region, to data centres and underwater internet cables. They say the fighting will be neither quick nor limited.



While the United States is assembling a massive arsenal that will be fully in place by early November, diplomatic efforts have continued, as US negotiators use the potential return to war as leverage with Iran to make progress on their demands on its nuclear program and control over the Strait of Hormuz. The United States will not have its full complement of military assets – including three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces – in place until early November. So far, however, Iran’s negotiators have been unwilling to make concessions on the nuclear program, insisting on deferring that issue until later in the talks. Some US planners are convinced that an intensive three-day campaign could cause enough economic damage to change the Iranian position. But US officials have frequently predicted Iran’s collapse, and other Western officials noted that Iran’s government has so far weathered the pressures on its economy. “At this point in the war, what is clear is that the conventional military campaign waged to date, and the current punishing economic sanctions and American naval blockade, have not brought the regime back to the negotiating table in a meaningful way,” said Dana Stroul, who served as the Pentagon’s top Middle East policy official in the Biden administration.



Neither Trump nor Netanyahu “has made a compelling case for how more war would change this strategic dilemma in an increasingly unstable and conflict-ridden region,” said Stroul, who is now with the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Israel’s election on Tuesday could complicate the plans. If Netanyahu loses, he will become a caretaker prime minister, and it will be difficult for him to launch a war, experts say. But some analysts believe that Netanyahu could leverage the prospect of an imminent joint US-Israel strike to pressure his rivals into joining a unity government to manage the war, which would extend his hold on power. After Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, Netanyahu formed a unity government that brought some opposition members into a war Cabinet to help make national security decisions. “He could use this to call for a broad emergency government, but he will face deep suspicion from his political rivals,” said Mazal Mualem, an Israeli political commentator and the author of a biography of Netanyahu.



“If Iran attacks, that’s one thing, but initiating an offensive strike would be extremely difficult for him.” Related Article Opinion

US politics When Trump gets a thrashing at the midterms, four words will come back to haunt him Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Officials say there is a small possibility that Trump could decide to begin a campaign this month, but there are many political reasons that he is likely to wait until after the US election – not least his own promise early this month not to strike before the vote. The United States will not have its full complement of military assets – including three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces – in place until early November. The US military prefers to conduct attacks under the cover of night, and there will be increasing hours of darkness over Iran early next month. There are also concerns that the war could spiral into a larger conflict. On Wednesday, the US State Department ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, as the Iran-backed Houthi militia continues to attack sites there.



A White House official said on Wednesday that the administration does not comment on military plans “that may or may not exist.” Trump, the official added, was keeping all options on the table to ensure that Iran cannot acquire nuclear weapons. Some officials say the targeting will avoid refineries and oil infrastructure because Trump is eager to prevent even higher gas prices. The Iranian regime has effectively used its Houthi allies in Yemen to keep the pressure on key US allies in the region. AP Both the US and Israel militaries are drafting plans for operations against Iran’s nuclear program, according to people briefed on the work. That could include an attack on Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried nuclear site that Iranians call Kooh Kolang. Trump said last week that he was considering using a 22,000-pound GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB, against Pickaxe. Officials say Trump is enamoured with the weapon in part because of its nickname, Mother of All Bombs.



But weapons specialists say that the MOAB explodes above ground, producing a wide blast, and would not likely destroy an underground site like Pickaxe, which is composed of granite. Military officials also warn that the bomb must be delivered by a slow-flying MC-130 transport plane that would be vulnerable to Iranian anti-aircraft fire. Israel and the United States came close to striking Iran early this month, but Trump again decided at the last minute to postpone the attack, according to US and Israeli defence officials familiar with the details. The decision came shortly before the operation was to begin, after both militaries had made extensive preparations and placed their air forces on the highest state of alert. The repeated planning efforts followed by Trump’s decisions against new attacks has caused “day-to-day whiplash” among military planners, said one commander, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, as they try to stay poised to carry out whatever military option Trump decides in the coming weeks. Loading In each round of the war so far, Iran’s leadership has become less conciliatory, convinced that the ultimate US and Israeli goal is to topple its government.



Iran’s new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, remains an enigma to US and Israeli intelligence officials. Some officials say he is not as powerful as his father, who was killed early in the war, and that hard-line members of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard make key decisions. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘I’m afraid of civil war’: The voters travelling from Australia to vote against Netanyahu Iranian officials say they are aware of the US war planning and have been developing their own new targets and tactics. Peiman Salehi, a political analyst in Tehran, said that if Pickaxe is attacked, part of Iran’s plans to retaliate would be to strike major oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, including Aramco because that would immediately spike oil and energy prices. “The war has made us understand that the best leverage for pressuring Trump is increasing oil and energy prices because it will hurt the American people,” Salehi said.



Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran’s negotiator General Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, said on social media this week that the idea that the United States would wrap up another round of strikes on Iran within 72 hours was a “fantasy” and that Iran would determine when the war would end. He noted that Trump said in February that the war would last two weeks. “Our attacks will be more fierce, creative and different,” Mohammadi said. “We are determined and confident and strong planning has been put in place.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country. That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks. Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.



CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 6.6 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

Warning: Graphic content A Killara man allegedly raped a 14-year-old boy at a popular north shore reserve in what detectives are treating as a random attack. Alan James Caradus, now aged 70, was arrested on Thursday after heavily armed tactical police raided his Killara home, seizing several electronic devices for forensic examination. Loading The alleged sexual assault occurred after Caradus, then 68, approached the 14-year-old at Echo Point Park by the Roseville Bridge in 2023, allegedly raping the boy and inciting the child to perform a sex act on him.



Detectives do not believe Caradus and boy knew each other, and are working to verify the circumstances leading to the alleged assault. Echo Point Reserve in Roseville. Ku-Ring-Gai Council Investigations began in December 2025, about two years after the alleged assault, leading to the arrest of the Killara man on Thursday. Caradus, wearing a T-shirt and track pants, was led out of his home by detectives, while general duties officers carried devices seized in the raid from the property in brown evidence bags. The man was led into Hornsby Police Station by two officers. NSW Police



He was taken to Hornsby Police Station, where he was charged with having sex with a child aged between 14 and 16, sexually touching a child aged between 10 and 16, and inciting a child aged between 10 and 16 to perform a sexual act to them. Caradus appeared in Hornsby Local Court on Thursday, where his application for bail was refused by Justice Rodney Brender. He will remain behind bars until at least November 4, when he will next appear in court. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. British actress Judi Dench says her eyesight has deteriorated to the point that she can no longer act on stage or in films.

Dench, 91, has had macular degeneration for more than a decade.

Judi Dench says she is no longer able to act due to macular degeneration. AP

“I can’t be on stage, I can’t do a play any more, I can’t do a film any more, I can’t read any more,” she told BBC Radio on Thursday.

“So you’ve got to adjust to all that, and make allowances for it and just get on and don’t think about it too much.”

World.title: ‘Landmark moment’: Sydney scientist’s world-first cancer breakthrough revealed
World.content:
Breaking NationalCancer ‘Landmark moment’: Sydney scientist’s world-first cancer breakthrough revealed Rachel Rasker and Kate Aubusson October 23, 2026 — 9:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A world-first mRNA cancer vaccine has dramatically cut the risk of melanoma recurrence and death in a landmark large-scale trial that signals a new era in personalised cancer medicine. The Australian-led Phase 3 trial found that adding a tailor-made cancer vaccine reduced the risk of the recurrence of melanoma or death by 42 per cent, compared with patients who were only given the immunotherapy drug, pembrolizumab (sold as Keytruda). Professor Georgina Long’s trial results have attracted widespread international attention. Tim Bauer Principal investigator, Professor Georgina Long, said she almost fell off her chair when she got the phone call relaying the trial results. “I’m not one prone to exaggeration, but this really is a very, very big leap forward in cancer,” said Long, who pioneered immunotherapy treatments that transformed melanoma from a death sentence to a treatable disease.



“It’s all the clichés: landmark moment, moon landing, first flight – it really is a foundational shift,” she said from her apartment in Lisbon, Portugal, on sabbatical from her medical director role at the Melanoma Institute Australia, affiliated with the University of Sydney. Related Article Explainer

Cancer Why is cancer so hard to cure? Trial participants had all previously undergone surgery to remove their melanoma tumours. All 1137 were given pembrolizumab. Two thirds were also given the personalised mRNA therapeutic vaccine designed to enable their immune system to recognise and destroy their distinct cancer cells, while the remaining patients were given a placebo injection. The trial, funded by Merck and Moderna, found that at two years, 82 per cent of trial patients who received both treatments were alive and melanoma-free, compared with 70 per cent of those who received pembrolizumab alone. Australian mRNA Cancer Vaccine Hub Director Associate Professor Seth Cheetham said the combination of immunotherapy and the personalised cancer vaccine was an “incredible breakthrough” that would help usher in a new era in cancer research and treatment.



“This is the first really large trial that’s shown definitively that this technology works, it reduces the risk of recurrence or spread and results in better outcomes compared to standard of care,” Cheetham said. “This is really the gold standard, and it’s what the entire field’s been waiting on,” he said. Professor Georgina Long and Professor Richard Scolyer were named joint Australians of the Year in 2024. Alex Ellinghausen Before checkpoint immunotherapies such as pembrolizumab, advanced melanoma was largely a death sentence, with most patients surviving less than a year. Today, about half of patients with advanced melanoma are alive and effectively cured, but around half still die from the disease. Long has dedicated her career to the mission of zero deaths from melanoma, and to finding a cure for these treatment-resistant patients. She won Australian of the Year in 2024 with her colleague and friend, the late Professor Richard Scolyer.



The new therapeutic vaccine is not for people who have never had cancer – it’s designed to help protect patients against their melanoma recurring once their tumour has been removed. Pembrolizumab helps the body hunt down cancerous cells, which can evade the immune system by mimicking healthy cells. The vaccine goes a step further, by telling immune cells exactly what the cancer cells look like. The personalisation of the vaccine is critical, Long said. Trial researchers sequenced the genome of each person’s tumour and compared it with their healthy cells to pinpoint the unique combination of mutations on the surface of their cancer cells, called neoantigens. They used this information to create tailor-made vaccines that would teach the immune system how to recognise those neoantigens as a threat to be destroyed.



Related Article Cancer Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize Cheetham said: “It really is the antithesis of a one-size-fits-all approach, which has dominated cancer care for a long time.” “It’s pioneering a new kind of medicine, in which we are looking at each tumour individually and crafting a unique treatment for it,” he said. Manufacturing such a personalised drug will be a logistical challenge, Cheetham said, especially for sick patients who will need timely access. The trial’s interim analysis will be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology on Sunday, ahead of publication in the New England Journal of Medicine.



In August, news of the trial’s success saw Moderna’s shares surge more than 170 per cent in a single trading day. But on Friday, after the trial’s results were leaked by an oncology website ahead of embargo, the company’s shares plunged by more than 25 per cent, in a phenomenon stockbrokers call “buy the rumour, sell the fact”. The vaccine was generally well tolerated in patients. Long said she hoped the findings could also help patients with active advanced melanoma or other cancers, but research is ongoing. Cheetham said melanoma cells were among the most promising targets, due to their abundance of mutations that make them appear quite distinct from healthy cells, whereas other cancers may not be as susceptible. But early trials of mRNA vaccines to treat lung and pancreatic cancers have some researchers optimistic, Cheetham said. Queensland MP Amanda Camm has stepped down as a cabinet frontbencher. The member for Whitsunday held two portfolios in the Crisafulli LNP government, standing as Families, Seniors and Disability Services Minister, and Child Safety and the Prevention of Domestic and Family Violence Minister. Amanda Camm says her decision to step down from cabinet was her decision, and she was not pushed. Brisbane Times / Cameron Atfield Camm said she informed Premier David Crisafulli of her resignation late on Thursday and the decision was “mine and mine alone”. She said the attack on Helen Haines also affected her decision, as did her recovery from recent surgery.





She came under more scrutiny in August amid revelations that statements made during estimates might have been flawed. And in September, reports revealed the group said to have taken up the work of a dumped domestic violence reform oversight office had not given Camm any progress update in the 16 months since it was set up. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli confirmed Camm would step down from cabinet. Brisbane Times / Cameron Atfield Later in the month, child safety workers walked off the job alongside employees from the Department of Youth Justice. While she was resigning from cabinet, Camm said she would continue to serve as the member for Whitsunday.



Crisafulli said Camm came in to a broken system. “I constantly saw her put the concerns of vulnerable women and children above all else,” he said. Related Article LNP Crisafulli under fire over ministers’ extramarital affair The minister was also caught in a public grilling when her undeclared romantic relationship with Sport Minister Tim Mander was brought to light earlier this year. Questions centred on whether the pair had fulfilled their obligations to report any conflicts of interest and adhere to the parliamentary code of conduct.



The extramarital affair was again scrutinised when the Australian Federal Police investigated reports Mander had not been living at his declared address – which had been the home he shared with his wife Gayle, before their marriage ended in April 2025. We’ve collected all the chef, front-of-house and restaurant finalists into one handy cheat-sheet ahead of the Good Food Guide Awards on Monday, October 26.

While there has certainly been an increase in fancy potato scallops and shimmering Korean soups in 2026, the biggest restaurant trend of the past 12 months has been previously bold and ambitious operators dialling back risk. We’ve never seen more steakhouses, sandwich shops or generic Italian joints sweep Sydney. If at first it doesn’t work, flip to pizza.

Osteria Luna in the Sydney CBD. Jennifer Soo

And we get it – restaurants have become ferociously expensive to run, and the cost-of-living crunch is real. Whether you’re a restaurant investor or a diner, no one’s overly keen to roll the dice on untested pitches right now.

But.

At the same time, young talent and veteran restaurateurs continue to open personal, singular venues because having a point of view – telling a story or sharing a history – is still more important than the profit margins on farmed kingfish and steak frites. Great restaurants find a way.
