Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume accused the prime minister of having a “tenuous” relationship with the truth after he denied suggestions yesterday that his office had compiled a “dirt sheet” on Helen Haines.

“There is no doubt that his office circulated this file that didn’t just list the projects that Helen Haines had requested, they also implied that she had some sort of conflict of interest,” she told Sunrise this morning.

“But the prime minister’s tenuous relationship with the truth is becoming a pattern of behaviour … The fact is, the prime minister has denied that there was any problem with this. Just own it. If he can justify its existence, justify it. If he can’t, he should own it and just apologise. But he seems to be unable to do that.”

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume. Dominic Lorrimer

Appearing alongside Hume on a regular panel was Health Minister Mark Butler, who said he had seen dirt sheets during his time in parliament and that this was certainly not one.

“Dirt sheets tend to sort of imply, you know, scandalous behaviour, and say things that people aren’t willing to say in the parliament,” he said.

“There was a list of the projects that Helen was advocating for in the lead-up to the election, like every lower house member … I just don’t think there’s anything remarkable about that.”

World.title: US and Israel are planning to hit Iran again once elections are over
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war US and Israel are planning to hit Iran again once elections are over Julian E. Barnes , Eric Schmitt , Farnaz Fassihi , Natan Odenheimer and Ronen Bergman October 23, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: The US and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the American midterm elections, according to US officials and other people briefed on the deliberations. As planning for a short but intensive operation progresses, the US and Israeli militaries have stepped up exercises, flying planes over Iraq to practice strike manoeuvres. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss new strikes, US officials said. Iran’s regime remains defiant despite the concerted military action undertaken against it by the US and Israel. AP Photo/Vahid Salemi The targets would be likely to include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Some officials say one more big round of attacks could push Iran’s economy over the brink and force the country to make diplomatic concessions after nearly eight months of conflict. Still, there are reasons to be sceptical that a renewed war would be any more successful than the first phase of intense US-Israeli strikes between February and April. Those rounds of fighting drove up energy prices and inflation around the world, eroded security in the Middle East and severely strained the Pentagon’s supply of missile interceptors.



It is also far from certain President Donald Trump will approve fresh strikes. Repeatedly this year he has vetoed plans for a return to major combat operations, including this month when the US and Israeli militaries were nearly ready to attack. Related Article US midterms Long lines, late nights, adulation: What it’s really like inside Trump’s midterm election rallies All of the officials interviewed for this story spoke on condition of anonymity to candidly discuss military planning. Iranian officials have promised to retaliate this time by expanding their targets beyond commercial ships and energy infrastructure in the region, to data centres and underwater internet cables. They say the fighting will be neither quick nor limited.



While the United States is assembling a massive arsenal that will be fully in place by early November, diplomatic efforts have continued, as US negotiators use the potential return to war as leverage with Iran to make progress on their demands on its nuclear program and control over the Strait of Hormuz. The United States will not have its full complement of military assets – including three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces – in place until early November. So far, however, Iran’s negotiators have been unwilling to make concessions on the nuclear program, insisting on deferring that issue until later in the talks. Some US planners are convinced that an intensive three-day campaign could cause enough economic damage to change the Iranian position. But US officials have frequently predicted Iran’s collapse, and other Western officials noted that Iran’s government has so far weathered the pressures on its economy. “At this point in the war, what is clear is that the conventional military campaign waged to date, and the current punishing economic sanctions and American naval blockade, have not brought the regime back to the negotiating table in a meaningful way,” said Dana Stroul, who served as the Pentagon’s top Middle East policy official in the Biden administration.



Neither Trump nor Netanyahu “has made a compelling case for how more war would change this strategic dilemma in an increasingly unstable and conflict-ridden region,” said Stroul, who is now with the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Israel’s election on Tuesday could complicate the plans. If Netanyahu loses, he will become a caretaker prime minister, and it will be difficult for him to launch a war, experts say. But some analysts believe that Netanyahu could leverage the prospect of an imminent joint US-Israel strike to pressure his rivals into joining a unity government to manage the war, which would extend his hold on power. After Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, Netanyahu formed a unity government that brought some opposition members into a war Cabinet to help make national security decisions. “He could use this to call for a broad emergency government, but he will face deep suspicion from his political rivals,” said Mazal Mualem, an Israeli political commentator and the author of a biography of Netanyahu.



“If Iran attacks, that’s one thing, but initiating an offensive strike would be extremely difficult for him.” Related Article Opinion

US politics When Trump gets a thrashing at the midterms, four words will come back to haunt him Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Officials say there is a small possibility that Trump could decide to begin a campaign this month, but there are many political reasons that he is likely to wait until after the US election – not least his own promise early this month not to strike before the vote. The United States will not have its full complement of military assets – including three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces – in place until early November. The US military prefers to conduct attacks under the cover of night, and there will be increasing hours of darkness over Iran early next month. There are also concerns that the war could spiral into a larger conflict. On Wednesday, the US State Department ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, as the Iran-backed Houthi militia continues to attack sites there.



A White House official said on Wednesday that the administration does not comment on military plans “that may or may not exist.” Trump, the official added, was keeping all options on the table to ensure that Iran cannot acquire nuclear weapons. Some officials say the targeting will avoid refineries and oil infrastructure because Trump is eager to prevent even higher gas prices. The Iranian regime has effectively used its Houthi allies in Yemen to keep the pressure on key US allies in the region. AP Both the US and Israel militaries are drafting plans for operations against Iran’s nuclear program, according to people briefed on the work. That could include an attack on Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried nuclear site that Iranians call Kooh Kolang. Trump said last week that he was considering using a 22,000-pound GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB, against Pickaxe. Officials say Trump is enamoured with the weapon in part because of its nickname, Mother of All Bombs.



But weapons specialists say that the MOAB explodes above ground, producing a wide blast, and would not likely destroy an underground site like Pickaxe, which is composed of granite. Military officials also warn that the bomb must be delivered by a slow-flying MC-130 transport plane that would be vulnerable to Iranian anti-aircraft fire. Israel and the United States came close to striking Iran early this month, but Trump again decided at the last minute to postpone the attack, according to US and Israeli defence officials familiar with the details. The decision came shortly before the operation was to begin, after both militaries had made extensive preparations and placed their air forces on the highest state of alert. The repeated planning efforts followed by Trump’s decisions against new attacks has caused “day-to-day whiplash” among military planners, said one commander, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, as they try to stay poised to carry out whatever military option Trump decides in the coming weeks. Loading In each round of the war so far, Iran’s leadership has become less conciliatory, convinced that the ultimate US and Israeli goal is to topple its government.



Iran’s new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, remains an enigma to US and Israeli intelligence officials. Some officials say he is not as powerful as his father, who was killed early in the war, and that hard-line members of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard make key decisions. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘I’m afraid of civil war’: The voters travelling from Australia to vote against Netanyahu Iranian officials say they are aware of the US war planning and have been developing their own new targets and tactics. Peiman Salehi, a political analyst in Tehran, said that if Pickaxe is attacked, part of Iran’s plans to retaliate would be to strike major oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, including Aramco because that would immediately spike oil and energy prices. “The war has made us understand that the best leverage for pressuring Trump is increasing oil and energy prices because it will hurt the American people,” Salehi said.



Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran’s negotiator General Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, said on social media this week that the idea that the United States would wrap up another round of strikes on Iran within 72 hours was a “fantasy” and that Iran would determine when the war would end. He noted that Trump said in February that the war would last two weeks. “Our attacks will be more fierce, creative and different,” Mohammadi said. “We are determined and confident and strong planning has been put in place.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. World.title: Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni resigns
World.content:
Audio player for " Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni resigns over gang campaigning " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2095491%2Flabour-candidate-kerrin-leoni-resigns

Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni resigns over gang campaigning Nine To Noon Download MP3 4m

Labour's Tāmaki Makaurau candidate Kerrin Leoni has resigned after a video emerged of her campaigning alongside Mongrel Mob members.

The footage showed Leoni, wearing a Labour Party jacket, talking to gang members about enrolling to vote and changing the government.

A photo from the same event - published by Newsroom - showed the former Auckland councillor posing with a group of people including some in Mongrel Mob regalia pulling hand gestures associated with the gang.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the footage was "inconsistent" with the standards he expected from his candidates.

"I have made it very clear that campaigning alongside gangs is unacceptable," he said in a statement released on Friday.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407256721112

Speaking to reporters later that morning, Hipkins said Leoni had displayed "very very bad judgement" and had paid a "very high price" for that.

"It is a clear violation of the very clear standards that I have set out for our MPs and candidates," he said. "Her position had become untenable."

Hipkins said he had a brief conversation with Leoni on Friday morning, in which she apologised and conceded she had not handled the situation well.

"Clearly, this has been very, very difficult for her. This is her family who we're talking about."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins. RNZ/Baz Macdonald

Hipkins said Leoni had not given the party the "full information" about the gathering and had not managed the conflict appropriately.

But he said he bore her no "ill will" for the mistake and became emotional while expressing his frustration at the "unfortunate" circumstance.

"All of us navigate family situations in politics, and it's bloody hard," he said.

"In her case, she should be really proud of what she has been able to achieve. She has grown up in an environment where she's been surrounded by gang members. She is not a gang member herself. She has made a good life for herself.

"She has made a mistake here, and she has paid a high price."

Hipkins said he also believed there was an element of "racism" to the reaction and chided National for "crowing" and "salivating" over the candidate's mistake.

"Our Māori MPs get held to a very different standard to others."

Hipkins said he was "very disappointed" in the situation and acknowledged it was "not helpful at all" to the prospects of a centre-left coalition.

He said he was not aware of any other Labour candidates visiting gang pads during this election campaign.

Hipkins had earlier condemned Green and Te Pāti Māori candidates for taking photos with gang members at a Mongrol Mob pad during the campaign.

He ruled out giving law-and-order portfolios to MPs from either party, saying it was unacceptable for politicians to "go out and celebrate with gangs".

Leoni herself criticised Te Pāti Māori rival Oriini Kaipara for the visit during an electorate debate on Wednesday. Kaipara hit back, accusing Leoni of having visited a gang pad the week before her, which Leoni denied.

Te Pāti Māori candidate for Tāmaki Makaurau Oriini Kaipara. VNP/Phil Smith

In a Facebook post on Thursday, Leoni said she had not visited a gang pad during the campaign but admitted attending a "whānau function" in early October where some close relatives who were gang members were present.

"I will not turn my back on them or pretend they are not my whānau because of their associations," she wrote. "I've always tried to be a role model for my whānau."

With nominations already closed, Leoni's name will remain on the ballot paper, despite Hipkins saying she no longer represents Labour.

The video - first reported by Whakaata Māori but also independently obtained by RNZ - showed a patched Mongrel Mob member advocating for the gangs to stop fighting each other and to instead turn their attention to the government.

The footage then cut to Leoni, addressing those present: "Some of them you might know that aren't enrolled to vote and they can have the power to change this government."

The Post reported that the event had been advertised online as a "fundraiser for the Mongrel Mob's Rogue Chapter". But Hipkins told reporters he had been reassured that the function was not a fundraising event.

Labour MP Priyanca Radhakrishnan. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Speaking earlier on Friday on NZ Herald's Ryan Bridge Today, Labour MP Priyanca Radhakrishnan defended Leoni, saying she had been visiting family.

She said she was willing to accept Leoni's version of events: "She was there at a whānau event, and that's the information that I have."

Hipkins also initially stood by Leoni on Thursday - before further footage emerged - saying she was entitled to interact with her own family.

World.title: 'I trusted him all those years': Luxury car dealer disappears amid abrupt business closure
World.content:
The end of a luxury car dealership in Petone has blindsided financiers and Wellington elites, including philanthropist Sir Mark Dunajtschik, who says he considered the business owner to have been like a son.

The man behind the children's hospital told RNZ he hadn't given up on Simon O'Reilly, who he said owed him a "substantial amount" of money, and was now rumoured to be in Europe.

Car dealership O'Reilly's Garage was on Wednesday placed into receivership, with Avanti Finance appointing receivers BDO.

Sir Mark told RNZ earlier this week he loaned O'Reilly the capital to start the dealership in 2018 and "was surprised like everybody else".

O'Reilly had always kept up with the interest on the loan, Sir Mark told RNZ, however, he'd subsequently taken what steps he could to protect himself financially.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"I trusted him all those years like he was my son and I haven't given up faith in him," he said.

Sir Mark said he last heard from O'Reilly about six months ago and believed he was now in Greece, but he wasn't going to chase him.

"It doesn't make a difference to me, whether he is on the moon or in Greece ... why should I spend my time trying to fathom out where he is? He's not here."

Do you know more? Email mary.argue@rnz.co.nz

O'Reilly has not responded to RNZ's phone calls and messages, and a former employee at the car dealership declined to comment.

No one answered the gate buzzer when RNZ visited O'Reilly's Khandallah property on Thursday, but a neighbour said they'd seen two moving trucks outside the home a week ago. Another neighbour said there had been packing up activity at night.

The street's residents hadn't seen the family for a couple of weeks, but mentioned they had some "nice" looking cars.

The dealership on Hutt Road is currently up for lease and promoted by listing agent Bayleys as an "outstanding opportunity to secure a high-profile showroom". When RNZ visited this week, the doors were closed and the car lot was empty.

O'Reilly's Garage - renowned for its high-end luxury cars - also bought and sold vehicles on consignment for Wellington's supercar-loving community.

While the business's website remained live, zero cars were listed for sale. Its previously sold section boasted a range of vehicles, including a 1997 Aston Martin AMV8, 2022 Porsche 718 Cayman GT4 RS, and a 2010 Ferrari California.

RNZ / Supplied

O'Reilly's Garage also became a dealer for Foton - spruiking the Chinese-made ute on its Facebook page - but Foton NZ confirmed the dealership ended the arrangement recently.

This week, the O'Reilly's Garage Facebook page appeared to have been taken down.

Well-known property investor and supercar enthusiast Steve Goodey, who said he'd had dealings with O'Reilly in the past, was less sanguine about the developments and the position in which Sir Mark found himself.

"In Wellington, he's the closest thing we've got to a saint right?"

Goodey has complained to the Registrar of Motor Vehicle Traders at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) over the sale of his Ferrari Portofino.

In recent correspondence seen by RNZ, Goodey told the MBIE Registrar he wasn't chasing his money.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"That's gone. I'm writing so it's on record that your office had this man in front of it two years ago and let him walk."

When RNZ asked MBIE about criticism that it did not do enough to investigate O'Reilly, registrar Duncan Connor said it had received two complaints.

"The first, received in 2024, was investigated and closed after no breach of the [Motor Vehicle Sales Act] was identified."

He said a second complaint had only just been received this month and was "currently under assessment".

Goodey said while the abrupt end to O'Reilly's Garage wasn't a surprise to him, it had shocked others.

"Other people had very different relationships with Simon O'Reilly. You know, a lot of people just didn't see it coming. He's a real smooth guy."

Mark Dunajtschik Supplied

Financiers scramble

According to the NZ Companies Register, the last annual return for O'Reilly's Garage was filed in May this year.

The Personal Property Securities Register records 36 financing statements registered against O'Reilly's Garage Ltd, with Avanti Finance a secured party on 29 of them. "Motor Vehicles" are included in the assets held as security.

Director of MTF Finance at the Lower Hutt Franchise, Geoff Kenny, said he had two secured loans with O'Reilly.

He said while a boat - a halmatic 22 metre - had been found through a "little bit of detective work", the motorhome was a different story.

"We have walked away from the security because the customer bought that motorhome off O'Reilly's Garage in good faith, and paid for it in good faith."

Kenny said any claim on the loan would have to be with O'Reilly directly.

"He should never have sold the vehicle while he had money owing on it to us."

He said up until last week, when he learned the business and O'Reilly had apparently gone, there'd never been any issues.

"It's just a sad situation. And I'd say just about everybody was blindsided because this was a guy who most people thought was a great guy, a good car dealer, and financially strong.

World.title: Ikea staff in Auckland to strike for first time over lack of weekend rates
World.content:
About 300 Ikea workers are set to strike for the first time on Saturday.

Workers First Union deputy secretary Rudd Hughes said the staff wanted to be given pay increases that kept up with inflation and time-and-a-half at the weekend.

He said Ikea had been given credit when it arrived in New Zealand for paying staff living wage.

"Now they've kind of stepped back from that saying well we never guaranteed it. It was always just a happy coincidence… so the current pay offer they've got on the table is less than CPI so we see that as a pay cut."

He said Ikea's Australian staff were paid overtime rates.

"What we're asking for even at weekend rates is less than what they get in Australia which is double time."

He said Ikea argued they had a legal mandate to pay overtime in Australia.

"What they are saying is that 'New Zealanders are second-class citizens and we're going to treat them worse than we treat our Australian workers'. We're not happy with that."

Ikea has been approached for comment.

"Ikea came to this country trumpeting their 'progressive' attitude concerning industrial relations, but talk is cheap and so is their offer to workers," Hughes said.

"Retail workers deserve to be recognised for the work they do, and weekend work should attract a top rate because of the time people have to spend away from their families and friends to earn their wages.

"Ikea need to step up and show they value New Zealand workers in the same way they value Aussie workers."

He said retail in general was a tough environment for workers.

"Retail is incredibly poorly paid in this country. You can live on a retail wage in Australia, you cannot live on it here. Part of that is aroudn the fact that people get overtime, get penal rates on the weekends."

World.title: Marama Davidson says attack on Australian MP Helen Haines a chilling warning
World.content:
Marama Davidson says she experienced "a chill" up her body when she learned about Australian politician Helen Haines who was mowed down outside her office by a car.

The Independent MP for Indi lost both her legs after she was struck by a Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office on Monday.

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson in an interview with Mata with Mihingarangi Forbes said she wanted to express her sympathy and aroha to Helen Haines, her family and her community.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407216854112

In 2023, Marama Davidson was injured when a motorcycle associated with Destiny Church clipped her stomach as she was crossing the road. She had been crossing at a pedestrian crossing she told The Spinoff and had put her hand out to warn him to slow down but they didn't stop.

Davidson was part of a counter protest group sending a message to anti-trans campaigner Posie Parker at Auckland's Albert Park.

The collision was captured on camera and Marama Davidson told Mata a person associated with Destiny Church was identified and charged.

Despite this, she was clear she wanted politicians to be accessible here in Aotearoa.

Her colleague Tamatha Paul who is also been the target of abuse, posted on social media that when debates are held in Wellington North, there are four uniform police officers and two parliamentary security guards on hand.

Paul told her followers Aotearoa needs to stop focusing on how women can keep themselves safe and start focusing on the perpetrators. She said the focus should be on misogyny, rape culture and how it manifests in our society, normalising violence against women.

Marama Davidson said: "There is a responsibility for all of us in politics to understand the power and the influence of our platform. To make sure that we are using our leadership roles to calm down the rhetoric, to calm the divisiveness, to not tolerate from anyone, including our own supporters, any threats or harm towards anyone else."

Marama Davidson discussed a range of topics including the attack on Australian politician Helen Haines and whether the Green Party would be part of the next government. Supplied

In a wide-ranging interview with Mata with Mihingarangi, Davidson said if the Greens were to be part of the next government, they would advocate for blocking Israel from attending the 2027 Pacific Islands Forum which is to be hosted in New Zealand.

This week RNZ reported Israel had joined the Pacific Islands Forum, the region's principal political organisation, as a partner.

Davidson said Aotearoa had a role to support and uphold the independence of the Pacific.

On the policy of Kiwimart, she said while the publicly owned supermarkets were one thing, there would need to be a national food strategy that included local growers and kai sovereignty. The Greens proposed $150 million a year for a food fund supporting more cooperatives, market gardeners, community gardens, kai sharing initiatives and projects.

On where all this kai is going to be grown, Davidson suggests co-ops that share land alongside the Hoki Whenua Mai policy which seeks to free up 26,000 hectares of land locked up under perpetual leases.

In a quick fire, Davidson couldn't pick between "Te Whakaputanga" or "Te Tiriti" but she chose to "reduce" rather than "recycle" or "reuse".

Threw a bouquet to Eugenie Sage for best Minister of Conservation but said the current Minister for Conservation Tama Potaka was "not effective" rather than "effective".

She wouldn't pick between James Shaw and Chlöe Swarbrick for best co-leader but she chose "kaupapa skirts" over "tino tees" and "Ardern" over "Hipkins".

World.title: Green Party releases fiscal plan, promises to increase health spending by $3 billion each year
World.content:
The Green Party has released its fiscal plan, promising to increase health spending by $3 billion each year.

Co-leader and finance spokesperson Chloe Swarbrick released the plan at Parliament this morning.

It includes operating allowances of $4.5b to $4.7b a year, and a slower return to surplus in 2029/30, and an increase to net core Crown debt to 44 percent of GDP in 2030/31, which she says is well within responsible fiscal ranges compared to other countries.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407256033112

"By the end of the forecast period, Crown expenses are 40 percent of GDP and revenue is 40.1 percent of GDP. This is well within a responsible fiscal range compared to other OECD countries," Swarbrick said.

The plan projects a nearly $8b a year increase to government revenue from a range of taxes including the party's "super-rich" tax, capital acquisitions tax, big corporations tax, major banks levy, enforcement of a tax on big tech companies, and reversal of the changes the party has labelled "tax cuts for landlords".

This would be balanced with cuts to income taxes and moves to add 64,000 more jobs than the 220,000 Treasury currently forecasts.

Unlike both National and Labour, the plan also promises to fund climate emissions mitigation through the purchase of offshore credits through unallocated spending.

Treasury estimates this to cost up to $5b - although that total would be lowered by however much nationwide emissions can be reduced in line with international commitments.

The party estimates a 1 percent increase to GDP after four years from its policies.

"Cutting public spending deepens economic downturns and inequality, pushes up unemployment and reduces output. The current government's fiscal track is made possible only through underinvestment in core public services," Swarbrick said.

"Our sensible long-term investment approach turns this around and tackles real risks to fiscal sustainability head on with genuine investments such as lowering exposure to imported fossil fuels, in turn reducing New Zealanders' cost of living and future imported inflation."

She said public debt was low compared to other countries.

"By the end of the forecast period, Crown expenses are 40 percent of GDP and revenue is 40.1 percent of GDP. This is well within a responsible fiscal range compared to other OECD countries."

Swarbrick said every one of the party's policies had been fully costed, but the Greens remained committed to a Parliamentary Budget Office that could cost every party's policies on the same basis.

"The Greens are the party of real economic responsibility. That means we will fix the basics and build the future in the real world, not just by moving numbers around a page as our emergency departments are left in crisis."

On the health spending, she said governments proposing to declare a surplus while children were having cancer treatments delayed were "failing".

"The Greens have heard the call of our nurses for safe staffing levels. We are committing $3 billion more every year for the next four years to bring investment up to the level necessary not just to deal with immediate pressures, not just to rebuild lost capacity, but ensure our health system is fit for purpose for patients and health workers.

World.title: Lawyer subject of ‘unprofessional and inappropriate’ messages in police group chat
World.content:
A lawyer was the target of "unprofessional and inappropriate" remarks in a police group chat, including comments about a photo of him being put in a headlock by a police officer.

In response to the photo, one staff member said "a bit tighter & a bit longer please", and "cock your wrist more to the right too".

In a separate exchange, when discussing the fact the lawyer had a girlfriend, a staff member shared a photo of a pig. This was accompanied by "meat Mrs [lawyer's surname]".

Staff also called the lawyer an "idiot", "f….wit" and a "dick".

Police say an investigation found no basis for a criminal investigation, but further steps were taken in relation to a number of staff. Police have apologised to the lawyer and his partner for the "inappropriate and unprofessional" comments.

The lawyer, who RNZ has agreed not to name, made a request under the Privacy Act in March after discovering that a photo of him being put in a headlock by a police officer had been shared in a group chat involving Whangarei PPS [Police Prosecution Service] staff.

The lawyer says he consented to the headlock as a joke, but not to a photo being taken, or shared in the group chat.

He received a copy of the photo, as well as the names of the people who were party to the chat.

He later requested all commentary about him by Whangarei PPS staff.

Police recently provided the material, which includes messages dating from October 2022 to this year.

In March 2024, the photo of the lawyer being put in a headlock was shared in the group chat followed by a series of comments.

Someone in the group said "I hope he's been charged with assaulting police", while another message said "a bit tighter & a bit longer please".

"A bit of man love if ever I saw it with [redacted] being the dominant!" one staff member said.

Other messages in relation to the headlock included "cock your wrist more to the right too", "Judge [redacted] has assessed the matter and determined 'no offence there'", and "still more tighter and longer".

The final message said "no matter how tight or restrictive, still wouldn't have shut him up".

In one exchange, when discussing the fact the lawyer had a girlfriend, a staff member shared a photo of a pig. Supplied

In December 2023, a member of the Whangarei PPS group chat said they had been told the lawyer was set to leave to work somewhere else due to his girlfriend's work.

"1st thing I questioned was [the lawyer] having a girlfriend".

A member then shared a photo of a pig and a message was sent saying "meat Mrs [lawyer's surname]".

Another message said "you can actually put lipstick on a pig."

In another message, dating back to 2022, a police officer refers to a matter in court involving the lawyer and said "oh my god that [lawyer] is a dick..".

In another exchange in April 2023, a staffer says "as you know [the lawyer] is an idiot" when discussing another court matter.

In February, this year, a staff member asked a colleague "how's f….wit, I mean [lawyer's surname] behaving?"

"I haven't seen the little [poo emoji] this morning," the staffer replies.

The Privacy Act response includes comments from Police's Executive Director of service victims and resolutions Rachael Bambery, who said the group chat was created to "facilitate work-related matters and has become a way for team members to informally chat with each other".

She said police acknowledged there were "unprofessional communications" in the group chat.

"The comments were made privately between colleagues, were not intended for a wider audience, and reflected the kind of coping mechanisms that can develop among Police staff working in a difficult and often confronting environment."

The lawyer told RNZ that the headlock came about after he had been threatened by a client, and the police officer offered to show him some restraint methods.

He said he agreed but did not know that a photo was taken.

The lawyer was "extremely distressed" when he read the comments about the photo.

"They are cold. They are serious. There is no LOL, no emojis. They are delivered in a sinister and serious manner," he said.

"Nobody calls out anybody for the behaviour in the group chat. It was obviously never reported ... and it is truly sad that no one had enough integrity to do something about it when they read those horrible messages."

The lawyer also told RNZ he believed the photo of a pig, shared alongside a message about his partner, had racist undertones as he had told some staff she was Polynesian.

"It's also concerning that people who are prosecuting other people for strangulation, serious violence, and threats of violence are behaving in the very behaviour that they prosecute and know and see the impact of on a daily basis in their work."

A series of messages sent in the chat about the headlock. Supplied

He wants the officers involved to be charged and "held accountable for their behaviour".

"If the shoe was on the other foot, and myself and other defense lawyers, or my clients, for example, gang members said the same things about their police staff in a group chat, they would almost invariably be charged with threatening behaviour," he said.

"Police should be held to a higher standard, given their requirements around integrity and conduct."

In response to questions from RNZ, police's chief of staff Cassandra Anderson said the code of conduct set "clear expectations for the behaviour of all police employees".

"Police acknowledges that a group of staff shared pictures and commentary about [the lawyer] in group chats that were unprofessional and inappropriate. This conduct did not meet the standards expected of police employees."

In relation to the photograph, Anderson said police staff described a request from the lawyer, during a break between court sessions, for staff to demonstrate a headlock on him.

"Believing this to be in good humour, at [the lawyer's] instigation, our staff obliged. Our staff described that the photo was taken with [the lawyer] knowledge and that he subsequently requested a copy of it.

"Regardless of the original purpose of the photo and regardless of who suggested the idea, Police reiterates its view that subsequent commentary in a closed group chat by our staff, was not appropriate and was unprofessional."

Police leadership became aware of the messaging when the lawyer raised concerns that he believed such material existed, Anderson said.

"This was then the subject of an investigation, which found no basis for a criminal investigation, but further steps were taken in respect of a number of Police staff.

"For privacy and employment reasons the detail of those steps cannot be shared. This matter was also reported to the Independent Police Conduct Authority (IPCA) in accordance with the Memorandum of Understanding between Police and the IPCA."

Anderson said police had apologised to the lawyer.

"We reiterate that apology to him … and to his partner for any offence and upset the comments have caused them."

Police initially apologised in writing in June when they confirmed the existence of a photo and "unprofessional and inappropriate commentary" in the chat.

The director resolutions also apologised in person when they met with the lawyer in Hamilton two days later.

"Police subsequently agreed to a request to support [the lawyer] to access professional services to assist him with the impact this matter had on him."

Anderson said police apologised again in writing on October 16, when they responded to the lawyer's revived information request.

"On this occasion all the information contained in the various communications was provided to [the lawyer] so the full context of the apology was clear."

Anderson said she wanted to be clear that the commentary in the exchange was "inappropriate and unprofessional".

"While we cannot disclose the detail of steps taken in relation to individual staff, appropriate action has been taken and the expectations of staff regarding professional and appropriate communication have been reinforced."

Police Minister Mark Mitchell said in a statement "as police have themselves said, these comments fall short of expectations and standards".

World.title: Few remain at homeless encampment in Whangārei as deadline to leave site looms
World.content:
Just three or four people remain at a homeless encampment in Whangārei as the council's new deadline for leaving the site looms later today, RNZ understands.

Up to 50 people have lived in tents and makeshift shelters at the disused Old Boys' sportsground since 2023, though that number dropped to 10 after Kāinga Ora opened a new housing complex in June.

The remaining rough sleepers were ordered on leave on 8 October but the eviction notices were put on hold following a public outcry.

MSD, Kāinga Ora and social service providers such as Arataki Ministries and Whare Āwhina have been working intensively to find homes for them since then.

RNZ understands that has been successful for all but a few people with the most complex needs.

Whangārei District Council said it had been forced to act by increasing health and safety risks, as well as complaints from nearby businesses.

The encampment backed onto Semenoff Stadium, leading to concerns for public safety during major sporting events.

The council said the area around one of the stadium's emergency exits was strewn with broken glass.

After mayor Ken Couper met the residents on site on 8 October, the eviction was paused and two new deadlines were set.

All tents and other belongings had to be moved off the grass onto a parking area by the end of 23 October, and the site had to be vacated completely by 20 November.

The original 10-day eviction notice was issued on 28 September under the council's new Public Spaces Bylaw.

Since then, advocates for the sportsground-dwellers said rubbish had been removed, grass around the stadium had been checked for broken glass, and a portable toilet had been provided by a member of the community.

More than 50 supporters took part in a peaceful protest at the sportsground on 8 October, the original eviction date.

Around 20 people, including four of the Old Boys' residents, took part in a protest march on Thursday from Laurie Hall Park to the council's headquarters on Rust Avenue.

Couper said the council was responsible for essential maintenance at all its reserves and public spaces.

"A number of emerging risks and hazards were making the former Old Boys' site unsafe for normal public use, contractors and maintenance staff. As landowner of that area, council has a requirement to maintain the grounds to help reduce fire and other safety risks, while securing emergency and operational access for events at Semenoff Stadium."

Couper said agencies including the Ministry of Social Development, Mahitahi Hauora PHE, and the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport were working directly with each person remaining at the Old Boys' site to identify housing and support suited to their circumstances.

Local hapū Te Parawhau had also been engaged as part of the response.

"Homelessness is a complex issue facing communities across Aotearoa, and there is no quick or simple solution. We need a coordinated, compassionate approach that supports people into individualised, appropriate pathways while addressing the concerns of the wider community," Couper said.

World.title: England stunned as Sri Lanka chases 430 after Brook's record ODI knock
World.content:
Sri Lanka has chased down 430 in a thrilling one-day clash against England despite Harry Brook scoring the fastest double-century in ODI history.

Brook's double-century helped England post a mammoth score of 4-429 before Sri Lanka chased down the target with two wickets and one ball to spare.

Sri Lanka's chase is the second-highest of all time in ODI cricket, trailing only South Africa's chase of 435 against Australia in 2006.

The 27-year-old captain rewrote the record books by racing to his double hundred in 114 balls, surpassing the previous mark of 117 deliveries set by India's Shubman Gill.

Brook's double-century was the fastest of all time and he also eclipsed England's highest individual ODI score of 182, previously held by Ben Stokes.

He made 202 from 116 deliveries, peppering the Sri Lanka attack with 21 fours and 10 sixes before departing to warm applause from the crowd.

The defeat leaves England bottom of the standings after losing both their matches, with Brook saying they need to win their next two games to reach the final in Lahore.

Harry Brook's record-breaking double-century was ultimately in vain as Sri Lanka chased down the target of 430 with a ball to spare. (Getty Images: Sameer Ali)

"Unfortunately, it [the record] doesn't matter now. I thought we were going to be in a good position but, unfortunately, it doesn't even count," Brook said after the game.

"Heartbreaking. I think you've hit the nail on the head there. It's very disappointing that we haven't been able to defend 430, but that's life, that's cricket," he added.

"You don't see many teams chase down 430 and hats off to Sri Lanka. They've played exceptionally well. We couldn't execute our skills enough with the ball and, again, they've just played an absolute blinder there.

"We'll have a good chat about it now and over the next couple of days. We've got a good opportunity in the next couple of games to really try and get to that final in Lahore."

Pavan Rathnayake top-scored for Sri Lanka with 130 from 106 deliveries, while opener Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka both fell three runs short of centuries.

Needing six runs from the final two deliveries, Sri Lanka sealed victory when Janith Liyanage launched Josh Tongue over long-off for six, leaving Brook's record-breaking innings all in vain.

Tongue was England's most successful bowler with 3-79.

England lost by 87 runs at the same venue in Rawalpindi on Tuesday to Pakistan, who lead the table with two wins from two.

Reuters

World.title: Wallaroos great inspired by mantra 'you can't be what you can't see'
World.content:
As Emily Chancellor runs out for her final Test, she will know she has fulfilled one of her ambitions as a Wallaroos representative.

Upon making her Test debut in 2018, Chancellor wanted to help increase the visibility of the Wallaroos among young fans.

Even though she followed rugby growing up, the Wallaroos were not on her radar as the women's game lacked adequate support and promotion.

Chancellor only began playing as a 21-year-old university student, admitting earlier this week "rugby wasn't an option" during her childhood.

At Canberra Stadium this evening, there will be young girls among the spectators eagerly watching the Wallaroos play Scotland.

They will be cheering on their heroes and dreaming of playing for the national women's rugby team, proving Chancellor has taken giant steps in accomplishing her mission.

Inspiring young fans has been at the forefront of Emily Chancellor's mind. (Getty Images: Robbie Stephenson)

"You can't be what you can't see," Chancellor told ABC Sport on the eve of her Test farewell.

"I feel like that is something that has driven me so hard; to want to keep playing and pushing the image of the Wallaroos to a wider audience.

"I feel like I've had a positive impact on that over the last eight years. I love seeing the kids in the crowd, with their parents, excited.

"What excites me is that there has been so much growth when I look back over the last eight years, considering where I was when I was a kid and the visibility of the game in the women's world [at the time].

"It's come so far. I'm really proud of where we've got to and how many young girls are turning up to games."

Tight bond

After 42 Tests, Chancellor will leave the game as a Wallaroos great.

The 35-year-old appeared in two World Cups and captained the team during the 2025 season.

A stellar domestic career with the NSW Waratahs and stints playing club rugby in the UK and Japan are also among her most cherished experiences.

Emily Chancellor captained the Wallaroos in 2025. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Aside from her on-field achievements, nothing means more to Chancellor than the tight bond she enjoys with her Wallaroos teammates.

She describes the close-knit squad as a "sisterhood".

"We're all struggling or thriving with the challenges rugby faces, particularly in the women's space," said Chancellor, who will start at openside flanker against Scotland.

"Be it pay, the lack of professionalism, or the striving for both of those things, I think that bonds you together massively."

'Limitless' future

The Wallaroos's semi-professional status has made it difficult for the squad to compete with the likes of England and New Zealand, both of which benefit from having full-time programs.

The Wallaroos are in the process of becoming full-time in the build-up to the 2029 World Cup, which will be hosted by Australia.

Emily Chancellor made her Test debut against New Zealand in 2018. (Getty Images)

Chancellor believes the team's opportunities will be "limitless" when this is finally achieved.

"You see how much natural ability the girls have, how much we do with so little in terms of game time at the moment," she said.

"I get excited by what Rugby Australia did with the Aussie women's sevens team when they went full-time.

"A bit more hard work and time together … wow, I think it will be exciting."

Chancellor will be enjoying retirement once the next World Cup rolls around, but her commitment to the Wallaroos's cause shows no signs of diminishing.

The drive to increase visibility of the Wallaroos and women's rugby will remain.

"We've still got a long way to go, and I don't plan on letting up on that goal of making it as visible as possible when I step away from playing," she said.

World.title: Quick hits: Bavuma hides from Smith implosion as Boland outdoes batters
World.content:
Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while nightwatchman Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha.

Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Head passes 100 but can't go on

Travis Head began day five needing 13 runs for a gritty, fighting century.

And after a two-hour rain delay, the punchy southpaw reached three figures with relative ease, bringing up the milestone with two leg-side boundaries against South African destroyer Marco Jansen in the sixth over of the day.

Travis Head scored his 13th Test century. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

His celebrations were understandably muted given the state of the game, with his helmet staying in place as he raised his bat and a grin not even threatening to peek through his grill.

It was just Head's second overseas ton after his effort in the 2023 World Test Championship final at the Oval against India, and first against a team on its home patch.

But Head was unable to set up for the long haul his team so craved, with the Australian departing just after the first drinks break, chopping on while attempting a cut shot that was never there.

Head was out for 121 and Australia was 5-209.

2. Boland shows batters how it's done

By now, Australian cricket fans should know better than to doubt Scott Boland.

But even the most optimistic of those watching back home surely wouldn't have expected the nightwatchman to outlast both Head and Steve Smith, take his innings deep into the day and soak up a staggering 166 deliveries.

Boland found the middle of the bat more often than not during his heroic vigil. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

There were a couple of streaky moments, sure, but Boland made his luck more than he rode it, defending with the kind of authority and simplicity his more celebrated batting teammates were so desperately lacking throughout the Test.

He even played a few memorable shots, including an immaculate straight drive back past South Africa spearhead Kagiso Rabada.

But finally, in the second over after tea, Boland's marathon vigil was over, with Wiaan Mulder producing a jagging peach to have the brave nightwatchman bowled through the gate for a new Test best of 40.

3. Bavuma can't watch as Smith throws it away

It was the moment — and didn't Temba Bavuma know it.

The South Africa captain just couldn't watch as Steve Smith top-edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer high into the blue Gqeberha sky, turning his back completely as Matthew Breetzke raced back and settled under the ball.

Bavuma couldn't watch as Breetzke took a dramatic juggling catch. (Fox Cricket)

It was a rash, ugly shot from Smith, and certainly not one befitting of a man tasked with saving a Test match.

But for a moment, it looked like he was going to get away with it.

Having just-about settled underneath the ball, Breetzke juggled once and then twice before securing the wicket that was destined to end the Australian resistance.

Smith, perhaps still struggling with his neck issue from day four, was out for 3 and Australia was 6-255.

4. Mulder does damage after tea

With four wickets still in reserve, Australia reached tea still with a sniff of pulling off one of the great escapes.

But in removing Australia's best two batters, the Proteas had already done the hard part, and there would have been no panic as they readied themselves for the game's final stanza.

And in the opening exchanges of what was being sold as a marathon, 44-over evening session, all-rounder Mulder struck not once, but twice.

First, he ended Boland with that divine off-cutter; then he produced something similarly inspired to send the newly-arrived Pat Cummins packing for 4.

At 8-262, it was all beginning to unravel.

There was only one thing that could save the Aussies now ...

5. South Africa beats descending gloom

All of a sudden, things were beginning to darken in Gqeberha.

With ominous clouds gathering on the outskirts of the oval and ground staff poised to pounce at the boundary rope, the South Africans were in a race with the elements.

Clouds were gathering ominously with the Proteas in search of their final two wickets. (Fox Cricket)

Two wickets were needed.

Well aware of the descending gloom, Bavuma threw the ball to his premier spearhead.

And Rabada delivered in the first over of his spell, bowling Mitchell Starc with the tailender attempting an ugly and wholly unnecessary slog.

But with the skies continuing to intimidate, we were treated to surely one of the most farcical drinks breaks in Test history.

Those five lost minutes, however, were not enough to save the Australians.

The heavens never did open, and number 11 Josh Hazlewood was promptly caught behind the wicket, confirming a chastening innings and 31-run defeat for Australia and a richly deserved series-levelling triumph for the South Africans.

World.title: Cummins admits Australia 'long way from our best' as South Africa levels series
World.content:
Australia has fallen to defeat by an innings and 31 runs against South Africa in the second Test at St George's Park in Gqeberha.

Brave innings from Travis Head (121) and night watchman Scott Boland (40) were not enough for Australia, as the Proteas levelled the series at 1-1.

"We were a long way away from our best," Pat Cummins said at the presentation.

"Across the board just not enough of us contributed.

"Ideally we'd be scoring more runs. The pitch was pretty good out there."

The two teams will now head to Newlands in Cape Town for the final Test on Tuesday with the series on the line.

The hosts came into the final day needing just six wickets for victory, but were made to wait to get on the field after the first session was washed out by rain.

The persistent drizzle, interspersed by heavier squalls, may have given Australia hope that they may be able to orchestrate a great escape.

Even once play eventually resumed, every over that Head and Boland successfully negotiated raised hopes even further.

Head's 13th Test century was the first by an Australian batter in a follow-on innings since the 1980s and added to the pressure South Africa must have been feeling, with Anrich Nortje's injury leaving the Proteas a bowler down.

"I thought there was some good fight today," Cummins said.

"Scotty Boland and Trav [Head] both played their roles really well, but it was a fair way to come back from and it wasn't quite enough."

Travis Head scored his 13th Test century. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Once Head chopped on to Wiaan Mulder just before the second new ball was due, the writing may have been on the wall.

Steve Smith, batting at seven after being hampered by a sore neck on day four, initially looked sprightly, before he top edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer to Matthew Breetzke when on 3.

Boland's brave, 166-ball vigil came to an end soon after, a brilliant off cutter from Mulder taking the top of his off stump.

Pat Cummins followed in the same way for just 4 to leave South Africa just two wickets from victory.

Still, Australia had hope as clouds gathered and threatened yet more rain to rescue an unlikely draw.

But then Rabada returned, bowling Mitch Starc for 11, before Marco Jansen extracted an edge from Josh Hazlewood for a duck.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Schutt banned for two matches after prescription medication failure
World.content:
Australian women's fast bowler Megan Schutt has been banned for two matches for failing to meet guidelines on the use of prescription medication.

Cricket Australia confirmed Schutt's suspension in a release on Thursday afternoon.

"The breach was a failure to adhere to requirements under the Sports Science and Sports Medicine guidelines with regard to prescription medication," Cricket Australia said.



"This relates to a single incidence which occurred while out of competition and was not for performance-enhancing purposes."



The two-match ban applies to all international and domestic cricket.

Schutt starred in the recent three-match ODI series against Bangladesh. She had series figures of 10-71.

She has not played in a three-match T20 international series against New Zealand, which wraps up tonight at North Sydney.

Schutt released a statement acknowledging the breach and accepting the penalty.

"I fully accept the penalty handed down and apologise for failing to meet the standards expected of me," Schutt said in her statement.

"I'm sorry for the attention this has caused and appreciate the support I've received.

"While this occurred out of competition and was not performance related, I understand that I am responsible for following the Sports Science and Sports Medicine Guidelines, which players receive regular education on, and I should have adhered to these guidelines."



Cricket Australia said it would continue to provide "appropriate support" to Schutt and to reinforce standards and responsibilities expected of all involved in the game.

World.title: Aussie Borlase on winning side as Atlanta Dream leads WNBA Finals
World.content:
Angel Reese recorded 21 points and 12 rebounds to help the Atlanta Dream secure a 97-71 home victory over the Golden State Valkyries, giving the Dream a 2-1 lead in the WNBA Finals after Game 3.

Rhyne Howard added 16 points, and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who also host Game 4 on Sunday (AEDT).

Australian guard Izzy Borlase played a solid role for the Dream on Wednesday night, local time. She played 26 minutes, finishing with 12 points, including one three-pointer, plus five rebounds, two assists and a block.

Another Australian Opals star, Miela Sowah, sat on the bench for the Valkyries and will remain there throughout the finals due to her restricted status as a development player.

The Dream highlighted one of Borlase's drives to the basket on its social media.

It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for its first-ever victory in the Finals. She now has a double-double in each game of the Finals.

"It feels good when you're in the finals. It's a long season, and you play against everybody and go through and push through, but when you can do it at the highest level, this is what you live for, this is what the off-season is for," Reese said.

"I put the work in for this moment, and I'm just happy I could lead the team to a win. We're feeling good going into Saturday."

With the game tied at 49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes's lay-up, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter, scoring 12 of the final 14 points.

With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who got fouled.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Golden State could never recover. Gabby Williams scored 15 points, and Hayes added 14 for the Valkyries.

"Protect home court," Howard said of the team's focus. "Giving our fans a show. We fought for this arena so we had to protect it. It's big. We went and stole one, but we can't let them come in and do the same thing."

The game was moved from the Dream's home Gateway Center Arena to the NBA's Atlanta Hawks home arena. Wednesday night's game was sold out, with more than 17,000 fans attending, as is Game 4 on Saturday at the same venue.

The game got off to a slow start as Atlanta led 9-1 after the first five minutes. Golden State missed its first eight shots before Aminata Gueye scored the first basket with 4:39 left.

They got within 13-10 before Naz Hillmon hit consecutive 3-pointers and then Reese hit one. The Dream led 23-15 after the opening quarter.

Atlanta built its lead to 37-26 midway through the period. Golden State was able to hang around and only trailed 46-40 at the break as the teams combined to shoot 15-for-31 (48 per cent) from behind the arc.

That was more completed 3-pointers in the first 20 minutes than in either Game 1 or Game 2.

Game 1 and 2 had huge ratings, with the opener on NBC averaging 2.1 million, the most ever for a first game of the Finals. Game 2, which was broadcast on USA Network, averaged 1.33 million viewers.

AP/ABC

World.title: Amid the hunt for World Cup glory one of Tonga's greats is not done yet
World.content:
As Tonga's World Cup campaign prepares to hit fever pitch, Tui Lolohea cannot stop smiling even when the young bulls give him stick.

After a training session in the lead-up to Friday's match against Lebanon it is rising prop Demetric Vaimauga, who is the kind of guy you hear before you see, that gees Lolohea up.

"Awwww yeah, it's Mr I Ain't Done Yet!" Vaimauga crows as he grabs Lolohea by the shoulders.

That's what they called Lolohea in an Instagram post after he came off the bench for an injured Latu Fainu to set up a try in Tonga's 30-12 win over England last week and he's been copping it ever since.

It was a cameo Lolohea, at 31 and with Tonga enjoying more depth and talent in the halves than ever before, thought would never come.

But once it did it added to an already sterling legacy in the red jersey, tacking an extra chapter on a story that, against all odds, is still being written.

Lolohea has already played for Tonga more times than any other player in history and against the Cedars he'll extend his own record with his 23rd cap.

Along with Jason Taumalolo, Lolohea is the only player to have appeared in each of Tonga's five wins over Tier 1 nations, making them the only two constant faces in every image of Tonga's greatest days.

Loading Instagram content

Lolohea has been wearing these colours when those days were still just a dream. When he debuted for Tonga back in 2015, Fainu, the man he replaced last week and will partner in the halves on Friday, was only nine years old.

Vaimauga himself had just turned 11 and as the giant youngster runs away cackling, Lolohea fires back in Tongan through a grin and shakes his head.

"I knew I'd get stick for this. Mr I Ain't Done Yet — they're always taking the piss out of me," Lolohea said.

"I hope he gets banged next time he goes off the back fence, so I can go laugh at him.

"They joke around, but I am one of the oldest in the team and it's good to show you can run around with the young bucks."

Jason Taumalolo and Tui Lolohea have played in every one of Tonga's wins over Tier 1 nations. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yueng)

Lolohea and Taumalolo are the elders this time around as the two longest-serving players in the team by a mile and while Taumalolo dragged Tonga into a new world, Lolohea is very much a product of the old.

Watching his debut from 11 years ago against Samoa on the Gold Coast is a measure of how far things have come.

When the two meet again next week it will be in front of a sold-out crowd at Parramatta Stadium, which they probably could have filled twice over, and both sides will boast some of the best players in the world.

Back on Lolohea's first day, a little over 12,000 came through the gates and both nations had to choose between grey beards, who wanted to give back to their community, journeymen who knew this would be as good as it got, or youngsters before their big futures came for them.

International rugby league has come a long way since Tui Lolohea's Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Lolohea was one of the latter and at the time he was counted as one of rugby league's brightest prospects, with feet so fast tackling him was like trying to grab a handful of smoke.

So much has transformed since those times but according to Lolohea, the most important things have stayed the same.

"Why you're doing it, what you're representing, that never changes," Lolohea said.

"We're a little dot on the map and there's always talk about financial stuff but the pride of our island nation, the proud culture we put out to the people, we've built that over the years and the support from the people is massive.

Why Jason Taumalolo is still more than just a man for Tonga In the NRL, we only talk about what Jason Taumalolo can't do anymore. But when he pulls on the red of Tonga it's a reminder of what he still is and always will be for the island nation and for Test rugby league.

"That's what we want to represent, our people and our family names, where we come from.

"I was just a little kid back then. I remember the passion, for Tonga and Samoa, and we're on the big stage now but the passion is still there even though it was a long time ago."

Plenty of familiar faces from that night are still around. Kristian Woolf is still the coach, Sika Manu, Lolohea's first captain, is in camp as an assistant and Konrad Hurrell is the team's media manager.

But only Lolohea is still playing, making him the last son of the olden days before the heroes came back home.

He remembers frantically messaging Taumalolo in 2017, asking if he really was going to come back to Tonga and marvelling at what followed.

He cannot forget his intercept try in the win over New Zealand, head cocked back and laughing as he went over, or his late score in the semi-final against England that gave Tonga hope of a miracle, or of the trip back to the islands that followed, where the team was given medals of honour at the royal palace.

Amid a good NRL career for the Warriors and Wests Tigers before a lengthy stint in Super League, where he's spent the last eight seasons, including the last five with Huddersfield, Lolohea might never have fulfilled the club expectations he carried into his Tongan debut.

Instead, his finest hours have come for Tonga itself, for whom he is both pioneer and icon.

They've never won a big game without him and his reward has been honours that are usually bestowed on heroes of ancient wars.

His people have named trophies after him and he has been granted lands outside the family village of Lapaha by King Tupou VI.

The team's official nickname is Mate Ma' Tonga, which translates to "die for Tonga" but the memories Lolohea has helped create for his nation are immortal, like the win over Great Britain in 2019 or the breakthrough victory over Australia the following week.

Tui Lolohea has carved out a fine legacy in Tongan red. (Getty Images: Kai Schwoerer)

On the back of those glories a whole new generation of stars chose Tonga and players like Isaiya Katoa, Robert Toia, Leka Halasima and Tolu Koula have not just become part of the cause, they have taken it further.

They beat New Zealand again in the Pacific Championships two years ago and pushed Australia to the limit in the final. Lolohea, of course, played in both and set up a try in the latter.

Tonga are not here to compete anymore, they are here to win — against Australia, New Zealand, England, Samoa or anybody else who wants some.

Taking the World Cup itself back to Nuku'alofa is not an idle fantasy. It's a dream Tonga can hammer into reality as part of a new world order Lolohea and his generation helped create and somehow, he is still part of it.

Apart from Taumalolo, his only fellow survivor from 2017, the other legends from the old days are done.

Tui Lolohea has played in England for close to a decade now. (Getty Images via PA Images: Martin Rickett)

Between Katoa, Fainu and Junior Amone, Tonga have more class and options in the halves and the nation had every right to move on from Lolohea years ago.

But Lolohea himself is still here, refusing to be swept away, a lot older and a bit slower but as he showed against England, still capable of making a difference for the better.

"To still be here after all this time, I'm fortunate to be here again and running around with the young guys and some of the superstars of our game," Lolohea said.

"It's an honour, every time.

Rugby League World Cup quick hits From Kalyn Ponga's magnificent Test debut to a mighty Tongan victory years in the making here are the quick hits from week one of the Rugby League World Cup.

"It's crazy to think, because I watch these guys every week and now I'm playing alongside them and I remember when we didn't really have any halfbacks at all.

"The depth we have now, it's such a big positive not just for now but for the years to come."

Lolohea knows this World Cup might be his last. He's finished up at Huddersfield and is still sorting out where he'll play next.

He is expected to drop back to the extended bench for next week's clash against Samoa and barring injury, it will be the same for the knockout stages.

This game against Lebanon could be it, the last time the legend of Tui Lolohea as a Tongan hero happens in front of us and not in our memories and that makes it worth savouring.

Tui Lolohea is hoping to build on his cameo appearance against England. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

He played rugby league for Tonga more times than any other person who has ever lived but it is still a privilege to him, a prize beyond what he can ever say.

Even after all these years it still makes his father, Paul, smile and get as emotional as he ever does.

Growing up it was just the two of them. Lolohea's mother died when he was just one year old due a heart condition and if Friday is the end, father and son will be together for it.

But there might be a truth in the jokes the young fellas tell: Lolohea isn't done yet.

"He [Lolohea's father] flew in Tuesday morning, he'll be here for the next couple of weeks to enjoy the last ride, no matter what happens," Lolohea said.

"But we never know these days, do we? I'm just buzzing I got on the field again. I'm glad I got to play my part."

World.title: Potential PNG signing helping to heal Cooper Bai's family rift
World.content:
Marcus Bai has explained how he and son Cooper moved past the rift that fractured their family, as the Gold Coast forward edges closer to signing a deal with the PNG Chiefs.

Cooper was warmly greeted by his father at Port Moresby's Jacksons International airport yesterday after being granted permission to explore his options ahead of the opening of the November 1 contracting window.

The 19-year-old has been high on the Chiefs' list of targets since the club got the green light to enter the NRL in the 2028 season, with the forward proving a hit with local crowds in Papua New Guinea across his two-Test international career.

PNG Chiefs unveil new logo ahead of 2028 NRL entry The PNG Chiefs logo brings together elements representative of the country ahead of its NRL debut in 2028.

But Cooper's journey hasn't always been smooth, and last year he invoked the ire of his legendary Kumul father when he turned down a deal with Melbourne Storm to remain at the Titans.

"He promised one thing … and then he went and did the other thing, and I was cranky with him," Marcus told AAP.

"I said you've got to be fair and square, that's not how you treat the clubs and people.

"It's not good for us as a family, I was really pissed off with him for that, and I was really angry at him.

"Now [with the chance to join the Chiefs], I said go and have a look and you and your girlfriend sit down and [think through] before making a decision."

Cooper Bai angered his father Marcus (pictured) by going back on his word with regards to signing for the Storm. (Getty Images: Shannon Morris)

Marcus said Cooper had shown maturity by speaking to the Gold Coast to ask permission to visit the Chiefs.

Cooper was due to visit PNG on a family holiday after he was ruled out of the Kumuls' World Cup campaign with a hamstring injury.

"He's only young. He's still finding his feet, and if he comes here there will be a lot of pressure on him," Marcus said.

"The crowd here are tough, they tell you straight up [if they're not happy]."

The chance for Cooper to join the Chiefs would represent a full circle moment for the Bai family.

Marcus left Papua New Guinea in the 1990s to pursue a career as a professional rugby league player, going on to win titles in the NRL and Super League.

He would likely stand down from the Chiefs board if Cooper was to sign a deal to join the club for its inaugural season in 2028.

"I'm proud of his achievements, it is hard to do what he's done and to be able to have an interest from many clubs, it's pleasing for me as a father," Marcus Bai said.

AAP

Tech.title: Canva’s first AI image model plans designs before generating them
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Canva is diving even deeper into AI with the launch of an image generation model that competes directly with those from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google. The model, called Canva Craft, uses a two-stage architecture that allows it to plan a design before generating an image, allowing for “greater precision, consistency and control,” according to an announcement on Thursday.

Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios. In addition to generating social media posts and marketing content, it’s also supposed to create realistic scenes, digital art, environmental imagery, and more. The model’s two-stage system allows it to more accurately generate complex images that require legible text and precise object placement, according to Canva.

Previous Next







1 / 5 An image generated by Canva Craft. Image: Canva

The new AI model builds on Canva’s big push into AI. In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it. The design tool also brought layers to AI-generated images, which let you make changes to part of an image while leaving the rest untouched.

Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus. The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs. It sits behind OpenAI’s GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, GPT-Image-2.5 Flare, and GPT-Image-2.

Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future.

Canva Craft is available now to all users globally. You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab.

Tech.title: PC shipments dropped over 20 percent in Q3 due to RAM price hikes
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Demand for new PCs took a hit after months of price hikes, with Counterpoint Research reporting global PC shipments fell 21 percent year-over-year in Q3 2026. That’s in line with earlier reports from IDC and Omdia. It’s not just PCs, either — that same quarter, smartphone shipments also hit a 14-year low.

Counterpoint linked the decline in PC shipments to higher component prices. Up until Q2 2026, PC shipments had been growing for over two years straight. But over the last several months, RAM, SSDs, and chips from Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm have all gotten more expensive, leading to price hikes on everything from MacBooks to Raspberry Pis. Counterpoint senior analyst Minsoo Kang noted that some companies are shifting to “prioritize configurations that can better absorb component inflation,” leaving fewer affordable options for price-sensitive buyers. Some companies are even reviving older tech, like DDR4 RAM and 4GB GPUs, to help mitigate price hikes.

Counterpoint also says Q3 2025 included “purchases ahead of the Windows 10 support deadline and tariff-related inventory adjustments,” which added to the sharp year-over-year drop this past quarter. The PC market might not bounce back anytime soon, as Counterpoint associate director David Naranjo says, “With global shipments expected to plunge 27% in Q4 2026 and remain broadly flat in 2027, stabilization should not be mistaken for recovery.”

Tech.title: Fall 2026 earnings watch
Tech.content: Every company is suddenly an AI company. Compute is an asset. Cars are flying. We’ve been promised robots — again. It’s time again to dig through earnings reports, listen to investor calls, and call out the latest wins and losses from around the tech sector and what it means for where the companies go next.

Tech.title: Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge — but legal experts say these changes aren’t enough to address their concerns. “This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, tells Nieman Lab.

Initially, Meta’s new terms for business accounts appeared to give the company permission to train its AI on news sites. The terms, which go into effect October 30th, stated that Meta “may use any content” from the websites associated with a business account to “develop, research” and “train” Meta’s products. At the time, legal experts told Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” such as the robots.txt file that has historically told scrapers (including search engines like Google) what they are allowed to crawl.

Following fierce backlash from the publishing industry, Meta removed language saying it would “train” its products with scraped content. But the tweaks might not be enough to rule out that possibility. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train,’” Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, tells Nieman Lab.

Meta has maintained that its new terms aren’t designed to scrape news content for free.
