Tech.title: TextNow’s $150 Yello Phone Is Customized for Kids and Pairs Up With a $20 Monthly Plan
Tech.content:
Low-cost carrier TextNow launched its first child-friendly phone on Tuesday, pairing a Motorola handset with a software portal that lets parents control who their kid can call or text.

Yello is a customized 2024 edition of the Moto G Play that costs $150 and comes with a $20 monthly plan, with no other required contracts or service commitments. It’s a simple 4G-only Android phone with a 6.5-inch display, but TextNow makes a number of software changes to restrict most access to the internet.

The phone doesn’t include Google’s Play Store and doesn’t allow users to install additional apps or services. It’s designed primarily for calls and texts with parent-approved contacts, which parents can manage through a web-based portal that also lets them check the phone’s GPS location. Kids can call or text those contacts from a menu of large icons reminiscent of Netflix’s profile selection screen.

More from CNET

Yello’s software only lets kids call or text parent-approved contacts. TextNow

Other software available on the phone includes access to the cameras — a 50-megapixel main camera and an 8-megapixel front-facing camera — along with the calculator, clock and a weather app. Seven preloaded games can be enabled, which include phone classics such as Snake, Mines and Tic-Tac-Toe. Photos taken on the phone can only be shared with parents.

This more restrictive approach should let kids stay in touch with approved friends and coordinate pickups with parents while limiting distractions and access to content inappropriate for young children.

The 2024 Moto G Play is a good choice for Yello’s software approach. Its 5,000-mAh battery should easily get through a day or two of use, and its IP52 certification should keep it resistant to light splashes of water. The phone has a limited amount of storage at 64GB, but that might work out fine considering the deliberate constraints placed on this device.

It’s worth noting that Motorola is only providing security support to this older model of the Moto G Play through 2027, but TextNow’s website says that its Yello software will continue to be built upon as the carrier gets user feedback. Since Motorola’s official support period for this phone is almost over, it will be important for TextNow’s Yello software to step in as it builds up features for this phone for kids.

Despite the name, the Yello phone is available in just one color: the same sapphire blue that’s on every 2024 Moto G Play.

Most US carriers offer their own versions of child-friendly devices such as Yello. AT&T, for instance, has repurposed the Samsung Galaxy A16 into the AmiGo Jr with similar parental controls. There are also a number of child-friendly smartwatches, which may be a better option depending on your family’s needs for connectivity. But Yello does offer a lot of flexibility, since it doesn’t require a more expensive unlimited data plan or a minimum service commitment.

The Yello phone is now available on TextNow’s website.

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story cited that Yello was using a different edition of the Moto G Play. TextNow clarified the model after Yello’s announcement, and the story has been updated accordingly.

Tech.title: Anthropic Introduces Claude Duet: A New Agentic AI App for Professionals
Tech.content:
Anthropic is dropping yet another AI product into our laps: Claude Duet, a dedicated app for professionals and business owners to handle tasks they would otherwise have to do manually. While agentic AI isn’t new, this app caters to a group that likely needs those capabilities most. Anthropic has always targeted the professional sector, and Duet, while specific, feels very on-brand for the company.

Claude Duet is designed around Opus 5.5, and the app is aimed at streamlining your daily operations. Not unlike Claude itself, Duet allows you to connect with the software you use for your work, and will continuously look for things that need your attention. This means you can connect your Gmail, calendar, Slack and thousands of other work and productivity apps.

Like other agentic tools, Duet is a proactive assistant that will help you prioritize things that it deems are most important and worthy of your attention first. The “proactive” part of Duet is that you don’t always have to prompt it to do something for the future; it’ll assess and assemble what you need to know by looking through your work apps. It’ll also do the opposite, and tell you when things can wait for later so you can focus on higher-priority tasks.

More from CNET

Anthropic says that Claude Duet prioritizes your privacy. As much as an AI tool can, at least. There are specialized safety protocols and measures to make sure sensitive information doesn’t go out into the world unless you want it to. Duet will automatically reject highly sensitive information, like credit card numbers, ID information and more. With other sensitive information, like health and finance information, Duet will ask before it sends anything out.

Duet is currently available in a research preview, but only for the Pro or Max subscription plans. You can join the waitlist now.

Tech.title: FTC Imposter Scam Threatens to Unplug Your Phone Number
Tech.content:
The scam du jour sounds like a real brain twister. According to a Federal Trade Commission alert issued Thursday about the newest imposter scam, fraudsters pretending to be from the FTC are calling to “warn” you that your phone number is being used to commit scams in another country and that if you don’t reply to them ASAP you run the risk of your phone getting deactivated.

And it sounds like a pretty intricate hoax. According to the alert, the caller will transfer you to a phony police officer and provide a search query to find the (fake) phone number to file a “report,” and if you call, more scammers pick up. And once you’ve handed over your personal information, they’ll tell you you have to travel to the relevant country to resolve it, unless you fork over a “security deposit.”

This is just one of the latest in the raft of scams we face daily, and frequently fall for. I know the recents list on my phone is mostly pages and pages of suspected-spam-labeled calls.

More from CNET

Just picking up provides scammers with the knowledge that your phone number is active and that you may be more likely to fall for the next step down a fraud’s path. Answering adds value to your personal information and a link to it all in its own.

I think scams like these rely on a series of adrenaline-fueled responses — the little spikes you get when you hear the phone ring, then see the ID (it’s the government!) and, if you pick up, the succession of scary warnings. Ignoring unexpected calls from strangers gives you time to think rationally about claims, if they leave a voicemail, and if they don’t, that’s telling as well.

In this case, it could start with the realization that it’s truly unlikely the FTC would be contacting individuals about this, especially before issuing a public statement that there’s a problem.

Tech.title: Soon You Won’t Have to Do Dishes at an Airbnb (Unless You Really Want To)
Tech.content:
You’re checking out in an hour, and there’s a pile of dishes. If it’s an Airbnb, don’t worry about it. The lodging platform recently updated its policy about what hosts can ask guests to do, and some cleaning chores are now off the list.

In the Reasonable House Rules and requests page on its website, Airbnb says hosts cannot “ask guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.”

Airbnb said there could be exceptions — “We understand every home is unique” — such as asking guests to limit water use if there are local restrictions due to drought, or to put trash in a bear-proof container at a woodsy lodging.

More from CNET

The app said the new regulations will apply to reservations booked on or after Nov. 20.

When laying out house rules and guest requests, many hosts require or ask guests to either clean dishes or put them in the dishwasher and run it. They may also ask guests to bag garbage and recyclables, place them in containers outside, and remove sheets and pillowcases from beds and towels from bathrooms, then pile them up for the cleaners.

Some hosts clapped back at the updated policy on the app’s community forum page. René, a host in Berlin, posted, “Seven days of dirty dishes covered in leftover food. Sugar ants and other pests have moved in. The guests check out. But will the pests check out too?” San Francisco host Adam said he would have to raise his cleaning fee by 30 to 50%, and Michelle in Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, commented that “the burden of cost has been switched to the hosts.”



The updated policy is the latest evolution in what has been one of the main complaints about Airbnb — cleaning fees and requirements. In November 2022, Airbnb changed its app and website so that guests could see cleaning and service fees when searching listings. There was a “Display total price” toggle near the top of a search results page that let you see prices that included all fees (but not taxes).

It was a response to years of complaints that listings did not include those fees upfront, in effect masking the true cost of a rental. For example, you go for a lodging at $100 per night, but in the final stages of making your payment, find out it’s actually $200 per night with all the fees included.

Then, in April 2025, Airbnb mandated that all listings worldwide must have the total price upfront, including all fees but not taxes, saying, “We know that clear, upfront pricing improves the Airbnb experience for both guests and hosts.”

Airbnb, which launched in 2008, says it has 5.5 million hosts globally who have served 2.5 billion guest arrivals in nearly every country for all types of lodgings — mansions, cottages, cabins, RVs, teepees, whatever. The platform’s competitors include Vrbo, Booking.com, Expedia and HomeToGo.

Host sees ‘both sides’ of it

Sam Eitzen, CEO and co-founder of experiential marketing platform Snapbar, operates a guest house in Washington listed on Airbnb where I stayed recently (yes, I did the dishes). He said he understands both sides of the issue — as a host and as a guest himself.

“I have been at Airbnbs that make the checkout instructions almost scary, and you worry about getting things wrong,” Eitzen told me. “We’ve never wanted to create that experience and treat the list of ‘chores’ as optional and helpful, but aim to never make guests feel worried about the process or make it sound like we’d come after them or charge them if they don’t.”

Eitzen said Airbnb is “walking a tightrope” in trying to please both hosts and guests. He said the new policy could create confusion, however.

“People will still post rules, lists and manuals in their Airbnbs, and those will most likely conflict with the app, and I think that runs the risk of confusing guests,” he said.

Tech.title: This New Device ‘Bricks’ Your Phone When You Enter Your Bedroom
Tech.content:
Brick, the maker of my favorite device for curbing doomscrolling, launched its first new product since the Brick on Thursday. Called Brick Night, it was designed to automatically block apps the moment you enter your bedroom to promote better sleep.

While 87% of US adults sleep with their phones in their bedrooms, studies have found that screen time in bed is associated with poorer sleep quality. Brick Night has the potential to prevent this.

How Brick Night works

First, in the Brick app, you create custom modes by selecting the apps you want to block and the time window you’d like them to stay blocked. Then, you define your bedroom space, up to 25 by 25 feet. Place your Brick Night in this space, like on your nightstand, and once Bluetooth detects that you’ve entered your bedroom, Brick Night will handle the rest.

More from CNET

Specifically, Brick Night uses your Bluetooth signal strength to estimate how close your phone is to the Brick Night through the Brick app. When you enter your bedroom, Brick Night automatically activates during your preselected time window; when you leave, it unblocks your apps based on your settings.

You select which apps get blocked once you set foot in your bedroom. Brick

Brick Night is battery-powered, so it doesn’t need to be charged and comes with batteries included. These last at least two years.

One Brick Night can also be shared by multiple users with their own Brick apps in the same bedroom. It is compatible with both iOS and Android.

How is Brick Night different from Brick?

Brick lets you create a boundary around your phone. Based on your different modes, it automatically blocks apps during your selected days and times. To unblock them, you have to physically tap your phone against the Brick.

Brick Night, on the other hand, is location-based. It automatically activates once you enter your bedroom (or whatever space you set) and deactivates when you leave it.

The Brick Night (left) and Brick (right). Brick

There is also a price difference. Brick costs $59, while Brick Night is $129. There is a bundle that allows you to purchase both for $169, saving you $19.

According to the company, Brick is ideal for work, studying, family time and mindfulness, while Brick Night works best for sleeping, winding down, waking up and employing a no-scroll zone.

Availability and price

Brick Night is now available in midnight blue for $129, exclusively on the Brick website.

Tech.title: New York and T-Mobile Settle Dispute Over 4G Plan Price Hikes. How to Get a Credit
Tech.content:
T-Mobile has come to an agreement with the New York State Attorney General’s Office over claims that the carrier did not honor price guarantees for T-Mobile One plans on its 4G network between January 2017 and April 2019. Those plans were advertised as being “Price Guarantee Plans.”

Affected active T-Mobile customers who leave the carrier will be able to collect a credit worth the last month’s payment and a $25 gift card.

Those who stay on and are still using an older phone can get a free 5G phone (worth up to $250) or credit up to $150 toward a more expensive 5G phone for lines that are still using 3G or 4G. Rates for their recurring monthly plans will stay the same until 2029.

More from CNET

As part of the agreement, T-Mobile is also making a one-time payment to the Attorney General’s office in the amount of around $98,000.

According to a press release issued by New York Attorney General Letitia James, an investigation by the office found that T-Mobile raised rates on those plans in 2024 by approximately $5 per line, a change that affected approximately 252,957 plans at the time. It also pegs the relief to be worth around $38 million in value.

“T-Mobile misled hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers by promising that it would never raise prices on their cellphone plans, only to do exactly that just a few years later,” said James in the release. “Consumers shouldn’t have to pay the price for a misleading sale.”

The office’s filed agreement notes that T-Mobile made the price guarantee in at least two press releases and during a CNET video interview with then-CEO John Legere in 2017. In that video, Legere said, “We also extended the Un-contract to T-Mobile One Unlimited, which means we will never raise your rate; we guarantee.”

The agreement notes that T-Mobile ran afoul of a New York State law that requires companies to disclose terms “clearly and conspicuously,” and that any disclaimers about the price guarantee were ineffective by “directly contradict[ing] what a reasonable consumer would understand the Price Guarantee Offer to mean.”

It also states that “Respondent [T-Mobile] neither admits nor denies the OAG’s Findings” that detail the investigation’s conclusions.

When asked about the agreement, T-Mobile sent the following statement to CNET: “The $38 million cited in the press release is an estimate of potential benefits that a group of long-standing T-Mobile customers may choose to take advantage of, not the amount in refunds or payments. The agreement provides for approximately $98,000 paid to the state and a range of optional customer benefits. We’re glad to have this matter resolved and remain focused on delivering value to our customers.”

Per the agreement, T-Mobile has 150 days starting Oct. 20 to identify and notify customers who are eligible for the relief. After they’ve been notified, customers will have 45 days to decide whether to cancel their T-Mobile account (getting the last month’s payment and a $25 cash card) or continue as a customer (getting a free or discounted 5G-capable phone for each affected line or the $150 credit toward a new phone). For the latter, T-Mobile will also not charge any costs such as transfer or activation fees.

Tech.title: An Entire Swedish TV Show Got Deleted, and AI Got Blamed
Tech.content:
A system failure at Swedish broadcaster TV4 has wiped out hundreds of hours of production footage for the celebrity reality series The Challenge, placing future seasons on hold. According to Sweden’s Aftonbladet newspaper, insider sources at production company Mastiff point the finger at a rogue AI agent. TV4, however, denies that AI was to blame for the tech catastrophe.

The Swedish series was due to return on Nov. 22, but has been delayed indefinitely, TV4 said in a statement. “We have to recut it from scratch. All the raw material is still there, and all that,” program director Mia Lindqvist said on the network’s website.

The TV4 network denies the Aftonbladet report that an AI agent deleted the episodes. “We don’t have the exact details of what happened yet, but it’s not true that this was caused by an AI agent. The main issue is that the production company’s backup system failed caused by a human error,” Lindqvist told CNET by email.

More from CNET

The program features stars of other Swedish reality programs, such as the country’s version of The Bachelor and Farmen, a reality show about (wait for it…) contestants on a farm. The Challenge: Sweden first aired in 2023.

AI is increasingly a part of editing and production workflows across movies and television, with entertainment giants, including Netflix, leaning on the technology to produce content more quickly and at lower cost. How much AI is involved in production and at which stages it’s used has been unclear.

If an AI agent were somehow responsible, that would seem to have negated any of AI’s time-saving benefits for The Challenge: Sweden and its production team, who now have to spend time rebuilding the episode edits that were lost. But technical issues caused by human error have a long history in TV and film, including the notorious Pixar incident in which a stray file system command wiped out 90% of Toy Story 2 during production (which was only recovered thanks to a supervising director who had taken her work home after a pregnancy, as The Next Web recounted).

Worries about AI agents taking unwanted action have spiked in recent months. The biggest flash point came over the summer when it was discovered that an OpenAI agent hacked the Hugging Face software repository. Shortly after that, the Australian government said that an agent, also from OpenAI, hacked into a government health site.

While TV4 said an AI agent was not to blame, it did not clarify whether another type of AI might have had some role in the deletion.

Tech.title: I Tried Automating My Relationships Using AI Agents. Muse and Dots Overstepped
Tech.content:
Most people revel in milestones. Turning the yearly page on birthdays, holidays and anniversaries is an opportunity for big parties, exchanging nice gifts and celebrating the ones we love. It can also be a minefield of missed connections and hurt feelings if you forget the dates.

If you’re ever sent a “happy belated birthday” message, neglected to recall your own anniversary or simply struggle to keep in touch with people, this guide might be for you. Granted, you’ll have to put your trust in an AI agent to do the heavy lifting, but you might never need to remember to send a card again.

While AI may not understand human connection and happiness, what it does well with is rote tasks. I tried to use ChatGPT and a few other AI tools to automate the upkeep of my personal and professional relationships — but here’s where it all went wrong.

More from CNET

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

‘Happy belated birthday,’ no more?

The penalties for being terrible at remembering birthdays increase as one gets older. Soon it’s not just your friend’s birthdays that slip your mind, but also their kids’ birthdays and your grandkids’ birthdays and on and on as the wheel of reproduction turns.

I used ChatGPT — which appeared to be the only AI tool among the three I tested that could automate this entire process for me — to identify key birthdays of friends and family and develop an automation system to make sure I never miss another important date.

Claude was able to access and draft emails as well as create birthday cards and greetings, but not automate the sending.

Claude/Screenshot by CNET

Gemini seemed like it could only work with me in the chat to draft emails and generate custom cards, not actually work inside my inbox. Only some people have access to Google’s AI agent, Gemini Spark, right now.

Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

I authorized ChatGPT and its agentic offering, Dots, to look through my Google Calendar and Gmail to find and match dates to the birthdays of the people most important to me. You can do this by navigating to your profile icon in ChatGPT, clicking Settings and then opening Plugins.

ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

I also gave ChatGPT authorization to read, compose and send emails on my behalf.

Then I asked ChatGPT to look through my calendar and Gmail and find as many important birthdays as it could.

ChatGPT correctly analyzed my inbox and discovered a great deal about the birthdays, personal habits and interests of my loved ones. (Surnames and birthdays redacted for privacy.) ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

ChatGPT was able to use my inbox to boil down my friends’ and family’s interests to a broad, yet specific, enough set of data points to create custom digital birthday cards that actually fit all their personalities. Even the one friend ChatGPT know much about still got a digital card that fit her pretty much to a T.

ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

Automating all my love

Now comes the most crucial element — setting up ChatGPT to automatically send digital birthday cards and greetings to all the important people in my life so I don’t screw it up. I tested this feature by asking ChatGPT to generate a digital card and message for my dog’s birthday and send the email to my husband.

ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

The chat limit was reached here, and ChatGPT also surfaced an alert that asked for my permission to send an email on my behalf. And while it can be good in general for an AI agent to ask for your permission before sending an email, I had tasked it with sending those specific emails by itself automatically each time.

Beyond my email task, I also asked Meta Muse, the social media giant’s AI agent, to send memes and check-ins to a few of my friends on Instagram. This ended up being more trouble than it was worth; the content Muse selected to send along was based on seemingly nothing specific, just random posts sourced from around the platform that might be construed as mildly amusing.

The bottom line on AI agents overstepping

This is where things get a little fuzzy. The amount of work it took to optimize Dots and Muse so they would send relevant, plausibly functional correspondence was not worth it. If it takes more time to review, revise and approve a simple email or DM than it would for me to do it myself, the whole prospect and promise of agentic AI falls flat.

Ultimately, you should also be aware that once you’re working with an AI agent, it may also start to overstep in the chat. I had to tell both Muse and ChatGPT’s Dots to back off — because while I’d given them permission to peruse my emails and social media accounts, I had only asked them to complete certain, very specific, actions while doing it.

ChatGPT/Meta/Screenshot by CNET

Dot took it upon itself, totally unprompted, to alert me to a timing snag in my evening, going through my emails and letting me know a movie I’d bought tickets for conflicted with my Japanese class that night. This might have been useful, had I not already sent an email to my teacher right after buying the tickets, letting them know I’d be missing class.

Muse started sending me unsolicited updates about the weather and a fire in Malibu. Both undertook relentless efforts to get me to use more and more of their features while I had the apps active.

Overall, the experience didn’t leave me feeling more connected to anything but the AI companies.
